ex p Parkinson  (1995) 29 HLR 179;  R v North and East Devon Health Authority  ex p
Coughlan [2001] QB 213; R v Secretary of State for the Home Dept ex p Herbage (No 2)
[1987] QB 1077;  R v Secretary of State for the Home Environment e x p Percy Bilton
Industrial Properties Ltd [1976] 1 EGLR 141; SS Hontestroom (Owners) v SS Sagaporack
(Owners) [1927] AC 37;  Trinidad and Tobago Civil Rights Association v Manning
(Trinidad and Tobago HC, 7 December 2007); Ventose v Chief Electoral Officer  [2018]
CCJ 13 (AJ), (2018) 92 WIR 118 (BB); Ward v Walsh (Barbados CA, 28 November 2012).

Legislation referred to:
Guyana – Court of Appeal Act, Cap 3:01,  Judicial Review Act, Cap 3:06, Mining Act,
Cap 65:01, Mining Regulations, Cap 65:01.

Other Sources referred to:
Eversley C, ‘Legitimate Expectation and the Creation of Procedural and Substantive Legal
Rights in Commonwealth Caribbean Public Law’  (2004) 33 C omm L World Rev 332;
Roberts M, ‘Public Law Representations and Substantive Legitimate Expectations’ (2001)
64 Mod L Rev 112; Ventose E, Commonwealth Caribbean Administrative Law (Routledge
2013); Wright D, ‘Rethinking the Doctrine of Legitimate Expectations in Canadian
Administrative Law’ (1997) 35 Osgoode Hall L J 139.

JUDGMENT
of
The Honourable Justice Saunders, President and The
Honourable Justices Wit, Anderson, Rajnauth-Lee and Burgess

Delivered by
The Honourable Mr Justice Anderson
on 15 June 2022

Introduction
[1] The Guyana Geology and Mines Commission (‘the Commission’) is the statutory
body with power to grant and renew licences for quarrying any quarriable mineral
(including stones) in Guyana .1 On 14 August 2015 , the High Court  of Guyana
ordered the Commission: (1) to quash its decision to sub-divide the area which had
been the  subject of a Notice of Intention to grant a quarry licence to Diam ond
Quarry Inc (‘the first respondent’); (2) to grant the first respondent a quarry licence
for the said area; and (3) prohibited from issuing any licence to any other person in
respect of that area of land. The Commission appealed to the Court of Appeal ,
which on 19 January 2021, allowed the appeal in part. The Court of Appeal varied

1 Mining Act, Cap 65:01, ss 88, 89. Under the Mining Reg ulations, Cap 65:01 (regs 1, 41, 48) the President may refuse to grant a
concession or lease in respect of the separate categories of ‘gold and precious stones and valuable minerals and metals, their ores and
compounds other than bauxite and mineral oil, asphalt, coal and other substances of like nature.’

the orders of the High Court but only to the extent of remitting the issue of the grant
of the quarry licence to the Commission for it to decide the matter according to law.
The Commission now appeals the decision of the Court of Appeal upholding the
orders of the High Court  whilst the first respondent cross-appeals on the ground
that the Court of Appeal ought not to have varied those orders.
Background
[2] Certain facts are undisputed between the parties, but others are hotly contested. On
28 March 2014 , the first respondent applied, and paid the prescribed fees , for a
quarry licence pursuant to s 89 of the Mining Act, Cap 65:01 (‘the Act’) in respect
of approximately 848 acres of land in a part of the interior of Guyana known as
‘Monkey Jump’. The first respondent claims that prior to the application it did the
necessary research work to ensure that the land applied for was not legally held nor
applied for by anyone. According to the first respondent, the records available at
the Commission revealed that no one had any right or interest in the area for which
it had applied, and no one had ever applied for that land for quarrying purposes.

[3] On 19 July 2014, the Commission surveyed Monkey Jump and on 15 September
2014, issued a Cease Work Order against Baracara Quarr ies Inc (‘the second
respondent’) in respect of its occupation of  a portion of Monkey Jump for which
the first respondent had applied. On 16 September 2014, the Commission caused
to be published in the Official Gazette a ‘Notice of Intention to Grant Quarry
Licence to Diamond Quarry Inc.’ The said Notice contained the following clause:

Any person who claims he has any right or interest to the area to be granted
and will be injuriously affected by the grant of a Quarry Licence may within
twenty-one (21) days after publication of the first advertisement lodge with
the Guyana Geology and Mines Commission a petition objecting to the
grant of this Quarry Licence.

[4] There is no record of any one having lodged a petition  of objection  with the
Commission within 21 days, or at all. In the premises, no one objected to the grant
of the quarry licence to the first respondent.

[5] On 15 October 2014, the Commission wrote to the first respondent requesting
additional documents pursuant to the Mining Regulations Cap 65:01, regs 225(1),
226(1), 227(1) namely: an Environmental Bond to be lodged as determined by the
Commissioner in Form 19 of the first schedule ; an Environmental Management
Plan for a period not less than 5 years; and submission of a Closure Plan. The first
respondent supplied all the requested documentation. Further, the said letter of 15
October 2014 indicated to the first respondent that ‘the Guyana Geology and Mines
Commission has favourably considered your application and an “intent to grant
quarry licence” will be published.’

[6] The first respondent claimed that at subsequent meetings with the Commission it
was told that its application would be fast tracked as Guyana was experiencing great
difficulty in securing enough stones for its infrastructural activities. The first
respondent also clai med that it was given all assurances by the Commission that
the licence would be granted to it and that  it should start preparations for
commencement of operations.  The Commission denied making  such promises to
the first respondent.

[7] On 10 February 2015, the first respondent attended a meeting convened by the
Commission at which the second respondent was also present. At that meeting the
Commission represented that ‘many, many years’ earlier the second respondent had
applied for the same land for which the first respondent had made its application.
The first respondent claims to have vehemently objected to this representation.
However, a report of the meeting compiled by the Land Administration Manager
of the Commission represented that the Commission had accepted two quarry
licence applications for the same area and that the outcome of the discussions was
that t he area would be divided into a northern portion granted to the second
respondent and a southern portion granted to the first respondent. Upon receipt of
the report, the first respondent immediately dispatched a reply to the Commission
that it had never agreed to any subdivision of the land for which it had applied. A
subsequent meeting at the Commission on 3 March 2015 failed to resolve the issue;

the first respondent claimed that the meeting ended abruptly with the Commission
indicating that it would proceed with the subdivision.

High Court Proceedings

[8] The first respondent applied to the High Court of Guyana  by way of Notice of
Motion supported by an affidavit sworn by its Managing Director, Mr Doodnauth
Samaroo, for writs of Certiorari, Mandamus , and Prohibition . The application
alleged that the Commission’s decision to subdivide the land between  the second
respondent and the first respondent was grossly unfair, discriminatory, and based
on mala  fides and favouritism. The first respondent submitted that the decision
bordered on criminality in that the Commission sought to protect  the second
respondent when the second respondent had no proof of ever applying for a quarry
licence for the area of Monkey Jump for which the first respondent had applied.

[9] The second respondent was not a party to the High Court Proceedings. However,
the Commission submitted an affidavit in answer sworn by Mr Donald Singh, its
Land Administration Manager. The Commission alleged that a portion of the area
for which the first respondent had applied had been occupied by the second
respondent for several decades  and that the second respondent  had conducted
quarrying activities on that area of land . A report was attached to illustrate  the
extent of the quarrying work done by the second respondent . The Commission
admitted that the second respondent did not have a licence for the area of land it
occupied, which was part of the land applied for by the first respondent.

[10] Presiding in the High Court, Chang CJ (Ag) found that:2

(a) The second respondent did not make an application for a quarry licence  in
respect of the same area of land applied for by the first respondent and that
any quarrying that the second respondent was undertaking on the land was
illegal being carried out without a licence from the Commission.

2 Transcript of oral decision, The Commissioner of the Guyana Geology and Mines Commission v Diamond Quarry Inc (Court of Appeal
of Guyana, 19 January 2021) at [10]–[12].

(b) There was no legal obstacle to the grant of the licence to the first respondent
in respect of the portion of land that it had applied for.

(c) There was no legal basis for the land to be subdivided merely to allow the
second respondent to continue to carry on the illegal quarrying operations
and the desire of the second respondent to preserve a part of the land for its
operations could not have been a proper basis for subdivision. The decision
to subdivide the land was unlawful and made for a purpose that was not
relevant, and highly improper.

(d) The first respondent’s application for a licence should have been granted as
it was not opposed by the second respondent or any other person.

(e) No public interest reasons were advanced as a ground  for the decision to
subdivide.

[11] The Chief Justice made absolute three orders which he had provisionally granted
in Chambers on 12 March 201 5: (1)  An order of  certiorari directing the
Commissioner to quash  its decision to subdivide the land  for which the first
respondent had applied; (2) An order of mandamus directing the Commissioner to
grant the first respondent a quarry licence to quarry for stones over the said land;
and (3) An order of prohibition preventing the Commission from granting a quarry
licence or any other licence under the Act to any other person or corporate entity in
respect of the said land.

The Court of Appeal Proceedings

[12] The Commission was dissatisfied with the decision and orders of the High Court
and appealed to the Court of Appeal , repeating in many respects, its argument s
before the High Court. The Commission took especial issue with the finding by the
Chief Justice that it had decided on a sub division of the land for which the first
respondent had applied.

[13] By way of Notice of Motion dated 23 October 2015, the second respondent applied
for and was granted leave to intervene in the appeal on the basis that its interests
could be irreparably injured by the judgment of the Chief Justice. The application
was supported by the affidavit of Mr As hik Rahaman , a shareholder and the
managing director of the second respondent. Mr Rahaman deposed that the second
respondent had been in sole and continuous possession and occupation of land s at
Monkey Jump since 1965, and that on 19 September 1974, the second respondent
had been issued with a quarry licence by the Commission to occupy and use a
portion of lands located at Monkey Jump  for quarrying purposes. 3 (It ought to be
noted here that it was agreed on all sides that the  licence granted in 1974 was not
in respect of , and therefore had nothing to do with , the land  for which the first
respondent had applied. ) The deponent further claimed that it occupied the land
applied for by the first respondent which was home to 12 employees of the second
respondent and their families and  that the second respondent had undertaken
substantial infrastructural work  on th e land. The Commission had routinely
conducted inspection of the second respondent’s operation at least once yearly and
had undertaken an assessment to determine the amount of stone in the ground and
the quarrying life expectancy.

[14] Finally, Mr Rahaman deposed that the second respondent  had in 2006 made a
Monkey Jump Licence Application and that the application was gazetted on or
about 13 November 2006. However, the deponent claimed that the publication was
in error in that the coordinates gazetted by the Commission were different from that
contained in its Monkey Jump Licence Application. The deponent asserted that he
sought to correct the mistake through several interventions with the Commission.
It was only in January 2015 that he learnt that the first respondent had applied for
a quarry licence over land which  encroached on the land occupied by the second
respondent. The deponent claimed that he was summoned to a meeting by the
Commission on 10 February 2015 at which the  first respondent was present and
where the Commission proposed the subdivision of the land. However, by letter

3 ibid at [3].

dated 10 March 2015, the second respondent indicated that the second respondent
was applying for the proposed extension to be included in its current licence.

[15] The second respondent  sought an order in accordance with s 7(1) an d (2) of the
Court of Appeal Act, Cap 3:01 setting aside the judgment of the High Court in its
entirety, or alternatively, an order remitting the matter to the High Court for further
hearing. The application also sought leave for the second respondent to intervene
in such further hearings.

[16] The Court of Appeal allowed the Commissioner’s appeal in part. The court upheld
the decision of the Chief Justice in all respects except for the order that  the
Commissioner issue the licence to the first respondent. Instead, the Court of Appeal
remitted the application to the Commission for its consideration according to law.
However, the Court of Appeal made clear that the first respondent was entitled to
the licence as a matter of fact 4 and that the second respondent could have had no
legitimate expectation to the land. As the second respondent had no licence it could
not now seek to lay claim to t he area in respect of which  a Notice of Intention to
grant the licence to the first respondent had been issued, and to which it had not
objected. In relation to the procedure of utili sing Judicial Review , the Court of
Appeal held that it was permissible to hear the application despite the availability
of common law remedies.

[17] It is worthy of note that  the second respondent has not appealed against these
decisions of the Court of Appeal all of which were contrary to its interests and the
affidavit evidence it had presented to the court.

Caribbean Court of Justice

[18] By Notice of Appeal filed on 3 November 2021 the Commissioner appealed against
the entirety of the judgment of the Court of Appeal. Attorneys for the first
respondent filed an Acknowledgement of Service on 12 November 2021 and a
Notice of a Cross-Appeal on 18 November 2021.

4 Transcript  (n 2) at [14].

Grounds of Appeal

[19] In summary the Commissioner filed the following grounds of appeal:

(a) The Court of Appeal erred in failing to consider or in rejecting the
contention that the Commission  made no decision to subdivide the land
which is the subject matter of the first respondent’s application and on
which basis the orders of certiorari and prohibition were made.

(b) The Court of Appeal erred in failing to consider that no promise was made
to the first respondent to grant it a quarry licence under s 88(1) of the Act
notwithstanding the publication of the Notice of Intention to grant a Quarry
Licence by the Commissioner.

(c) The Court of Appeal erred in relying on or upholding findings of contested
facts on affidavit evidence in a public law matter namely:

(i) that the Commission decided to subdivide the land;

(ii) that the Commission decided to award a quarry licence over the said
land or part thereof to a person other than the first respondent; and

(iii) that the Commission unconditionally promised or decided to award
a quarry licence to the first respondent.

(d) The Court of Appeal erred in deciding or upholding the decision that the
second respondent was illegally conducting quarrying activities when the
evidence shows that the second respondent could have been found to have
had a bare license which would have afforded it a defence to a claim for
trespass by the Commission.

(e) The Court of Appeal erred in varying the order of mandamus to the extent
that the matter is remitted to the Commission to consider the application by
the first respondent.

(f) The Court of Appeal erred in failing to consider that fairness in public
administration includes issues such as the national need for production of
quarry material as referred to with implied approval.

[20] The relief sought by Commission on appeal is as follows:

(a) That the judgment of the Court of Appeal is reversed and/or set aside;

(b) That the appeal to the Court of Appeal by the Commission be upheld;

(c) That the orders made by the High Court be discharged; and

(d) That the Commission be awarded its costs in this Court and in the Courts
below.

Grounds of Cross-Appeal

[21] According to the Notice of Cross-Appeal, the first respondent appeals only that part
of the judgment of the Court of Appeal relating to the decision to set aside the High
Court’s order of mandamus directing the Commission to issue or grant the licence
to the first respondent. The grounds of the cross-appeal are as follows:
(a) Having approved the finding by the Chief Justice that the first respondent
was entitled to the grant of the quarry licence, the Court of Appeal erred in
law in finding that the Chief Justice had no discretion to grant the order of
mandamus to compel the issue of that licence; or alternatively,

(b) The Court of Appeal erred when and to the extent that it found that the Chief
Justice’s exercise of his discretion to compel the issue of th e licence was
sufficiently irrational or bad in law to warrant the intervention by the Court
of Appeal.

[22] It is again worthy of note that although the second respondent was served with the
Notice of Appeal, and with the Notice of Cross-Appeal, the second respondent did
not enter an Acknowledgment of Service and chose not to take part in the
proceedings before this Court.

Issues for Determination
[23] There are four issues that arise on the grounds of appeal and cross-appeal namely:

(a) Whether the second respondent had submitted an application to the
Commission in respect of the land for which the first respondent applied.

(b) Whether the Commission made a decision to subdivide the land for which
the first respondent had applied , between the first and the second
respondent.

(c) Whether the first respondent had a substantive legitimate expectation to be
issued a quarry licence.

(d) Whether the first respondent is entitled to an order of mandamus directing
that a quarry licence be issued to it.

[24] The first two issues are prim arily issues of fact and evidence; the third issue is of
fact and law; and the final issue is one primarily of law.  As the findings of fact by
the High Court , which were  upheld by the Court of Appeal , were all based on
affidavit evidence , it is necessary to draw attention to the important difference
between factual findings based on affidavit evidence as distinct from findings based
on viva voce evidence.

[25] Judicial findings of facts are often based on the live evidence given in court and the
cogency and credibility of the witnesses who give that evidence. When this is the
case, an appellate court will be reticent to differ from the trial judge who would
have had the advantage of observing and evaluating the witnesses.  In Campbell v
Narine5  this Court approved the view of Sumner LJ in SS Hontestroom (Owners)
v SS Sagaporack (Owners) 6 which emphasised that not having seen the witnesses
puts appellate judges in a permanent position of disadvantage as against the trial
judge and, unless it can be shown that the trial judge failed to use or has palpably

5 [2016] CCJ 07 (AJ) (GY), (2016) 88 WIR 319.
6 [1927] AC 37, 47, endorsed by the Privy Council in Harracksingh v A-G of Trinidad and Tobago [2004] UKPC 3, (2004) 64 WIR 362
(TT) at [10] and Beacon Insurance Co Ltd v Maharaj Bookstore Ltd [2014] UKPC 21, (2014) 84 WIR 478 at [14].

misused his advantage, the higher court ought not to reverse finding s of fact. As
regards the drawing of factual inferences, s 7(1)(b) of the Court of Appeal Act, Cap
3:01 provides that on the hearing of an appeal from the High Court in any civil
matter, the Court of Appeal shall have power to draw inference s of fact.  In
Campbell v Narine 7  this Court endorsed the view of Byron CJ in Grenada
Electricity Services Ltd v Peters 8 that an appellate court is generally in as good a
position to draw inferences or to evaluate evidence as the trial judge.

[26] The position is  significantly different where, as in t he present appeal, findings of
fact are made from affidavit evidence and there was no giving of viva voce evidence
and no cross-examination. In these situations, the trial judge has no real advantage
over an appellate court in making findings of fact. Where affidavit evidence
involves significant and outcome determining conflicts, the trial court ought not to
seek to resolve the matter on the papers but should rather avail itself of the
advantage of having the deponents cross-examined and thus be able to observe their
demeanor and make assessments of their cogency and cre dibility. In this regard s
10 of the Judicial Review Act, Cap 3:06 which provides that an interlocutory order
may be made for cross -examination, should be prayed in aid  by the parties in
appropriate cases.

[27] With these considerations firmly in mind, we shall now turn to examine the issues
that arise for determination in this case.

The Area Applied for by the First Respondent and the Area Applied for by the Second
Respondent

[28] A central issue in this appeal is whether the area of land in Monkey Jump for which
the first respondent applied to quarry stone s was also the subject of a similar
application by the second respondent. The Report of the 10 February 2015 meeting
(‘the 10 February 2015 Report’), authored by Mr Singh of the Commission, stated
that the Commission had ‘accepted two (2) Quarry Licence Applications from the

second respondent and the first respondent dated 26 June 2006 and 28 March 2014,

had not applied for a quarry licence and ‘that, if it was carrying on quarrying
operations on any part of the land which is the subject of the [ first respondent’s]
application to the Commission (G.G.M.C.), then it was doing so illegally. ’9This
finding was unanimously upheld by the Court of Appeal.

[29] Although cross-examination would have been useful, there was, in our view, ample
documentary evidence in the record to support the finding by the courts below that
the second respondent  had not made an application for any portion of the land
which was the subject of the application by the first respondent.

[30] The assertion by the Commission in the 10 February 2015 Report that both the first
and second  respondent had applied for the same area was disputed by the first
respondent and, it should be noted, is not unambiguously supported by the second

that: (1) its search at the Commission revealed that no application was ever made
for a quarry licence for the area by anyone; (2) there was no record at the
Commission to show that anyone had applied for a quarry licence of the said land;
(3) had there been any conflict with its application the Commission would not have
proceeded with its application and caused the Notice of Intention to be advertised;

appear, the second respondent claims that there had been an error in relation to its
application; the existence of an error in the second respondent’s application is also
supported by the Commission.

[31] It is very significant that in his affidavit before the High Court, Mr Singh of the
Commission did not repeat the assertion in the  10 February 2015 Report, that the
first and second respondent had applied for the same area of land . Nor did the

The Report was attached as Exhibit GGMC1.  It was in respect of this quarrying
work that the  Cease Work Order was issued to the second respondent by the
Commission on 15 September 2014.11

[33] In his affidavit before the Court of Appeal, Mr Rahaman, the Managing Director of
the second respondent, placed into evidence the application of 20 June 2006 for a

referenced a ‘copy of the occupation survey commissioned by  the second

in occupation since at least 1965. This occupation survey by the Commission

was marked as Exhibit G.  However, Exhibit G appears to designate a relatively
small area as the second respondent’s ‘existing occupation’ within Monkey Jump;

[34] Mr Rahaman acknowledged that on or about 15 September 201 4, the second
respondent received a Cease Work order from the Commission. He further deposed

with his 10 February 2015 Report). Evidently this evidence was preferred in the
Court of Appeal to Mr Rahaman’s representation that there had been mistakes in
the coordinates contained in the second respondent ’s Monkey Jump Licence

[35] There is no clear and compelling evidence that there was a mistake with respect to
the area of Monkey Jump for which the second respondent applied or of the area
which it occupied. None of the inspection reports refer to any issues concerning the
area inspected. On the other hand, t he clarity of the delineation of the 1,200 acres
on the map attached by the second respondent to its 2006 application, the evidence
from the Commission that the second respondent had applied for an area north of
the land on which it was found in occupation , and the Cease Work order issued
render untenable the assertion by the second respondent  that there had been a
mistake in its application.  The map depicting the  area for which the second
respondent had applied is attached to this Judgment as Annex 2. Even if there

was such a mistake or inadvertence on the part of the second respondent it would
amount at best to suggesting that the second respondent had intended to apply for
another or additional areas of Monkey Jump. Such an intention could not supersede
the actual application by the first respondent which , on Mr Rahaman’s own
affidavit, had preceded the discovery of the mistake or inadvertence by some six
months.

[36] There is another consideration that should be noted . The Cease Work Order was
issued 15 September 2014, the day before the Notice of Intention to grant the quarry
licence to the first respondent was published . The Commission obviously was
aware of the second respondent’s  occupation on the land for which the first
respondent had applied  before the Notice of Intention was published , and
nevertheless proceeded with its publication . The Cease Work Order specifically
stated that it was ‘absolutely necessary for the maintenance of the public peace and
for the protection of the interests of the STATE or of private persons  that all work
should cease ’. Th e issuance of that Order ought to have placed the second
respondent on enquiry and heightened diligence in the protection of its interests ,
including the checking of quarry licence applications published in the Gazette.

[37] In sum, therefore, we find no basis for disagreeing with the courts below that the
848 acres of land for which the first respondent applied  to conduct quarrying
operations had not been the subject of an application for a quarry licence by  the
second respondent. The Notice of Intent ion to grant the quarry licence to the  first
respondent specifically exempted ‘all lands lawfully held or occupied.’ There was
no indication that any portion of the land for which the first respondent had applied
was lawfully held or lawfully occupied by anyone. It appears tolerably clear from
evidence proffered by the Commission that the 1200 acres for which the second
respondent applied was to the north of the ‘flyspeck’ it occupied on the 848 acres
for which the first respondent had applied.

[38] The question of whether the Commission made the decision to subdivide the land
for which the first respondent had applied is one of fact to be decided upon the

support of the application by the second respondent to intervene and to be made a
party to the appeal . The court did not confront the specific issue of w hether the
Commission had decided to subdivide the land but quoted the findings and decision

[40] Before this Court, the Commission’s first ground of appeal was that the Court of

Substantive Legitimate Expectation to be Issued a Quarry Licence

[48] The first respondent’s claim to a legitimate expectation that it would be issued a
quarry licence  is that it had received the unambiguous assurance from the
Commission that its application had been favourably considered and that the Notice
of Intention to Grant the licence would be published. The Notice was published and
there was no objection to the grant of th e licence by anyone. The first respondent
had satisfied all the legal requirements under the Act for the award of the licence.
The Land Administration Manager of the Commission had represented to the first
respondent that the application would be processed as soon as all the statutory
documentation was submitted and verified, and the documents had been so
submitted. The case against  legitimate expectation is that the Commission had
made no express promise to  grant the quarrying licence, and that the grant of a
licence is always subject to overriding public interests.

[49] The doctrine of legitimate expectation is a relatively new and still evolving area of
public law. Some features are comparatively settled and others still in the process
of development. The cases suggest that there are two broad categories: procedural

legitimate expectation and substantive legitimate expectation  but it is not always
easy to keep these categories in water-tight compartments.

[50] The paradigm case of procedural legitimate expectation arises where a public
authority gives a clear and unequivocal representation, which could be in the form
of an express promise or an established practice, that it will give notice or conduct
consultations before changing an existing policy. In these circumstances, the court
will not allow the public authority to effect the proposed change without the
promised notice or consultat ion, ‘unless the want of notice or consultation is
justified by the force of an overriding legal duty owed by the decision -maker, or
other countervailing public interest…’14

[51] The archetypal case of substantive legitimate expectation arises where the publi c
authority gives the assurance that the claimant would enjoy the substance of the
existing policy and the court considers that it would be unfair to the claimant to
allow the public authority to change or abolish the policy notwithstanding the desire
of the public authority to do so. The distinction was explained in  R v North and
East Devon Health Authority  ex p Coughlan 15 by Woolf LJ who stated that a
promise or practice may induce a legitimate expectation of, for example , being
consulted before a particular decision is taken; in these cases, the court will require
the opportunity for consultation to be given unless there is an overriding reason to
resile from it. By contrast, cases of substantive legitimate expectations are different:

Where the court considers that a lawful promise or practice has induced a
legitimate expectation of a benefit which is substantive , not simply
procedural, authority now establishes that here too the court will in a proper
case decide whether to frustrate the expectation is so unfair that to take a new
and different course will amount to an abuse of power. Here, once the
legitimacy of the expectation is established, the court will have the task of
weighing the requirements of fairness a gainst any overriding interest relied
upon for the change of policy.16

14 R (Bhatt Murphy) v Independent Assessor [2008] EWCA Civ 755 at [30].
15 [2001] QB 213.
16 ibid at [57].

[52] This distinction was accepted by this Court in Attorney General v Joseph17 where
it was held on the facts that the substantive entitlement was to a procedure; namely
the procedure that should be followed before the sentences of death could be carried
out in respect of two condemned men. The leading judgment by de la Bastide PCCJ
and Saunders JCCJ held18 that the respondents had a legitimate expectation that the
State would not execute them without first allowing them a reasonable time within
which to complete the proceedings they had started to the Inter -American
Commission on Human Rights. This expectation di d not extend to requiring the
State to abide by the recommendations made by the Commission.

[53] It is necessarily a more complex and consequential exercise to decide whether there
exists a substantive right to enjoy the content or benefit of a policy as distinct from
a merely procedural right to be notified or consulted  before an alteration of the
policy is effected . In substantive legitimate expectation cases, the court must
necessarily balance the competing interests of the individual, who has the legitimate
expectation that the policy maker will be faithful to its assurance to apply the
existing policy, and that of the public authority who should generally not be
constrained in changing policy in the interest of the public. The public body will
only be restrained from acting contrary to its promise or representation if failure to
do so would amount to an abuse of power and would therefore be contrary to good
governance.

[54] The matter was put with admirable clarity in  Guyana Geology and Mines
Commission v Pharsalus Inc .19  Delivering the judgment of this Court,  Hayton
JCCJ acknowledged that it was ‘most unusual ’ for substantive legitimate
expectations to be recognised:

… because they lead to a body, whose function is to act in the public
interest, being required to make a particular decision rather than merely
restricting how a body should proceed to come to a decision of its own. The
courts recognise that, while the claima nt and the public have an interest in
persons being able to rely upon legal certainty and fair, good governance,

17 [2006] CCJ 3 (AJ), (2006) 69 WIR 104 (BB).
18 ibid at [118].
19 [2013] CCJ 10 AJ, (2013) 83 WIR 401 (GY).

authorities like the Commission and the Minister normally have to be
allowed discretionary leeway in the developing public interest to formulate
and re -formulate policy, balancing competing interests across a wide
spectrum and deciding the content and pace of change.20

[55] Nevertheless, recognition of substantive legitimate expectations was possible if the
necessary requirements were met. Specifically:

To ascertain whether a substantive legitimate expectation has arisen the
courts focus upon not what the claimant subjectively expects but upon what
the claimant is entitled to expect as a result of “a specific underta king,
directed to a particular individual or group, by which the relevant policy’s
continuance is assured,” so that the defendant’s conduct is “equivalent to a
breach of contract or breach of representation.”  There needs to be “a clear
and unambiguous rep resentation, devoid of relevant qualification” so that
effect can be given to such representation, it being clearly unfair to the
representee in all the circumstances for the court to allow this representation
to be defeated by the public interest (which i s never static) in changing the
policy reflected in the representation.

This undertaking or representation needs to be made by the decision-maker
who will be required to implement the undertaking or representation.21

[56] These stipulations were accepted by us in the subsequent case of Guyana Geology
and Mines Commission v BK International Inc  (BK International) 22. This Court
cited and relied on  its cases of Attorney General v Joseph ;23  Air Services L td v
Attorney General;24 Commissioner of the Guyana Geology and Mines Commission
v Pharsalus Inc;25 Gilharry v Transport Board26 in concluding that the doctrine of
legitimate expectation was firmly established in the jurisprudence of the Caribbean
Court of Justice (CCJ).  In BK International27 the claim for a procedural legitimate
expectation was upheld as an alternative basis  for grounding the Commission’s
obligation to comply with the provisions of the Procurement Act, Cap 73:05.

[57] Academic authority suggests that there may be a distinction between upholding a
substantive legitimate expectation in respect of a specific promise as contrasted
with a policy. Melanie Roberts argues28 that this is so because a promise made to a
person carries ‘a particular moral force’ and because holding the public body to that
representation is less likely to have serious constraining consequences for the
general administration of the policy.  The promise functions like an estoppel at
common law. By contrast, ‘general policy statements address to the world or large
numbers of people’ are less likely to genera te substantive legitimate expectations
because ‘it is in the nature of general policy that it may be changed’.29

[58] It may not always be easy to draw a distinction between policy statements and the
individual promise, but the paradigmatic case of the promise is tolerably clear. Ex
parte Coughlan 30 is an ideal substantive legitimate expectation claim precisely
because it involved a promise to an individual. Ms Coughlan was severely disabled
and was moved into the Mardon House nursing home on the promise that it would
be her ‘home for life’. Subsequently the health authority decided it could break the
promise if it seem ed reasonable taking economic factors and the needs of other
patients into account. The English Court of Appeal held that it was unlawful for the
health authority to break its promise to Ms Coughlan in the absence of an overriding
public interest and compelling circumstances  and that these had not been
demonstrated by the health authority.

[59] Pharsalus also involved the allegation of a promise made to an individual.  Clause
2 of t he permit granted by the  Minister gave the claimant a right to apply to the
Commission for radioactive minerals and rare earth elements within its Permit area
and that application was to be treated on a ‘priority basis’. The claimant appears to
have expected that its application to the Commission for a prospecting licence for
radioactive minerals and rare earth elements within its Permit a rea would succeed
subject to satisfying the Minister and the Commission on certain provisions set out
in clause 2 of its Permit. The claim failed as any representation made by the

29 ibid 117-18.
30 Coughlan (n 15).

Minister in clause 2 was ambiguous (it was not necessarily clear what treating the
application on a ‘priority basis’ meant) and, having been made by the Minister ,
could not bind the Commission against whom it was invoked.

[60] In the present appeal, the undisputed premise for engendering the legitimate
expectation consisted of unambiguous assurances given by the Commission to the
first respondent and publication by the Commission of  the Notice of Intent ion to
Grant the licence. There was no objection to the Notice of Intention to the grant of
the licence by anyone. The Land Administration Manager of the Commission had
represented to the first respondent that the application would be processed as soon
as all statutory documentation was submitted and verified . All the statutory
documents were submitted.  In these circumstances, the Commission could not
simply change its mind and withhold the grant of the licence in the absence of
important public interests which compelled the withholding of the licence. In the
absence of such interests, it would be unfair and an abuse of power to frustrate the
legitimate expectation and interests of the first respondent.

Mandamus to Enforce Substantive Legitimate Expectation
[61] Where there has been a violation of constitutional rights a court, in pursuance of
the general re dress provisions in the Constitution, may, in appropriate
circumstances, order the grant of the specific remedy claimed by the claimant. For
example, in Observer Publications Ltd v Matthew31 where violation of the right to
freedom of expression had been established, the Privy Council ordered that a radio
broadcasting licence must be issued to the complainant. Similarly, in Central
Broadcasting Services Ltd v Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago32 in relation
to a similar breach, the Privy Council considered that the only appropriate remedy
was a mandatory order requiring the Attorney General to do all that was necessary
to procure and ensure the issue forthwith to the appellant the FM radio broadcasting
licence applied for. Similarly, mandatory orders have also bee n issued to direct a

31 (2001) 58 WIR 188 (AG PC).
32 [2006] 1 WLR 2891, [2006] UKPC 35 (TT) at [36].

public body to perform a duty specified in legislation. 33 Spectacularly, in Ventose
v Chief Electoral Officer, 34 this Court ordered the Chief Electoral  Officer of
Barbados to register or cause to be registered Professor Ventose as  an elector by
noon two days after the judgment was delivered or be held in contempt of Court
and imprisoned or fined.

[62] In substantive legitimate expectation cases , the public body has a policy to
implement or a discretion to exercise. The present question is whether the doctrine
of legitimate expectation has developed to the point where that expectation is
regarded as a legal right capable of being specifically enforced by mandamus
notwithstanding the discretion resident in the public body . This is yet another
evolving area of law with divergence in the  decided cases  and attended with
conceptual difficulty. As David Wright has pointed out:35

Although giving substantive effects to  legitimate expectations seems a
natural evolution from giving procedural effect to this kind of promise, this
raises very different issues about the use and fettering of discretion, and the
extent to which public authorities should be bound by their declarations of
policy.

[63] In the earlier cases on substantive legitimate expectation the courts often gave their
opinion on the issue , including finding that a legitimate expectation had been
established, and then remitted the matter for reconsideration by the public authority
sometimes with a statement of the expected outcome. This was the approach
adopted in the present case by the Court of Appeal. Having found that as a matter
of fact the first respondent was entitled to the grant of the quarry licence the court
nonetheless varied the order of the Chief Justice directing the grant of the licence
to the first respondent, and instead remitted the matter to the Commission for the
exercise of its discretion according to law.

33 R v Secretary of State for the Home Environment ex p Percy Bilton Industrial Properties Ltd  [1976] 1 EGLR 141; R v Secretary of
State for the Home Dept ex p Herbage (No 2) [1987] QB 1077.
34 [2018] CCJ 13 (AJ), (2018) 92 WIR 118 (BB).
35 David Wright, ‘Rethinking the Doctrine of Legitimate Expectations in Canadian  Administrative Law’ (1997) 35 Osgoode Hall L J
139, 156.

[64] In taking this approach the Court of Appeal relied principally on the 1971 decision
of Camacho v Collector of Customs.36 In that case the applicants’ importation of
certain goods required a licence issued by the Controller of Customs who refused
to issue the licences on the instruction of the Minister of Trade, Industry and
Commerce. The Trial Judge held that the person to whom the law granted the power
to grant or refuse the licence was the Controller of Customs and not the Minister.
The Judge held that the Controller of Customs had not applied his mind to the
applications and granted an order of mandamus directing that the  application be
remitted to the Controller of Customs for consideration and determination
according to the provisions of the relevant Ordinance.

[65] The applicants were not satisfied with this order and contended before the Court of
Appeal of the West Indies  Associated States Court of Appeal (WIASC) that the
Judge should have granted an order directing the Collector of Customs to issue to
them the licences for which they had applied. The WIASC accepted that the
Minister had acted based on political prejudice against the applications and that in
acting on the ministerial edict, the Controller of Customs had failed to exercise his
independent discretion and had also breached s 12(2) of the  Antigua Constitution
Order 1967  (guarantee against d iscriminatory treatment). However, the court
refused to grant  an order of  mandamus directing the grant of the licences to the
applicants. Lewis CJ explained the approach taken by the courts to the grant of
mandamus in the following terms:37

In this connection it may be appropriate also to quote the words of Lor d
Morris of Borth-y-Gest in Padfield v Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and
Food ([1968] AC 997, [1968] 1 All ER 694, [1968] 2 WLR 924) ([1968] 2
WLR at p 950):

‘Where some legal right or entitlement is conferred or enjoyed, and
for the purpose of effectuating such right or entitlement a power is
conferred upon someone, then words which are permissive in
character will  sometimes be construed as involving a duty to
exercise the power. The purpose and the language of any particular
enactment must be considered.’

36 (1971) 18 WIR 159.
37 ibid 177.

Here, the language of s 4 of the Ordinance… does not specify any particular
person or class of persons for whose benefit the power conferred  on the
Collector of Customs may be exercised…. Before the power in the Collector
of Customs can be held to be one that he was bound to exercise  (as the
appellants are in effect contending) it would have to be shown that  the
section gave them a “right” in law to have the power exercised in their
favour.

[66] Legitimate expectation was not canvassed in Camacho, and, in any event, the
doctrine has developed by leaps and bounds over the intervening 50 years. Even,
so the cases are legion that the finding of a legitimate expectation d oes not
necessarily yield the award of mandamus to give effect to that expectation. In the
case of Leacock v Attorney General 38  the applicant was a police officer who
applied for study leave from his employer, the Royal Barbados Police Force
(RBPF) to study at the Hugh Wooding Law School after completing his studies at
the University of the West Indies. The RBPF denied his application for study leave
as they found that he had a poor work ethic; was regularly absent from work
ostensibly on sick leave while he was attending the University of the West Indies,
and generally had an uncooperative attitude.  The court found that the appellant had
a legitimate expectation to be granted study leave based on a practice that had
developed over many years that officers who had successfully completed the LLB
were granted study leave to complete their LEC at the Hugh Wooding Law School
and that t here was no overriding consideration to justify a departure from the
practice. Despite these findings Sir David Simmons CJ found that the ‘merits of a
case will often involve policy considerations’ but that ‘Such considerations are not
for the courts.’39

[67] This decision was criti qued by Professor Ventose who opined that despite the
court’s bold finding that the practice created a substantive legitimate expectation
the court adopted a rather conservative approach on the remedies granted. Professor
Ventose stated that the Chief Justice:

38 (2005) 68 WIR 181 (BB).
39 ibid at 51.

… emphasized that it was no part of his function, or indeed any court’s in a
judicial review application to substitute the court’s decision for that of the
competent authority.  But this statement really misses the point, for the very
acceptance of substantive legitimate expectation means in those very
limited circumstances the courts may think it justified to interfere with the
decision of the public authority , and, consequently, take a more intrusive
role than they ordinarily would where there has been an abuse of power by
the public authority40.

[68] There are many other cases in which courts have issued ancillary orders in addition
to making strong statements affirming the existence of legitimate expectations but
have stopped short of ordering mandamus to fulfil th ose expectations. See, for
example, Trinidad and Tobago Civil Rights Association v Manning; 41 and Pan
Trinbago Inc v National Carnival Commission of Trinidad and Tobago.42 The latter
case has been subject to strong academic criticism.43

[69] Whilst it remains t rue that it is not in every case that a finding of a substantive
legitimate expectation engendered by a public body will warrant the grant of
mandamus to give it effect, there are some cases in which the court may conclude
that there is only one lawful outcome in which case it may give a mandatory order
to require that result. In these circumstances , the court may well grasp the nettle
and issue mandamus to give effect to the substantive legitimate expectation.

[70] In R v Ealing London Borough Council, ex p Parkinson 44 Laws J stated:

There are, it is true, rare cases where the public law court is able to conclude
that only one result was legally open to the body in question, and in that
case an order of mandamus may issue to require that result to be arrived at.
Even there, however, the court does not undertake the role of primary fact-
finder, substituting its judgment on the merits for that of the body reviewed.
It merely recognises the existence of a situation in which a public authority,
properly directing itself on the facts according to the law, has only one
choice legally open to it.

40 Eddy Ventose, Commonwealth Caribbean Administrative Law (Routledge 2013) 214.
41 (Trinidad and Tobago HC, 7 December 2007).
42 (Trinidad and Tobago HC, 14 December 2017).
43 Calvin Eversley, ‘Legitimate Expectation and the Creation of Procedural and Substantive Legal Rights in Commonwealth Caribbean
Public Law’ (2004) 33 Comm LWorld Rev 332.
44 (1995) 29 HLR 179 at 185.

[71] This approach was also adopted in the case R (S) v Secretary of State for the Home
Dept.45 In this case an asylum seeker came to UK from Afghanistan in September
1999. At the time when he arrived, there was a favourable policy in place treating
with Asylum seekers from Afghanistan in which they were granted exceptional
leave to stay for four years and indefinite leave thereafter. In January 2001, a ‘public
service agreement ’ was entered into betwee n the Home Department and the
Treasury, setting targets for dealing with asylum claims lodged on or after 1 January
2001.  A decision was made to postpone indefinitely consideration of older
applications, such as th at of the  claimant, so that the Departmen t could meet its
targets under the agreement.  The claimant ’s application was not considered until
March 2004.  By that time, there had been changes in the policy towards Afghan
asylum seekers, following the removal of the Taliban regime, and the asylum claim
was refused.  He exhausted all options of appeal and eventually filed for Judicial
Review. Carnwath LJ delivering the majority judgment of the court stated:46

[I]t was open to the court to determine that a legally material factor in the
exercise of that discretion was the correction of injustice. That proposition
did not require express statutory authority. It was implicit in the principles
of fairness and consistency which underlay the whole statutory scheme.
Further, in an extreme case, the court could hold that the unfairness was so
obvious, and the remedy so plain, that there was only one way in which the
Secretary of State could reasonably exercise his discretion.

[72] In Pharsalus this Court implicitly accepted that mandamus could be ordered to give
effect to a substantive legitimate expectation. We agreed with all members of the
Court of Appeal that no formalistic demand and rejection of the demand are needed
on which to base an order for mandamus, since it is ‘the substance of the matte r
that is important. ’47 The mandamus was no t ordered in Pharsalus because it was
found that no legitimate expectation arose since the undertaking and representation
contained in the permit were not unambiguous and were those of the Minister and
not the Commissioner.

45 [2007] EWCA Civ 546, [2007] Imm AR 781.
46 ibid at [46].
47 Pharsalus (n 19) at [27].

[73] In sum mary, on present law, the court will generally not issue an order of
mandamus to direct a statutory authority exercising discretion over its decision -
making or policy-implementation, to take a particular decision except in rare cases
where it considers that there was only one right conclusion that could reasonably
be reached in circumstances before it.

[74] We consider that the present case falls within these exceptional parameters. The
first respondent had applied for the quarry licence, paid the applicable fees, and in
response to the request from the Commission supplied all the statutorily required
documents. The first respondent was assured that its application had been
favourably considered and that a Notice of Intent to grant the licence would be
published. That Notice was published and no objection to the grant of the licence
was received. Even apart from the verbal assurance from the Land Administration
Manager of the Commission which allegedly led t he first respondent to expend
resources in preparation for operating the quarry, the course of conduct between the
parties and the written assurance given by the Commission represented a clear and
unambiguous promise from which the Commission could only resile for reason of
some overriding public interest. No such reason was presented to the courts below
or to this Court.

[75] In this case, the specific conduct of the Commission indicated that, barring proof
of overriding public considerations to the contrary, the Commission could not grant
a licence over the area for which the first respondent had applied to anyone else
without frustrating the legitimate expectation of the first respondent that it had
created. In these circumstances and considering the course that this litigation has
taken in which the second respondent could have but chose not to appeal against
the decision of the Court of Appeal adverse to its interests , we consider that it is
appropriate that mandamus should issue req uiring the Commission to grant the
licence to the first respondent for which it had applied.

Conclusion
[76] The appeal is dismissed, and the cross-appeal is upheld. The orders of the Court of
Appeal are affirmed except to the extent that those orders varied the orders of the
High Court.
Disposition
[77] The following are the orders of this Court:

(i) The Judgment and Orders of the Honourable Chief Justice (Ag) Ian Chang
dated 14 August 20 15 in Action No 2015-HC-Dem-CIV-M-18 be and are
hereby affirmed.

(ii) The costs in the fixed sum of [GYD]$500,000.00 be paid by the
Commissioner of the Guyana Geology and Mines Commission to Diamond
Quarry Inc. and costs fixed in the sum of [GYD]$1,500,000.00 be paid by
Baracara Quarries Inc to Diamond Quarry Inc.

[78] The Commission shall pay the sum of GYD$2,000,000.00 to the first respondent,
representing the costs of this appeal to the CCJ in accordance with Part 17.3 (c) of
the CCJ (Appellate Jurisdiction) Rules 2021.

items.title: CALVIN RAMCHARRAN v THE DIRECTOR OF PUBLIC PROSECUTIONS
items.full_text:
[2022] CCJ 4 (AJ) GY

IN THE CARIBBEAN COURT OF JUSTICE
APPELLATE JURISDICTION

ON APPEAL FROM THE COURT OF APPEAL OF GUYANA

CCJ Appeal No GYCR2021/001
GY Criminal Appeal No 42 of 2015

BETWEEN

CALVIN RAMCHARRAN                    APPELLANT

AND

THE DIRECTOR OF
PUBLIC PROSECUTIONS                      RESPONDENT

Before the Honourable:  Mr Justice W Anderson, JCCJ
Mme Justice M Rajnauth-Lee, JCCJ
Mr Justice D Barrow, JCCJ
Mr Justice A Burgess, JCCJ
Mr Justice P Jamadar, JCCJ

Appearances

Mr C A Nigel Hughes with Ms Savannah Barnwell and Mr Ronald J Daniels for the
Appellant

Mrs Shalimar Ali-Hack, SC, Director of Public Prosecutions with Mrs Diana
Kaulesar-O’Brien, Mrs Teshana Lake and Ms Natasha Backer for the Respondent

Criminal law – Appeal - Sentence - Appellant convicted of rape and causing actual bodily
harm – Sentences of 23 years and 3 years imprisonment to run concurrently – Whether
sentences manifestly exces sive - Sexual Offences Act Cap 8:03, s 3(3) - Criminal Law
(Offences) Act Cap 8:01, s 49.
Criminal law - Rape - Sentencing Principles - Failure to apply guidance in Pompey v DPP.

SUMMARY

Calvin Ramcharran (‘Ramcharran’) was tried before a jury and convicted of rape and
assault causing actual bodily harm. On the day  of the verdict, 16 November 2015, he was
sentenced to 23 years imprisonment for the offence of rape and 3 years imprisonment for
the offence of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, wit h the sentences to run
concurrently. On 11 January 2021 the Court of Appeal affirmed the decision of the trial
judge. Ramcharran appealed to this Court. The appeal was against sentence alone, this
Court having refused permission to appeal against conviction.

Before this Court Ramcharran contended inter alia  that the sentences were manifestly
excessive, that the judge failed to consider or to adequately consider the antecedents of the
appellant or any social report or any victim impact statement and that she failed to outline
or apply any principles and considerations upon which the sentences were determined. He
argued that the Court of Appeal erred in law when they found that although the trial judge
did not identify the process by which the penalties were arrived at the sentences did not
warrant any review or were appropriate.

The Court, in a majority judgment authored by Barrow JCCJ found that the sentence for
rape was manifestly excessive. The Court considered that the trial judge failed to hold a
separate sentencing hearing, to take a victim impact statem ent, to obtain mental health or
psychological assessments, to obtain a social report and to give reasons for and indicate
the process used to arrive at the sentence. While the trial judge did hear a plea in mitigation
and did not impose the maximum sentenc e of life imprisonment, because the judge gave
no reasons the appellate courts could only infer what the trial judge considered in arriving
at the sentences imposed.

The Court found that the Court of Appeal in reviewing the trial judge’s sentence erred i n
failing to follow the comprehensive guidance for trial judges in respect of sentencing in
rape cases in its earlier decision in Pompey v DPP (‘Pompey’). The Court was satisfied that
because the Court of Appeal failed to be guided by the precedent of Pompey, as it was
bound to do, it failed to apply the proper sentencing principles and objectives to the
determination of the issue raised by the appeal: whether the sentences were manifestly
excessive or wrong in principle. More fully stated, it failed to con sider if a different
sentence should have been passed.

The Court found that pursuant to the Caribbean Court of Justice Act it had jurisdiction to
review the sentences imposed. The Court considered the range of starting sentences for
rape, as well as the aggravating and mitigating factors and imposed a sentence of 12 years
imprisonment. In respect of the sentence for assault causing actual bodily harm the Court
found that because the sentence of imprisonment for 3 years for assault is to be served
concurrently there is no double punishment for this offence, and it may be left to stand for
its demonstrative and deterrent effect.

In a separate judgment, Rajnauth-Lee and Jamadar JJCCJ agreed that the sentence for rape
imposed and affirmed by the Court of App eal was excessive and needed to be reviewed.
The sentence was suspect, because no rational or evidence -based approach was taken to
sentencing. Neither the trial judge nor the Court of Appeal followed the methodology
recommended by the majority judgments of this Court in Pompey, with the result that the
sentence imposed was presumptively excessive and disproportionate.  The evidential
deficits and procedural shortcomings, taken together with the failure to follow the
sentencing approach explained by the majority in Pompey, resulted in a sentencing hearing
that was flawed and has arguably not met the threshold standards to constitute a fair hearing
that could produce a fit, proportionate, and just sentence. The deficits were arguably so
fundamental, that evidentially it was difficult for an appellate court to engage in a thorough
resentencing review and arrive at an appropriate new sentence. To overcome these
evidential deficiencies, this matter could have been remitted for a sentencing rehearing by
the trial judge guided by this Courts jurisprudence, including as set out in their opinion and
in the majority opinions in Pompey. However, given the passage of time from both the date
of the crime and the holding of the sentencing hearing, and in the interest of fairness
including to the victim, timeliness, and for pragmatic reasons, a sentencing re -evaluation
and reconsideration ought not to be remitted for rehearing and should be undertaken by
this Court. Rajnauth-Lee and Jamadar JJCCJ disagreed with the sentence imposed by the
majority and would have imposed a sentence of 16 years imprisonment for rape.

All judges of this Court agreed that the sentence for rape imposed by the trial court and
upheld by the Court of Appeal was excessive and needed to be reviewed. They agreed that
the sentences for the two offences should run concurrently and agreed with the lower courts
on the sentence for the assault charge. The majority also all agreed with the general
approaches to a sentencing hearing outlined in the joint opinion of Rajnauth -Lee and
Jamadar JJCCJ. The appeal was therefore allowed, and the Appellant sentenced to 12 years
imprisonment for rape. The sentence for assault causing actual bodily harm was affirmed.
The sentences are to run concurrently.

1994) UN Doc E/CN.4/Sub.2/1994/24 ; Weller P J, ’Mainstreaming TJ in Australia:

JUDGMENT
of
The Honourable Justices Anderson, Barrow and Burgess

and

JUDGMENT
of
The Honourable Justices Rajnauth-Lee and Jamadar

Delivered by
The Honourable Mr Justice Barrow
on the 18th day of February 2022
JUDGMENT OF THE HONOURABLE MR JUSTICE BARROW, JCCJ:

Introduction

[1] This appeal against a sentence of 23 years imprisonment for rape raises again basic
issues of sentencing principles and approach and the need for sentencing courts to
apply and further develop guidelines which have been established.

The Facts

[2] The appeal was against sentence alone, this Court having refused permission to
appeal against conviction. The appellant was tried before a jury and convicted of
rape and assault causing actual bodily harm. He was sentenced respectively to 23
years and 3 years imprisonment for the offences, with the sentences to run
concurrently. The Court of Appeal affirmed the decision of the trial judge.

[3] Because an appellate court is required to exercise its sentencing discretion, it is
necessary to set out fully the traumatic occurrence. T, the virtual complainant, went
to a football match on the night of 21 July 2012. T was 20  years old. Due to its
cancellation, she and three friends went to an open-air party and ‘Fish Fry Lime’ at
Calabash Alley, Soesdyke. While there, T went alone into an unfinished concrete
structure nearby to urinate. On her way in she saw someone stooping in the place,
she said good night and went to urinate. While she was urinating, the person got up
and went outside.

[4] On her way out she saw the appellant, also 20 years of age, standing outside the
structure. She knew the appellant for seven years prior f rom attending school with
him. The appellant held onto her hands, pulled her back into the structure and asked

Sentencing in the Courts below

[6] After the jury convicted the appellant on 16 November 2015, the trial judge heard
a plea in mitigation on his behalf and proceeded immediately to sentence him. The
Court of Appeal heard the appellant’s appeal on 18 and 30 June 2020 and on 12
January 2021 affirmed the conviction and sentence.

[7] The facts relevant to the sentencing exercise at first instance and before the Court
of Appeal are brief. As indicated, the trial judge failed to hold a separate sentencing
hearing, to take a victim impact statement, to obtain mental health or psychological
assessments, to obtain a social report and to indicate the process used to arrive at
the sentence. While the trial judge did hear a plea in mitigation and did not impose
the maximum sentence of life imprisonment, because the judge gave no reasons an
appellate court can only infer what the trial judge considered in arriving at the
sentences imposed.

[8] The Court of Appeal acknowledged the deficiencies of the sentencing exercise but
went only as far as observing that ‘the trial judge has not shown the process used to
arrive at the sentence, given the modern sentence guidance’.1 The Court of Appeal
indicated that there was ‘not much that the judge could have done in terms of a
smaller sentence’, considering the maximum sentence and the aggravating and
mitigating factors but failed to identify what these factors were.2

[9] The contention on appeal is that the sentences were manifestly excessive, and this
is summarised in the grounds of appeal. In brief, the appellant contended that the
judge failed to consider or to adequately consider the antecedents of the appellant
or any social report or any victim impact statement and that she failed to outline or
apply any principles and considerations upon which the sentences were determined.

The Guidance Pompey Provided

[10] This Court recently provided comprehensive guidance for trial judges in respect of
sentencing in rape cases in Pompey v DPP3 and while that decision came long after
the trial judge had done her sentencing, it was available before the appeal was heard.
The Court of Appeal acknowledged the decision in Pompey but placed no reliance
on that guidance. That failure to be guided by Pompey was critical because if the
Court of Appeal had so guided itself, it is likely it would have arrived at a different
decision.

[11] Four opinions from a seven -member bench were delivered in Pompey, with the
majority opinion being delivered by Saunders PCCJ and Rajnauth-Lee and Jamadar
JJCCJ each delivering a concurring opinion and Wit and Anderson JJCCJ
delivering a joint dissenting opinion. The upshot of the decision was that a sentence
of 15 years imprisonment for rape of a minor must be considered a stan dard
sentence in a case with no aggravating or mitigating features and that the sentence
would be lower for rape of an adult.

Re-exercise of Sentencing Discretion

[26] One of the fundamental principles the judgment in Pompey reiterated36 was that a
sentencing court needs to identify for itself and state for general information the
starting point or range of punishment for an offence of the type before it. Using the
starting sentence or range approach, it was decided in Pompey that a sentence of 15
years imprisonment for the rape of the minor was appropriate, with a higher
sentence of 17 years imprisonment for a repeat offence. The dissenting opinion
considered that a starting point of 5 to 8 years may have been appropriate, and this
is significant because it strengthens the force of the 15 years sentence in Pompey,
as being at the higher rather than lower end of the range. This stands in flat out
contradiction of the DPP’s suggestion in oral argument of a starting point, in this
case, of 23 years. The extensive summary, in this opinion, of the multiple opinions
from the full bench of this Court in Pompey was done deliberately to show that the
sentences decided in that case were arrived at after an ample and indeed exhaustive
consideration of relevant data and factors. It must also be observed that all opinions
in Pompey recognized that the most reliable way to arrive at starting sentences and
ranges was for the judiciary of Guyana to see to and be assisted in conducting the
necessary exercise for creating sentencing guidelines.37

[27] It is curious that the Court of Appeal acknowledged that Pompey decided that a
sentencing court should begin its decision -making on the sentence to impose by
identifying a starting point , but took no step in that dir ection. It may be that the
court failed to appreciate a significant dimension of its appellate function in a
sentencing appeal. In this regard, the Court requested and received supplemental
written submissions, post-hearing, from the appellant (the DPP declining to provide

Jurisdiction to Interfere

[31] In oral argument, the question as to the scope of the jurisdiction of this Court to
review the sentence imposed by the sentencing court was raised with counsel.
Section 11(6) of the Caribbean Court of Justice Act, Cap 3:07 provides that in
relation to any appeal to it this Court shall have all the jurisdiction and powers of
the Court of Appeal in relation to that case.  The primary grounds of this appeal, as
stated, were that the sentences of 23 years and 3 years were ‘manifestly excessive’.
The expression ‘manifestly excessive’, in appeals against sentences is a familiar
one in common law courts that expresses the proposition that the sentence imposed
exceeded the proper range of sentences after taking into account all the f actors
relevant to the offence and the offender. 40  The ground easily fits into the ambit of
s 13(3) of the Court of Appeal Act, Cap 3:01 discussed by  Wit and Anderson JJCCJ
in Pompey, at [128], as being in broad terms in providing that the Court of Appea l
“… if they think that a different sentence should have been passed …” may quash
the sentence passed at the trial and substitute another sentence warranted in law.

40 Sentencing Academy, ‘Sentencing Explained, Appeals Against Sentence’  13 February 2021 <https://sentencingacademy.org.uk/wp-
content/uploads/2021/02/Appeals-Explainer.pdf> accessed 17 January 2022.

[32] Counsel for the appellant submitted that there are several grounds upon which an
appellant may urge that a different sentence should have been passed and these
include that the sentence passed was manifestly excessive; wrong in principle; the
result of procedural error; based on improperly considered material; and others.
While there are these and other bases for urging error, such as an outright failure to
follow legal principles and precedent, it needs to be emphasized that the core
exercise the appellate court must conduct is to consider if a different sentence
should have been passed. The exercise is not that the appellate court should consider
if a particular error has occurred that may need to be corrected and then go on to
consider passing a different sentence. Rather, the exercise is that the appellate court
must consider the sentence pas sed and re -exercise the sentencing discretion to
decide if a different sentence should have been passed.

[33] This appeal provides a good example of how that difference may operate in
practice. When the appeal came to be heard and to be decided Pompey was fully
available to assist the Court of Appeal in performing its statutory obligation of
considering ‘if a different sentence should have been passed ’. The essential basis
of this appeal is that the Court of Appeal failed to consider, guided by the decision
of Pompey, if a different sentence should have been passed; it failed to consider
whether there were sufficient grounds for them to interfere with the sentence. The
court looked at the errors of the trial judge and decided she had done her best in the
circumstances. That approach was thought to be supported by the words of Massiah
C. in Williams v Walters41 that ‘… the court will not interfere with a sentence unless
it is manifestly excessive or wrong in principle.’

[34] With respect, the court gave no proper consideration to the requirements contained
in the Chancellor’s statement of the law because they did not consider or apply the
by-then established developments in sentencing practice and principle. That
advertence would have shown them that by reference both  to the precedent of the
recent sentence for rape and the applicable sentencing principles, as to which see

41 (Guyana CA, 18 July 1985).
[16] above, the sentence was both manifestly excessive and wrong in principle. Had
the court so adverted it would have recognized it was its duty, as an appellate court,
to quash the sentence because they could not think otherwise than that a different
sentence should have been passed.

Retribution

[35] Lock him up and throw away the key  was a familiar expression of an earlier
generation and the sentiment it contains continues to express popular reaction to
crimes especially of such abhorrence as rape. It must be appreciated that it is a
reaction that, while undoubtedly indicative of the societal disposition, has never
been a principle of sentencing because it has no judicial authenticity. No doubt, the
maximum sentence of life imprisonment that the legislation provides may seem to
the uninformed to amount to nearly the same thing, but now  it must be accepted
that a sentence of life imprisonment will be rare and imposed only in the worst of
the worse cases.

[36] This must necessarily be so because, as Pompey confirmed, modern sentencing
practice requires the court to begin its exercise by identifying a starting sentence or
range of sentence that has been established as standard for the offence, where the
circumstances of its commission are not particularly bad. The decision on the
sentence to impose must be a result of the process of fully considering the primary
aims and principles of sentencing which, as discussed by  Jamadar JCCJ42 drawing
upon this Court’s decisions in Lashley v Singh 43 and Alleyne v R 44, are the
prevention of crime (first and foremost), retribution, general and subjective
deterrence, preventing the particular offender from committing crime and
rehabilitation – retribution alone may not determine the sentence.

[37] The Court of Appeal’s approach that in Guyana we impose sentences that are not
altogether short expresses a reality that reflects the demands within the society for
retributive justice. But the full seven -member bench of this Court gave the matter
full consideration in Pompey and determined that insufficient weight may have
been given in previous sentenc ing exercises to sentencing objectives other than
retribution. It follows that the Court of Appeal was legally bound to guide itself by
the determination in Pompey. The ancient aphorism with which  Wit and Anderson
JJCCJ concluded their opinion in Pompey45 is apposite at this juncture: ‘A talent
for following the ways of yesterday is not sufficient to improve the world of today.’

[38] We are, therefore, satisfied that because the Court of Appeal failed to be guided by
the precedent of Pompey, as it was bound to do, it failed to apply the proper
sentencing principles and objectives to the determination of the issue raised by the
appeal: whether the sentences were manifestly excessive or wrong in principle.
More fully stated, it failed to consider if a dif ferent sentence should have been
passed.

Re-exercising the Sentencing Discretion

[39] The re-exercise of the sentencing discretion that this Court must perform begins
with identifying a starting sentence, which was a seminal principle that Pompey
further endorsed,46 following the Court’s earlier determination in  Persaud.47 The
sentence of 15 years imprisonment for the rape of a minor  in Pompey makes it
proportionate to decide on a starting range of sentence of 8 to 10 years for the rape
of an adult. As discus sed in Persaud48, a sentencing court must proceed by
considering the aggravating and mitigating factors; first those pertinent to the
commission of the offence and then those pertinent to the offender49.

[40] As regards factors pertinent to the commission of the offence, the violence used in

decision to separately charge assault occasioning actual bodily harm. The multiple

the violation and that strength of character, that right to resist, must be vindicated
by the Cour t treating the repeated violence used to overcome it as a significant
aggravating feature of the offence. The violence operates to increase the Court’s
sense of the overall criminality and the sentence that is appropriate in this case.
However, as Pompey was concerned to establish, care must be taken to ensure there
is no double punishment when sentences are being imposed for multiple offences
and the commission of one offence aggravates the other. That is not a concern in
this case because the two sentenc es are not consecutive, and care will be taken to
ensure that the sentence for the violence is not simply added on to the starting
sentence. Rather, as Pompey showed, the sentencing court must proceed with an
appreciation of the overall criminality of the conduct of the offender and impose a
sentence that is appropriate to that criminality.

court must respond as significantly and not incidentally increasing the feeling of
violation the victim must have suffered.

[42] In relation to the commission of the offence there were no mitigating factors. As

found guilty, the appellant offered no expression of remorse and he denied himself
the mitigation earned by genuine remorse.
