items.title: SASEDAI KUMARIE PERSAUD v SHERENE MONGROO
items.full_text:
[2023] CCJ 16 (AJ) GY

IN THE CARIBBEAN COURT OF JUSTICE
APPELLATE JURISDICTION

ON APPEAL FROM THE COURT OF APPEAL OF
THE CO-OPERATIVE REPUBLIC OF GUYANA

CCJ Appeal No GYCV2023/001
GY Civil Appeal No 127 of 2016

BETWEEN

 SASEDAI KUMARIE PERSAUD                                               APPELLANT

AND

 SHERENE MONGROO           FIRST RESPONDENT
 ZENOBIA ROSENBERG      SECOND RESPONDENT
 INDRANIE MULCHAND          THIRD RESPONDENT

Before:   Mr Justice Saunders, President
Mr Justice Wit
Mme Justice Rajnauth-Lee
Mr Justice Burgess
Mr Justice Jamadar

Date of Judgment:  15 December 2023

Appearances

Mr Hari Ramkarran SC, Mr Nikhil Ramkarran and Mr Kamal Ramkarran for the
Appellant

Ms Shaunella Glen, Ms Tamara Khan and Ms Paula Jones-Nicholson for the First
Respondent

Mr C A Nigel Hughes, Ms Savannah Barnwell, Ms Sophia Findlay, Ms Edrianna Stephen
and Mr Michael Jagnanan for the Second Respondent

Mr C V Satram, Mr Mahendra Satram and Mr Ron Motilall for the Third Respondent

Will – Contentious probate proceedings – Testamentary capacity of testator – Suspicious
circumstances surrounding  making of will  – Acknowledgement by testator of his
signature on will – Presumption of due execution – Establishment of due execution in
absence of presumption – Expert evidence as to testator’s signature – Grant of probate in
solemn form of copy of will – Two conflicting opinions in Court of Appeal – Third
opinion in Court of Appeal supporting both conflic ting opinions – Whether conflicting
opinions of Court of Appeal on certain issues result in defective judgment on those issues
– Court of Appeal overturning trial judge’s findings of fact – Distinction between
findings of primary fact and inferences drawn from primary facts – Wills Act, Cap 12:02,
s 4.

SUMMARY

The parties to this appeal were the appellant, Sasedai Kumarie Persaud (Sasedai or
Sasedai Persaud) who was the business manager, executor and principal beneficiary
under the will of Yusuf Mongroo (the deceased or Mr Mongroo). She had been employed
in the deceased’s business since 1999. The first and second respondents were Sherene
Mongroo (Sherene or Sherene Mongroo) and Zenobia Rosenberg (Zenobia or Zenobia
Rosenberg), the two daughters of the deceased, who challenged the will. The third
respondent was Indranie Mulchand (Indranie or Indranie Mulchand) who the trial judge
found, was the common law wife of the deceased, and who also benefitted under the
deceased’s will.  At the trial, evidence was al so led from Nyron Dexter Lathuillerie, who
claimed to be the son of the deceased, but who did not join Sherene and Zenobia in
challenging the will.

Mr Mongroo died on 15 August 2010 at the age of 83 years at the St Joseph Mercy
Hospital in Georgetown. He owned and operated a business called the Horseshoe Racing
Service at Lots 6 -7A Commerce and Longden Streets, Georgetown, Guyana. He also
owned a residential property at Lot 107 New Garden Street, Queenstown, Georgetown,
Guyana, and was known to have owned assets abroad including real estate and racehorses
in Barbados and a bank account in the Cayman Islands. He made separate wills disposing
of his assets in Guyana, Barbados and the Cayman Islands.

The Last Will and Testament of the deceased disposing of his assets in Guyana  (the
Guyana will) was allegedly executed on 12  August 2010 and is the subject of the instant
dispute. In the Guyana will, the deceased instructed as follows: (a) The property at Lots
6-7A Commerce and Longden Streets, Georgetown, be devised to Sasedai Persaud; (b)
Sasedai Pe rsaud to assume sole ownership, management and control of the Horseshoe
Racing Service, and the net proceeds of the business be apportioned: fifty -five percent to
Sasedai Persaud, and the remaining forty five percent to Indranie Mulchand; (c) The
property at 107 New Garden Street, Georgetown be devised to Indranie Mulchand;  (d)
The residue of the deceased’s estate in Guyana be bequeathed to Sasedai Persaud and
Indranie Mulchand in equal shares. The children of the deceased derived no benefit under
the Guyana will.

Proceedings were brought in the High Court by Sherene and Zenobia against Sasedai and
Indranie, contesting the validity of the Guyana will. The trial judge, George J , found that
the Guyana will was valid and effective, dismissed the claim, and amended the defence
and counterclaim to the effect that probate in solemn form was granted with respect to the
copy of the Guyana will presented to the trial court. On appeal to the Court of Appeal, the
decision of the trial judge was reversed and the Guyana will was held to be invalid and
ineffective.

On 28 February 2023, Sasedai Persaud appealed the decision of the Court of Appeal to
this Court. The following issues arise for the determination of th e Court. Firstly, whether
the conflicting opinions of the Court of Appeal on certain issues resulted in a defective
judgment on those issues which ought to be set aside ? Secondly, did the evidence led at
the trial support the findings of the trial judge on the following issues: (a) whether the
deceased possessed  the requisite testamentary capacity? (b) whether the Guyana will
complied with the requirements of s 4 of the Wills Act in that the deceased acknowledged
his signature in accordance with s 4? (c) whether the signature on the Guyana will was
that of the deceased in compliance with s 4 of the Wills Act, and whether the trial judge
ought to have admitted to probate in solemn form a copy of the Guyana will?

The Court made it clear that in its appellate jurisdiction it is a superior court of record
with such j urisdiction and powers as are conferred on it by the Agreement Establishing
the Caribbean Court of Justice, the Constitution or any other law of the Contracting Party.
The Court was of the view that  the conjoint effect of s 4(1) (b) and s 11(6) of the
Caribbean Court of Justice Act and s 7(2) of the Court of Appeal Act was that this Court
was empowered in an appeal from Guyana to ensure the determination o n the merits of
the real question in controversy between the parties. The Court therefore did not agree
that the conflicting opinions of the Court of Appeal on certain issues resulted in a
defective judgment which ought to be set aside for that reason alone. The Court st ated
that it was able to hear the case on its merits.

Before embarking on its analysis of issues which largely concerned findings of fact, the
Court explained that where a trial judge had properly utilised the distinct advantage of
having seen and heard the witnesses, had adequately evaluated the witnesses, and
weighed the facts and circumst ances of the case, an appellate court ought not to lightly
reverse findings of credibility arrived at by the trial judge. The Court pointed out
however that the importance of the distinction between findings of primary fact s and
inferences drawn from the findings of primary facts could not be overlooked. The Court
agreed with Burgess JA sitting in the Court of Appeal of Barbados in the case of Walsh v
Ward that an appellate court should exercise cautious reluctance before it reviewed
findings of fact which were based on assessments of the credibility of witnesses, but that
it was in as good a position as the trial judge when it came to drawing inferences which
involved evaluating evidence.

On the issue of the  deceased’s testamentary capacity , the Court observed that there did
not exist in the instant case circumstances which ought to have excited the suspicion of
the trial judge . The Court also noted that  ‘stricter proof of knowledge and approval’ by
the deceased in the making of the Guyana will was not necessary. The Court noted that
the trial judge accepted the evidence of Mr Vidyanand Persaud, Attorney -at-Law who
prepared the Guyana will, and of Dr Rohan Jabour, a medical doctor, who was o ne of the
witnesses to the Guyana will. The trial judge also found that Sherene and Zenobia had not
established that they enjoyed a close relationship with the dece ased. The Court was
therefore of the view that the evidence accepted by the trial judge provided a sufficient
basis on which  she could have found that the d eceased had the requisite testamentary
capacity.
As to  the requirement of due execution contained in s 4 of the Wills Act, the Court
expressed the view  that it was undisputed that the Guyana will was not signed in the
presence of the witnesses, as stated in the attestation clause. In those circumstances, the
Court observed that the presumption of due execution could not be applied. The Court
was however of the view  that having regard to the evidence accepted by the trial judge,
and in particular, the evi dence of Dr Jabour, the finding of the trial judge t hat the
deceased acknowledged his signature on the Guyana will in the presence of both
witnesses, who signed in the presence of the deceased,  and of each other,  could not be
faulted, and ought not to have been reversed. The Court thus held that due execution of
the Guyana will was established.

Additionally, t he Court concluded that  having regard to the contested expert evidence
examined in the light of the totality of the evidence accepted by the trial j udge, the trial
judge was correct to find that the signature on the Guyana will was that of the deceased.
Further, the Court was of the view that the exercise of the discretion by the trial judge to
admit to probate in solemn form a copy of the Guyana will, could not be faulted , as the
Court was of the view that the trial judge was seeking to do j ustice in the circumstances
of the case.

Accordingly, the decision of the Court of Appeal was set aside, and the judgment of the
George J in the High Court was r estored. The consent order which this Court granted on
3 May 2023, and which prohibited Sherene, Zenobia and Indranie (the Respondents)
from distributing the assets of the deceased pending the determination of the appeal, was
discharged.

JUDGMENT

Rajnauth-Lee J (Saunders P and Burgess and Jamadar JJ concurring)

RAJNAUTH-LEE J:

Introduction

[1] This appeal raises important issues in Guyanese contentious probate law. It
explores, among other things, the issues of testamentary capacity, compliance with
the requirements for due execution of a will under the Wills Act 1, and whether the
trial judge ought to have granted probate in solemn form of the copy of the will
tendered into evidence in the circumstances of this case. An overarching issue is

1 Cap 12:02
whether having regard to the evidence presented to the trial judge, the Court of
Appeal should have reversed certain findings of fact made by the trial judge.

[2] The parties to this appeal are the appellant, Sasedai Kumarie Persaud (Sasedai or
Sasedai Persaud) who is the business manager, executor and principal beneficiary
under the will of Yusuf Mongroo (the deceased or Mr Mongroo). She had been
employed in the deceased’s business since 1999. The first and second respondents
are Sherene Mongroo (Sherene or Sherene Mongroo) and Zenobia Rosenberg
(Zenobia or Zenobia Rosenberg), the two daughters of the deceased, who
challenged the will. The third respondent is Indran ie Mulchand  (Indranie or
Indranie Mulchand)  who the trial judge found, was the common law wife of the
deceased, and who also benefitted under the deceased’s will.  At the trial, evidence
was also led from Nyron Dexter Lathuillerie, who cl aimed to be the son of the
deceased, but who did not join Sherene and Zenobia in challenging the will.

[3] Mr Mongroo died on 15 August 2010 at the age of 83 years  at the St Joseph Mercy
Hospital in Georgetown.  He owned and operated a business called the Horseshoe
Racing Service at Lots 6 -7A Commerce and Longden Streets, Georgetown,
Guyana. He also owned a resi dential property at Lot 107 New Garden Street,
Queenstown, Georgetown, Guyana, and was known to have owned assets abroad
including real estate and racehorses in Barbados and a bank account in the Cayman
Islands.

[4] The Last Will and Testament of the deceased disposing of his assets in Guyana  (the
Guyana will) was allegedly executed on 12 August 2010 and was the subject of the
dispute. In the Guyana will, the deceased instructed as follows:

a.     The property at Lots 6 -7A Commerce and Longden Streets,
Georgetown, be devised to Sasedai Persaud, who was also appointed
executor of the deceased’s will;

b.     Sasedai Persaud to assume sole ownership, management and control of
the Horseshoe Racing Service , and the net proceeds of the business be
apportioned: fifty -five percent to Sasedai Persaud , and the remaining
forty five percent to Indranie Mulchand;
c.     The property at 107 New Garden Street, Georgetown be devised to
Indranie Mulchand;

d.     The residue of the deceased’s estate in Guyana be  bequeathed to
Sasedai Persaud and Indranie Mulchand in equal shares.

[5] The children of the deceased , and in particular, his two daughters, Sherene
Mongroo and Zenobia Rosenberg, derived no benefit under the Guyana will. Nyron
Dexter Lathuillerie also received no benefit under that will.

[6] Included in the Record of Appeal before this Court were two other wills, one dated
6 August 2010 disposing of the deceased’s assets situated in the Cayman Islands
(the C ayman Islands will). The other will was executed on 12 August 2010 and
dealt with the deceased’s assets situated in Barbados (the Barbados will).

[7] Proceedings were brought in the High Court by Sherene and Zenobia  against
Sasedai and Indranie contesting the validity of the Guyana will. The trial judge,
George J found that the will of Mr Mongroo was valid and effective, dismissed the
claim, and amended the defence and counterclaim to the effect that probate in
solemn form was granted with respect to the copy of the will presented to the court.
On appeal to the Court of Appeal , the decision of the trial judge was reversed and
the will was held to be invalid and ineffective.

[8] This Court has come to the conclusion that the trial judge was correct to uphold the
validity of the Guyana will and to order that a copy of the Guyana will be admitted
to probate in solemn form.  The consent order granted by this Court on 3 May 2023
whereby it was ordered that Sherene, Zenobia and Indrani e (the Respondents) shall
not distribute the assets of the deceased pending the determination of this appeal is
to be discharged.

The High Court Proceedings

[9] On 12 October 2010 Sherene Mungroo commenced proceedings against Sasedai
Persaud and Indranie Mulchand contesting the validity of the Guyana will on
various grounds which included forgery, non-compliance with the Wills Act,
suspicious circumstances, and undue influence. On 1 April 2011, Sasedai Persaud
filed a defence and counterclaim seeking among other things that the court
pronounce in solemn form for the last will and testament of the deceased dated 12
August 2010. On 18 November 2010, Indranie Mulchand  filed a separate defence
and counterclaim, asserting among other things, that claims made by her in a
separate action, High Court Action No 669 S/A of 2011, under the Family and
Dependants Provision Act,2 were entitled to priority of hearing and adjudication to
the claim herein made by Sherene Mungroo. Further, by order of George J dated 4
February 2013,  Zenobia Rosenberg  was adde d as a plaintiff to the action
commenced by Sherene. She filed a statement of  claim on 30 May  2013, making
similar allegations t o those made by Sherene. Further and consequential pleadings
were filed by the parties in this matter.

[10] In her written judgment delivered on 16 December 2016 , the trial judge expressed
the view that the case turned on the facts and the credibility of the witnesses .
Several witnesses, including the parties to the action, gave evidence before the trial
judge. The trial judge indicat ed at the outset that she accepted that Sherene
Mungroo, Zenobia Rosenberg an d Nyron Dexter L athuillerie were the children of
the deceased, a national of Trinidad and Tobago, but who had lived in Guyana for
many years. The trial judge found as a fact that Sherene, Zenobia and Nyron did not
establish that they enjoyed a close relationship with the deceased. In addition, the
trial judge observed that except for Zenobia there was no evidence that the other
children even knew that the deceased was ill.

[11] The sequence of events leading up to the making of the Guyana will commenced
with i nstructions allegedly given by the deceased to Mr Vidyanand Persaud ,
Attorney-at-Law (Mr Persaud) for its preparation. The trial judge  accepted and
relied heavily on the testimony of Mr Persaud, and of Dr Rohan Jabour (Dr Jabour)
in arriving at  findings of fact concerning the preparation and execution of th e
Guyana will. The findings and reasoning of the trial judge will be considered in

2 Cap 12:24.
further detail in this judgment.

[12] The trial judge found that there was no evidence advanced on behalf of Sherene and
Zenobia that either  Sasedai or Indranie was responsible for or had anything to do
with preparation or execution of the Guyana will. The trial judge concluded that all
the evidence pointed to Sasedai having nothing to do with the Guyana will, except
for taking it to Mr Persaud and then attending Messrs Cameron and Shepherd with
instructions to have the will probated. On the evidence, the trial judge found that
there was no collusion be tween Mr Persaud and either Sasedai or Indranie in
relation to the preparation and/or the execution of the Guyana will.

[13] In the circumstances, the court found that there were no suspicious circumstances
attendant upon the making of the Guyana will and that  there was no evidence of
undue influence on the part of either S asedai or Indranie  in relation to the
preparation or execution of the Guyana will. She further found that the deceased
possessed the requisite testamentary capacity to make the Guyana will, and that the
Guyana will was duly signed by the deceased and duly executed in compliance with
the Wills Act.

The Proceedings before the Court of Appeal

[14] On 10 November 2022, the Court of Appeal delivered its decision in the appeal,
allowing the appeal, and setting aside the orders of the trial judge. Cummings -
Edwards C (Ag) delivered an oral decision. A transcript of that decision was
provided to this Court. There has also been filed with this Court a written judgment
by Cummings -Edwards C dated 22 Novemb er 2022 and a written judgment by
Gregory JA which carries no specific date, but which sets f orth the date of 10
November 2022 as the last date of hearing.  Presumably, Gregory JA delivered her
written judgment on that date. The third appellate judge, Persaud JA, did not
produce a written judgment, but delivered an oral decision. A transcript of his oral
decision was filed with this Court. In his oral decision, Persaud JA stated that
having had the benefit of the opinions of Cummings-Edwards C and Gregory JA, he
fully agreed with their analysis and conclusions. He therefore agreed as  well to
allow the appeal and to set aside the orders of the trial judge.

Judgment of Cummings-Edwards C (Ag)

[15] Cummings-Edwards C identified several issues for determination by  the Court of
Appeal: whether there were circumstances of suspicion attending the preparation
and execution of the Guyana will; whether Mr Mongroo was subject to undue
influence; whether he possessed the requisite testamentary capacity; whether he had
given instructions to make the Guyana will; whether given his medical condition
the contents of the Guyana will had been confirmed by him ; whether the signature
on the Guyana will was that of Mr Mongroo; and whether the Guyana will was
validly executed in accordance with the Wills Act.

[16] Cummings-Edwards C did not agree with the submissions advanced on behalf of
Sherene and Zenobia that there were suspicious circumstances associated with the
making of the Guyana will. She was of the view that  if in fact there were suspicious
circumstances those were rebutted having regard to the evidence l ed at the trial. On
the totality of the facts and circumstances, she therefore agreed with the findings of
the trial judge on this issue.

[17] Further, Cummings -Edwards C observed that Sasedai Persaud had clearly been
trusted by the deceased, and such was particularly evidenced by the fact that she
held blank cheques signed by him. However, although Cummings-Edwards C
viewed this as evidence of some degree of control or influence exert ed by Sasedai
Persaud over the deceased, the Chancellor  was not satisfied tha t that by itself
proved that the deceased was subject to undue influence specifically leading to the
preparation of the will. Cummings-Edwards C noted that whether there was undue
influence was a question of fact and that the burden was on the party seeking to
invalidate the transaction to prove on a balance of probabilities that undue influence
was exerted. She concluded that on the balance of probabilities the issue of undue
influence had not been established by Sherene and Zenobia.
[18] Cummings-Edwards C ex pressed the vie w, however, that on the totality of the
evidence, she did not agree with the findings of the trial judge on the issue of the
capacity of the deceased to make the Guyana will.

Judgment of Gregory JA

[19] In her judgment, Gregory JA identified the specific issues for determination:
whether the evidence before the trial judge supported the finding of testamentary
capacity of the deceased, and due execution of the Guyana wi ll; whether the
evidence pertaining to a copy of the Guyana will was fairly e valuated by the  trial
judge; and whether there should have been a finding of suspicious circumstances
affecting the validity of the Guyana will . Gregory JA did not deal with the issue of
undue influence, presumably on the basis that this issue did not arise for
determination by the Court of Appeal.

[20] On the question of the testamentary capacity of the deceased, Gregory JA found
that the combined testimony of conversations and int eractions involving the
deceased during his hospitalisation at Woodlands Hospital from 20 July 2010 to his
discharge on 1 August 2010 and up to his admission on 9 August 2010 to St
Joseph’s Mercy Hospital, seemed to indicate a sufficiently lucid mental state to
express his wishes for the preparation of a will, this notwithstanding that his
physical condition might have been weak. Additionally, the judge drew support for
the proposition that the deceased had been in a sufficiently lucid state from the fact
that Dr Jabour specifically denied a suggestion that the deceased was in no st ate to
make or sign a will on 12 August 2010.

[21] Further, as to the assertions made on behalf of Sherene that the deceased had never
made a will before the Guyana will, and that the dispositions in the Guyana will
were therefore a significant change, depriving the children of the deceased from
making claims to his estate in Guyana, Gregory JA  observed that there was
insufficient evidence before the trial judge on which the deceased's  sentiments and
intentions regarding his relationships overall, especially wi th his children, could be
assessed. She reasone d: ‘The deceased having been a private person, there was
nothing reliable to support any inference  being drawn as to  testamentary capacity
on the basis of the significant change brought about by the will.’  Gregory JA
therefore concluded that the ground of appeal that the deceased lacked testamentary
capacity to make or sign a will and/or that the finding of testamentary capacity was
against the weight of the evidence must fail.

[22] At [100] of her judgment, Gregor y JA found that  the execution of the Guyana will
by the testator took place in the presence of neither of the attesting witnesses as the
will was taken to Dr Jabour's office as a pre-signed document. The judge went on to
suggest that her reading of authorities wherein wills were invalidated involved wills
having been signed before the attesting witnesses were both present, and that the
will in the present case was similarly defecti ve for non -compliance with the
requirements of s 4 of the Wills Act . The judge was of the vi ew that the testator's
subsequent acknowledgement of his signature to the attesting witnesses did not cure
such a defect.

[23] In all the circumstances, Gregory JA concluded that the presumption of due
execution did not apply, or alternatively, the presumption was displaced by the
formal defect in the manner in which the signature of the testator had been affixed
to the Guyana will, in that no attesting witness was present when he signed.

[24] Gregory JA turned to the question of suspicious circumst ances and expressed the
view that the sequence of events outlined by Mr Persaud about the preparation of
the Guyana will did not lead to the conclusion that the Guyana will was executed in
secrecy.

Judgment of Persaud JA

[25] As mentioned earlier, Persaud JA did not produce a written judgment, but delivered
an oral decision stating that, having had the benefit of the opinions of Cummings -
Edwards C and Gregory JA he fully agreed with t heir analysis and conclusions.
Persaud JA therefore agreed to allow the appea l and to set as ide the orders of the
trial judge.

Appeal before this Court

[26] On 28 February 2023, Sasedai Persaud appealed the decision of the Court of
Appeal.

[27] No cross appeal has been filed by Sherene and Zenobia. Accordingly, the issues
whether there were suspicious circumstances surrounding the making of the
Guyana will, and whether undue influence was exerted on the deceased in the
making of the Guyana will, do not arise for the determination of this Court.

Issues for Determination

[28] The following issues arise for the determination of this Court.

(1) Whether the conflicting  opinions of the Court of Appeal on certain issues
resulted in a defective judgment on those issues that ought to be set aside?

(2) Did the evidence led at the trial support the findings of the trial judge on the
following issues:

(a) whether the deceased possessed the requisite testamentary capacity?

(b) whether the will complied with the requirements of s 4 of the Wills Act
in that the deceased acknowledged his signature in accordance with s 4?

(c)  whether the signature on the Guyana will was that of the deceased  in
compliance with s 4 of the Wills Act, and whether the trial judge ought
to have admitted to probate in solemn form a copy of the Guyana will?

Issue 1 – Whether the Conflicting Opinions of the Court of Appeal on Certain
Issues Resulted in a Defective Judgment on those Issues that Ought to be Set
Aside?

[29] It was submitted on behalf of Sasedai Persaud that Cummings -Edwards C and
Gregory JA made con flicting findings as regard s the issues of the t estamentary
capacity of the deceased and the due execution of the Guyana will, and that Persaud
JA concurred with both appellate judges. Accordingly, it was argued that this
eliminates the issues of testamentary capacity and due execution of the Guyana will
for determination by this Court, and leaves only the issue of compliance with the
Wills Act and the standard of p roof. It was further submitted that the  opinions of
the Court of Appeal on the issues of testamentary capacity and due execution of the
Guyana will were therefore defective and ought to be set aside.

[30] On the issue of testamentary capacity, it was pointed out that Cummings -Edwards
C decided that the evidence adduced failed to prove that Mr Mongroo had the
requisite testamentary capacity at the time of making the Guyana will. Conversely,
Gregory JA concluded that the ground of appeal that the deceased lacked
testamentary capacity was against the weight of the evidence and must fail.  She
therefore found that the deceased had the requisite testamentary capacity.

[31] As to the issue of due execution of the Guyana will, it was submitted that there
were conflicting routes to the conclusions arrived at by Cummings -Edwards C and
Gregory JA. Cummings-Edwards C concluded that there was no evidence that the
deceased acknowledged his signature in the presence of Dr Kumar, or that the
witnesses signed in each other’s presence. She was of the view that the presumption
of due execution was displaced. On the other hand, Gregory JA came to the
conclusion that the wi ll had to be sign ed by the testator in the presence of the
attesting witnesses, and in the absence of this, the subsequent acknowledgement by
the deceased of his signature did not comply with the requirements of the Wills
Act. In effect, both judges agreed that the testator and the attesting witnesses had
not all signed in the presence of each other, but one judge foun d that the testator
had not acknowledged his signature in the joint presence of the attesting witnesses
while the other judge held that the t estator had done so but that this step did not
validate the will.

[32] In its appellate jurisdiction this Court is a superior court of record with such
jurisdiction and powers as are conferred on it by the Agreement Establishing the
Caribbean Court of Justice (the Agreement) or by the Constitution or any other law
of the Contracting Party. 3 By virtue of s 4(1)(b) of the C aribbean Court of Justice
Act (the CCJ Act) 4 the Court shall have appellate jurisdiction provided for in the
CCJ Act as is conferred on it in  accordance with the provisions of Part III of the
Agreement. By vir tue of s 11(6) of the CCJ Act, in relation to any appeal to this
Court, the Court shall have all the jurisdiction and powers possessed in relation to
that case by the Court of Appeal of Guyana. 5 The conjoint effect of the above
provisions and s 7(2) of the Court of Appeal Act6 is that this Court is empowered in
an appeal from Guyana to ensure the determination on the merits of the real
question in controversy between the parties.

[33] Accordingly, where the jurisdiction of this Court has been invoked by the filing of a
notice of appeal, it is  open to this Court to determine all matters it deems material
in resolving the issues before it, and so determine the real question in controversy
in the appeal. In the circumstances, we do not agree tha t the conflicting opinions of
the Court of Appeal resulted in a defective judgment which ought to be set aside for
that reason alone.  We are of the view that this Court’s jurisdiction to  determine
these issues cannot be excluded in this manner.  It is important to highlight,
however, that any confusion concerning the decision of a Court of Appeal in
similar circumstances should  be avoided by the third appellate judge indicating
with clarity the specific opinions with which that third judge was in agreement.

Issues 2 (a) – (c)

[34] Issues 2 (a) – (c) are primarily issues of fact which were de termined by the trial
judge on the evidence led before the court. As this Court observed in Commissioner
of the Guyana Geology and Mines Commission v Diamond Quarry Inc 7 judicial
findings of fact are often based on the evidence given in court and the cogency and
credibility of witnesses who give that evidence. In such a case, an appellate court
will be reluctant to differ from the trial judge who would have had the advantage of
observing and evaluating the witnesses. The Court further noted that in Campbell v
Narine8 this Court approved the view of Sumner LJ in SS Hontestroom (Owners) v
SS Sagaporack (Owners) which emphasised that not having seen the witnesses puts
appellate judges in a permanent position of disadvantage as against the trial judge
and, unless it can be shown that the trial judge failed to use or has palpably misused
their advantage, the higher court ought not to reverse findings of primary facts.

[35] Moreover, in Campbell v Narine 9, this Court endorsed the observations of the
majority of the Canadian Supreme Court in Housen v Nikolaisen:10

The trial judge has sat through the entire case and his ultimate judgment
reflects the total familiarity with the evidence. The insight gained by the trial
judge who has lived with the case for several days, weeks or even months
may be far deeper than that of the Court of Appeal whose view of the case is
much more limited and narrow, often be ing shaped and distorted by the
various orders and rulings being challenged.

[36]  It follows that where the trial jud ge has properly utilise d the distinct advantage of
having seen and heard the witnesses, has adequately evaluated the witnesses, and
weighed the facts and circumstances of the case, an appellate court ought not to
lightly reverse findings of credibility arrived at by the trial judge. Moreover, where
the trial judge has made a fair and reasonable assessment of the evidence before the

which are based on assessments of  the credibility of witnesses, but that it is in as

involve evaluating evidence. 12 We agree. It is also important to note that by virtue
of s 7(1)(b) of the Court of Appeal Act of Guyana 13 the Court of Appeal in civil

(a) Whether the Deceased Possessed the Requisite Testamentary Capacity?

[37] The test for testamentary capacity was laid down in the case of Banks v
Goodfellow14:

For a testator to be capable of making a valid will he must be able to
understand the nature of the act and its effects and the extent of the prope rty
of which he is disposing, and he must be able to comprehend and appreciate
the claims to which he ought to give effect and the manner in which his
property is to be distributed between them.

[38] In Loosley v Powell15 the Court of Appeal of New Zealand noted that the pr inciples
relating to the assessment of testamentary capacity were well -settled by that court
in Woodward v Smith.16 There the court re-stated the principles laid down in Banks
v Goodfellow. We note in particular the following dicta:

...Testamentary capacity does not require a sound and disposing mind and
memory in the highest degree; otherwise, very few could make testaments at
all…Nor must the testator possess such capacity to the same extent as

previously. His mind may have been in some degree weakened, his memory
may have become in some degree enfeebled; and yet there may be enough left
clearly to understand and make a sound assessment of all those things, and all
those circumstances, which enter into the nature of a r ational, fair and just
testament.17

[39] In her text, Non-Contentious Probate Practice in the English-Speaking
Caribbean18, Karen Nunez -Tesheira, notes that animus testandi or testamentary
capacity is a common law principle and has been given statutory force in S aint
Lucia, Barbados, The Bahamas, and in Trinidad and Tobago when the yet -to-be
enacted provision of the proclaimed Succession Act becomes law . Nunez-Tesheira
observes that in order to possess the necessary testamentary capacity, it must be
established t hat (a) the te stator ha d the mental capacity to make the will (b) the
testator knew and approved of the contents of the will (c) the will was that of a free
and capable testator, that is, the testator must have exercised genuine free choice in
the making of the will an d more particularly that the testator did not make the will
as a result of the undue influence or fraud of another. Further, commenting on the
degree of mental capacity, which is required of the testator, Nunez -Tesheira, citing
Banks v Goodfel low, observes that once it can be established that the testator has
sufficient intelligence to understand the testamentary act, this will be adequate even
though the testator’s mental powers are reduced below the ordinary standard.

[40] As mentioned earlier, Gregory JA expressed the view  that the combined evidence
of conversations and interactions involving the deceased during his hospitali sation
at Woodlands Hospital from 20 July 2010 to his discharge on 1 August 2010 and up
to his admission on 9 August 2010 to St Joseph’s Mercy Ho spital, seemed to
indicate a sufficiently lucid mental state to express his wishes  for the preparation of
a will, this notwithstanding that his physical condition m ight have been weak.
Gregory JA also noted that  the judge drew suppor t for the proposition that the
deceased had been in a sufficiently lucid state from the fact that Dr Jabour
specifically denied a suggestion that the deceased was in no state to make or sign a

17 ibid at [19].
18 (2nd edn, The Caribbean Law Publishing Co 2004) 34-35.
will on 12 August 2010.

[41] It has been noted that Cummings -Edwards C did not agree with the trial judge. She
thought that the issue to be determined was whether the deceased had testamentary
capacity to execute the will, assuming that the will was made by him. She relied
heavily on the testimony of  Dr Nehaul Singh (Dr Singh) Head of the Pathology
Department at  the Georgetown Hospital Corporation  in Guyana. Dr Singh had
performed the post -mortem on the deceased . He testified that the deceased was a
severely ailing person and that the mental functions of such a person, esp ecially an
83-year-old with cerebral atrophy, whether ill or not, would be impaired.
Cummings-Edwards C w as of the view that although Dr Singh did not see Mr
Mongroo alive or perform any medical examination on him, the evidence of his
post-mortem findings could not be discounted.

[42] Cummings-Edwards C expressed the view that testamentary capacity at the time
instructions are given for the preparation of the will, and knowledge and approval
of the contents of the will at the time of execution must go hand in  hand. She
observed that if indeed Mr Mongroo had signed the Guyana will when his medical
condition had w orsened (having regard to the evidence of Dr Singh) he may have
been liable ‘to be made the instrument of those around him’.

[43] Cummings-Edwards C relied on the Trinidad and Tobago case of Moonan v
Moonan19 and the judgment of Wooding CJ in the Court of Appeal. Wooding CJ
cited the statement from Halsbury’s Laws 20 that ‘stricter proof of knowledge and
approval is necessary where there was some weakness in the testator, which, though
not amounting to incapacity, renders him liable to be made the instrument of t hose
around him …’ Cummings-Edwards C was of the view that such strict proof was
lacking, and the deceased’s capacity to compre hend the extent of his property and
the claim of others who were excluded from the Guyana will, was not supported by
the medical evidence. Accordingly, on the totality of the evidence, she departed

19 (1963) 7 WIR 420 (TT CA) at 426.
20  Halsbury’s Laws of England (3rd edn, 1962) vol 39, para 1301.
from the finding s of the trial judge on this issue and concluded that Mr Mongroo
did not possess the requ isite testamentary capacity at the time of the making of the
Guyana will.

[44] As to the issue of mental capacity and state of health of the deceased, the trial judge
examined the evidence before her. She accepted the evidence of Mr Persaud, the
Attorney-at-Law, who prepared the Guyana will and who had been the deceased’s
lawyer for about six years. The trial judge found Mr Persaud to be a most credible
witness. Mr Persaud testified that the deceased had given him instructions to
prepare the Guyana will when t he deceased was a patient at the Woodlands
Hospital in Georgetown, towards t he end of July, in the words of the trial judge,
‘long before the said August 12’. The trial judge noted that there was no challenge
to Mr Persaud’s evidence that he met with and received instructions from the
deceased in relation to the preparation of a will.

[45] Additionally, the trial judge accepted the evidence of Mr Persaud that he visited
with the deceased at the St Joseph Mercy Hospital, where the decease d had been
hospitalised, and the deceased was able to correct the draft will that Mr Persaud had
prepared, when the draft was read to him.  The trial judge therefore observed that it
was clear that in correcting Mr Persaud, the deceased’s faculties were intact. The
trial judge also accepted Mr Persaud’s unchallenged evidence that on the 10 or 11
August, when Mr  Persaud visited the deceased at the St Joseph’s Mercy Hospital,
Mr Persaud gave the deceased the final version of two wills . Mr Persaud later
clarified that he had given t he deceased two copies of one will. He  explained to the
deceased what had to be don e to execute them. According to the trial judge, the
further unchallenged evidence of Mr Persaud was that the deceased confirmed to
him that the final version of the will conformed with his instructions and was
correct. In addition, it was the evidence of Mr Persaud that the deceased did not tell
him about any other wil l – whether Cayman Islands or Barbados. According to Mr
Persaud, he was not surprised at this, since he had advised the deceased to get
someone in those places to deal with the property he owned there.

[46] The trial judge also accepted Mr Persaud’s evidence that on his final visit with the
deceased, the deceased got up and sat on a chair next to his hospital bed, while Mr
Persaud sat on a chair in the room. They chatted about cricket and the security
situation in the country. The deceased appeared lucid and in good mental health,
according to Mr Persaud.

[47] The trial judge relied on the testimo ny of Dr Jabour as to the state of mind and
health of the deceased . She found that Dr Jabour was a credible witness, w ho had
known the deceased for more than 40 years. Dr Jabour communicated with the
deceased when the deceased was outside of Guyana, and although the deceased was
not his patient, the deceased would call, and Dr Jabour would go over to his house
to treat him for minor ailments.

[48] Importantly, the trial judge accepted Dr Jabour’s evidence that he received an
envelope containing the wills (Guya na and Barbados) at ab out 2 -3pm on 12
August. Later that afternoon, he went to visit the deceased. The trial judge acc epted
that the deceased confirmed the contents of the will to Dr Jabour. This was done by
Dr Jabour to ensure that the contents of the Guyana will reflected the wishes of the
deceased. In addition, the trial judge accepted the evidence of Dr Jabour that the
deceased was mentally fit, even if physically weak at the time of the execution of
the will. The trial judge noted that Dr Jabour had no thing to gain by givin g this
evidence about the state of health of the deceased, and nothing in this regard was
suggested to him.

[49] In the context of what the trial judge considered to be the highly credible evidence
of both Mr Persaud and Dr Jabour, she considered the testimony of Dr Singh. Dr
Singh's testimony had been to the effect that he had performed a post-mortem
examination on the deceased and that examination revealed that the deceased was a
severely ailing person . He gave the deceased’s cause of d eath as cerebral consu lar
herniation because of cerebral oedema and atrophy. Dr Singh testified that a person,
especially one at 83 years old with cerebral atrophy, whether ill or not, would have
impaired mental functioning. According to Dr Singh , such a person would have
memory problems; he wou ld have confusion, inability to comprehend, language
difficulty and communication problems. Dr Singh advised however, that the
examination of the brain to determine brain disorder dysfunction could only be
done on a live person and the pe rson best placed to diagnose the neurological
system would have been the attending physician , charged with ten ding to the
deceased, while he was alive.

[50] In those circumstances, the trial judge found that Dr Singh’s evidence did ‘not point
to total impairment so as to totally affect the mental and motor skills and
functioning.’ Physical impairment there clearly was, but nothing in the evidence
remotely suggested that this was such as to affect the ability of the deceased to
communicate and to sign the docume nts on 12 August. In addition, the trial judge
noted that the deceased had signed a blood transf usion form on the morning of 12
August. The trial judge t herefore found as a fact that the deceased was alert when
he acknowledged his signature to the doctors.

[51] It is important to highlight that the case of Moonan v Moonan cited by Cummings-
Edwards C was decided on very different facts. In that case, the will was made at a
time, when the testator had less than 24 hours previously undergon e a very serious
operation. He had received some sedation, which the surgeons thought would
debilitate him mentally. The genesis of the will occurred while the testator’s brother
and nephew were with the testator in the hospital where the surgery had been
performed. No one else was  with the testator. His brother and nephew invited a
solicitor to the hospital to make the will. The brother and nephew were named as
two of the four beneficiaries to take the whole of the testator’s estate. The testator’s
wife and child with whom he w as living in the ‘closest amity’ were omitted from
the will. For 19 years between the making of the will and the death of the deceased
the will remained in the possession of the testator’s brother, who was also named as
the sole executor of the will. Throughou t that long period, the wife and child
remained in complete ignorance that the testator had made the will. The solicitor
had never acted as solicitor for the testator and was therefore unaware either of the
extent of the testator’ s estate or of the per sons who might be expected to have a
claim on his bounty. In getting his instructions, he made n o inquiry and was given
no information concerning any of these essential matters. In addition, there was
evidence from Sir Henry Pierre, a well -respected surgeon in  Trinidad and Tobago,
that the testator had told him that for the first few days after the operation in the
hospital, he could not remember anything of what took place.21

[52] Wooding CJ concluded that the circumstances surrounding th e preparation of the
will, the contents of will, and its execution, ‘add up to circumstances which should,
and indeed did, excite suspicion …’ 22 There must therefore be sufficient evidence
which would remove that suspicion. Wooding CJ concluded however that that
suspicion had not been displaced.23

[53] This Court has noted that in this case the trial judge found as a fact that S herene,
Zenobia and Nyron did not establish that they enjoyed a close relationship with the
deceased. The trial judge observed that exce pt for Zenobia there w as no evidence
that the other children even knew that the deceased was ill. The trial judge also
found as a fact that both Sasedai and Indranie had nothing to do with the
preparation or execution of the Guyana will, and there was nothing to suggest that
there was any collusion  between Mr Persaud, the Attorney who prepared the will,
and either Sasedai or Indr anie. Moreover, it was undisputed that neither Mr
Persaud, Dr Jabour, Sasedai nor Indranie knew of the existence of the deceased’s
children. We reiterat e that these are very different circumstances to Moonan. We
therefore do not agree that there ex isted in this case circumstances which ought to
have excited the suspicion of the trial judge or that ‘stricter proof of knowledge and
approval’ by the deceased was necessary.

[54] This Court has come to the conclusion that the evidence before the trial judge, and
in particular, the evidence of Mr Persaud and Dr Jabour, which the trial judge
accepted, provided a sufficient basis on which the tr ial judge arrived at her findings
regarding the testamentary capacity of the deceased. We therefore agree with

21 Moonan (n 19) at 427.
22 ibid.
23 ibid at 429.
Gregory JA and the trial judge that the deceased had the testamentary capacity to
make the Guyana will. We therefore do not believe that, given the evidence before
the trial judge and h er findings of fact, an appellate court should have reversed
these findings.

(b) Whether the Guyana Will Complied with the Requirements of s 4 of the
Wills Act in that the Deceased Acknowledged his Signature in
Accordance with s 4?

[55] Section 4 of the Wills Act provides:

No will made in Guyana shall be valid unless it is in  writing and executed in
manner hereinafter mentioned; that i s to say, it shall be signed at the foot or
end thereof by the testator, or by some other person in his presence and by his
direction, and the signature shall be made or acknowledged  by the testator in
the presence of two or more witnesses  present at the same time, and those
witnesses shall attest and  shall subscribe the will in the pres ence o f the
testator, but no form of attestation shall be necessary.

[56] The trial judge accepted Dr Jabour’s evidence. She observed that Dr Jabour had
testified about the execution of two wills – the Guyana will and a Barbados will.
She found that both wills were executed at the same time. She noted that Dr Jabour
appeared to be unsure whether Dr Kumar, the deceased’s attending physician, had
signed the will in the hospital room in Dr Jabour’s presence and that of the
deceased on 12 August. She found, however, Dr J abour to be a credible  witness,
who could not remembe r exactly w hat occurred at the execution of the will,
because he was more focused on ensuring that the will expressed the deceased’s
wishes. The trial judge noted that Dr Jabour had testified that he and Dr Kumar
were together at the same time when the deceased confirmed that he had signed the
Guyana will. He had also testified that his recollection would have been better in
2011 than in 2014, the date of his testimony  in court. Dr Jabour therefore referred
to a document , the 2011 Barbados affidavit , which he had swor n to in January
2011, as evidence of what actually occurred in August 2010 . He preferred to refer
to that document, rather than rely on his memory. This affidavit was filed in
Barbados to prove due execution of the Barbados will,  but had been tendered into
evidence in this case by Sherene.

[57] In answer to questions from the trial judge, who allowed Dr Jabour to clarify his
evidence, Dr Jabour confirmed that Dr Kumar was at the foot of Mr Mongroo’s bed
in the hospital room when he signed the will; that there was only one place to sign
in the hospital room, the bed table. He signed and then Dr Kumar signed. He noted
that he was 68 years old at the time he was giving evidence and he saw an average
of 30 patients per day . This evidence was presumably led to explain Dr Jabour’s
faulty memory and his reference to what he deposed in the 2011 Barbados affidavit.

[58] In the circumstances of this case, the trial judge applied the presumption of due
execution and held that the Guy ana will had been properly executed in accordance
with the Wills Act.

[59] The Court of Appeal did not agree with the trial judge. Cummings -Edwards C
stated that there was no evidence that the deceased acknowledged his signature in
the presence of Dr  Jabour and Dr Kumar. The presumption of due execution ought
not to be applied in the circumstances of this case. Cummings -Edwards C
especially lamented the absence of Dr Kumar as a witness before the trial judge.
She was of the view that  Dr Kumar should have been c alled if he was available, to
prove due execution.

[60] On the other hand, Gregory JA thought that the will had to be signed by the testator
in the presence of the attesting witnesses, and in the absence of such signing, the
subsequent acknowledgement by the deceased of his signature did not comply with
the requirements of the Wills Act. Gregory JA placed reliance on several authorities
including Re Colling .24 She concluded that her reading of the authorities which
invalidated wills which were signed before the attesting witnesses were both
present, led her to th e view that the Guyana will was similarly defective for non -

24 [1972] WLR 1440.
compliance with s 4 of the Wills Act. She went on to state that subsequent
acknowledgement to the witnesses would not have cured the defect in the
execution. We do not agree. It is clear that s 4 of the Wills Act allows for a will to
be signed by the testator beforehand once  the testator’s signa ture is subsequently
acknowledged by the testator when both witnesses are present.25

[61] The principle omnia praesumuntur rite esse acta 26 or that all things are presumed
to be done rightly, applies where a  will is regular on the face of it, with an
attestation clause and the signatures of the testator and witnesses in their proper
places.27 This presumption of due execution applies where there is a proper
attestation clause, even though the witnesses have no recollection of having
witnessed the  will,28 and even though the attestation clause appears only on the
completed draft of a las t will.29 It may be rebutted b y evidence of the attesting
witnesses or otherwise, but the evidence as to some defect in execution must be
clear, positive and reliable.30

[62] It was argued on behalf of Sherene Mongroo that the presumption cannot be
applied where the attestation clause is clearly contradicted by the evidence in the
case, and does not accurately reflect the way the will was actually executed and
witnessed. Moreover, that the presumption of due execution was displaced where it
was disclosed in evid ence that the testator never signed in the presence of either of
the witnesses, but the attestation clause on the will states otherwise. In Wilson v
Lassman31 the court he ld that where it was known and agreed that the attestation
clause did not ref lect the facts of the execution and attestation , and where due
execution was alleged on another basis , there could be no room for the application
of the presumption. We agree. It is undisputed that the Guyana will was not signed
in the presence of the witnesses, as  stated in the attestation cl ause. The deceased’s

25 See R D’Costa, P Teverson, T Synak, Tristram and Coote’s Probate Practice (31st edn, LexisNexis 2015) para 3.107.
26 See Halsbury’s Laws of England  (5th edn, 2021) vol 103, para 898.
27 Vinnicombe v Butler (1864) 3 Sw & Tr 580; 164 ER 1400 at 1401 (Sir J Wilde).
28 Woodhouse v Balfour (1887) 13 PD 2.
29 Re Webb [1964] 2 All ER 91.
30 Croft v Croft (1865) 4 Sw & Tr 10, 164 ER 1418.
31 [2017] EWHC 85 (Ch).
signature was allegedly acknowledged by the deceased to the witnesses subsequent
to its being signed. The p resumption of  due execution could therefore not be
applied in this case.

[63] But that is not the end of the matter. It is still open to this Court to determine
whether the evidence presented to the trial judge was sufficient to justify the
finding that the Guyana will was acknowledged by the deceased in the presence of
Dr Jabour and Dr Kumar, who signed it  in th e presence of each othe r and the
deceased, and thus established due execution of the Guyana will.

[64] Gregory JA observed that it was within the trial judge’s domain to determine which
version of Dr Jabour’s evidence should be accepted. We agree. In other words, it
was within the domain of the trial judge to accept the evidence of Dr Jabour that
both he and Dr Kumar were present when the deceased acknowledged his signature
on the Guyana will, and that they both signed the will in the presence of each oth er.
We have examined the evid ence set out at [56] and [57]. In addition, we note that
the trial judge had  accepted the evidence of Mr Persaud that he had advised the
deceased to have his doctors witness the Guyana will. Further, we note the trial
judge’s conclusion  that Dr Jabour’s testimony that the deceased confirmed the
contents of the Guyana will was sufficient for a finding that the deceased
acknowledged his signature on the Guyana will.

[65] In all the circumstances of this case, this Court is of the vie w that the trial judge
was entitled to accept the evidence of Dr Jabour (including the evidence contained
in his 2011 Barbados affidavit) on the issue of the execution of the Guyana will.
There was therefore sufficient evidence on which the trial judge could have made
her finding as to the due execution of the Guyana will. Accordingly, the finding of
the trial judge that the deceased acknowledged his signature on the Guyana will in
the presence of both witnesses, who signed in the presence of the deceased a nd of
each other, cannot be f aulted, and ought not to have been reversed. Due execution
of the Guyana will has therefore been established.

(c) Whether the Signature on the Guyana Will was that of the Deceased in
Compliance with s 4 of the Wills Act , and Whether the Trial Judge
Ought to have Admitted to Probate in Solemn Form a Copy of the
Guyana Will?

[66] These two issues, one concerning a finding of fact by the trial judge, and the other,
an exercise of the discretion of the trial judge, can be conveniently dealt w ith
together. Whether t he signature on the Guyana will was that of the deceased is a
further aspect of due execution under s 4 of the  Wills Act. It was also a matter for
the trial judge to decide whether she ought to exercise her discretion to admit to
probate in solemn form a copy of the Guyana will.

[67] The trial judge heard the testimony of Mr Glen Parmesar, a highly experienced
document examiner from Trinidad and Tobago. He was retained by Sherene and
Zenobia to examine the signature on the Guyana will. He  had received a
photocopied will (from Zenobia) which he compared to several known signatures
of the deceased. He concluded that the signature on the  photocopied will was not
written by the person who had written the known signatures. Mr Parmesar agreed
that poor health was a factor that affected writin g habits in that control might show
some variability. He expressed the opinion however that the structural differences
that he saw suggested ‘somebody else[’s] writing rather than due to poor health’.

[68] In cross-examination, it was revealed that Mr Parmesar did not know the medical
conditions of the deceased that had been outlined in the evidence given by Dr
Singh, but he had been told that the deceased was in poor health. He agreed that
depending on the circumstan ces, damage to the brain cells would affect the motor
control of the writer. He stated that a lack of motor control was capable of creating
structural changes to handwriting. He indicated that his finding that the handwriting
on the will was less fluid and less firm than that in the known signatures could have
been the result of damage or disease of the brain. In addition, Mr Parmesar stated
that had he been aware of the circumstances of motor functions as indicated to him
in cross -examination, he would hav e requested more specimens closer in time to
the time when the questioned signature was written and which would have reflected
the person’s medical condition.

[69] Further, and also in cross -examination, Mr Parmesar agreed that the copy of the
will that h e had originally receiv ed from Zenobia was a poor copy. There were
parts of the signature that were not properly produced.

[70] As regards the blood transfusion form which had been signed by the deceased on
the morning of 12 August, Mr Parmesar was of the view that there were some
similarities but there was less writing control and ability in the blood transfusion
form. He explained that the line quality was less firm an d showed less control and
some of the letters were not uniformly formed. He noted that ‘bas ed on just
observations of the two signatures, assuming the same authorship, the will would
reflect a better writing quality or state of health than the blood transfusion
document’.

[71] Further, Mr Parmesar testified that he examined what purported to be an original
will of the deceased when he arrived in Guyana. That will was sourced from
Sasedai’s lawyer.  Mr Parmesar tendered that will into evidence. It was marked
GP3 (a) and (b). On examination of the document with a handheld microscope, Mr
Parmesar indica ted that the signatures  of the testator and the witnesses on the
second page appeared not to be original ink signatures. They appeared to be printed
versions of the signatures, and more likely a colour photocopy or a laser copy of the
original ink signatures. He saw what appeared to be dot -like patterns and not the
written lines of a pen.

[72] On the other hand, Mr Troy Whittaker, Inspector of Police and handwriting
examiner attached to the Guyana Police Force, testified on behalf of Sasedai. He
had received a request to examine several documents through the requisite channels
of the Guyana Police Force. He examined copies of the Guyana will, as well as
original letters and cheques tendered by Sasedai. Mr Whittaker was subsequently
given other documents which included the blood transfusion form and an
identification card. He said that from his ex amination of the blood transfusion form
(which he was seeing for the first tim e in court) he formed the opinion that the
person who wrote it was maybe ill or aged in tha t they did not have tho rough
control over the pen. He also said that the writing surface had to be factored in. He
concluded that taking into consideration that signatures are not identical and
factoring in illness, age and the writing surface, the person who signed the cheques
and the identification card (that was also examined by Mr Parmes ar) was one and
the same person who signed the Guyana will.

[73] The trial judge noted that while in court, Mr Whittaker, with the aid of a
magnifying glass, reviewed the s ignatures of the witnes ses to the will, and
signatures on other documents including the signatures on the deceased’s death
certificate, and stated that he saw a rainbow or spectrum of colours around the
signatures. He was of the view that this was caused by the use of the magnifying
glass as a feature of magnification and not as a feature of the handwriting itself.
The trial judge noted in this regard that the instrum ent used by Mr Whittaker was
not as high powered as the instrument used by Mr Parmesar.

[74] The trial judge remarked that a number of issues led her to the conclusion that she
could not accept Mr Parmesar’s evidence. She took into account her earlier findings
as regards the preparation and execution of the Guyana will. In addition, she noted
that Mr Parmesar had used a poor copy of the will which he had obtained from
Zenobia to determine whether the signature was forged. The trial judge observed
that the copy of the will used by Mr Parmesar to arrive at his conclusion s showed
that parts of the sig nature w ere missing. The trial judge also remarked that Mr
Parmesar had stated in his report that:

limitations were encountered in this examination due to the unavailability of
the original [will] … and the quality of the photocopy as well as to the lack of
additional specimen signatures  … The availability of the original [will] for
examination and the provision of additional contemporaneous specimen
signatures, if possible , should allow for a more conclusive forensic
handwriting determination to be made.

We note that there was no ev idence before the trial judge that this more conclusive
forensic examination had been carried out.

[75] Cummings-Edwards C did not agree with the trial judge. She was of the view that
on the totality of the evidence, and especially given the fact that only a copy of the
will was tendered into evidence, and the absence of the original will was not
properly accounted for, there was much merit in the ground of appeal that the
signature on the Guyana will was not that of the deceased.

[76] On the other hand, Gregory J A observed that the handwriting experts did not agree
on whether the signature on the Guyana will wa s that of the deceased. She
expressed the view that it was within the domain of the trial judge to find whether
the deceased had signed both the Guyana will and the blood transfusion form.

[77] We have come to the conclusion that the trial judge was correct to find that the
signature on the Guyana will was that of the deceased. The trial judge accepted Mr
Parmesar’s evidence that the  will tendered into evidence  was a copy. The trial
judge rejected Sasedai’s evidence that someone broke into her home, stole the
envelope in which the original wills were kept, and then returned to her the
envelope with copied documents. Nevertheless, she concluded that, given the chain
of evidence regarding the custod y of the document, the document produced to the
court represented the will of the deceased.

[78] In addition, the trial judge accepted submissions advanced on behalf of Sasedai that
it would be p assing strange for someone t o colour copy a forged signature, moreso
in circumstances where there is no evidence that the signat ures of the witnesses
were forged. Dr Jabour’s unchallenged evidence was that his signature was on the
Guyana will. The trial judge observed that Sherene and Zenobia had produced no
evidence to suggest that either Sasedai or Indranie copied or colour copied or
caused anyone, whether Mr  Persaud, Dr Jabour or anyone else to copy or colour
copy the will or the signatures on the Guyana will.

[79] Even more importantl y, the trial judge was of the view  that the facts and
circumstances surrounding the signing and execution of the Guyana will as found
by her, nullified Mr Parmesar’s evidence which was centred on the premise that the
deceased signed the will on 12 August when it is alleged that he was not in a
position to do so. It followed that, according to that premise, someone else must
have signed the will. This the trial judge rejected.

[80] It must be noted that the trial judge had accepted th e evidence of Mr Persaud tha t
the deceased was given the will on 10 or 11 August. She also accepted  Dr Jabour’s
evidence that he saw the signed will at about 2 -3 pm on 12 August. Having regard
to this, the trial judge drew a strong inference that the deceased had signed the will
before the witnesses would have signed it. On the totality of the evidence,
therefore, the trial judge preferred Mr Whittaker’s evidence which supported the
evidence already give n to the court and accepted by the trial judge. She w as
therefore satisfied that the signature on the Guyana will was that of the deceased.

[81] As to the copy of the will that was tendered into evidence, the trial judge found that
the will presented to the court was a copy. She noted that there appeared to be a
‘mix up’ on the part of Sasedai and her lawyers as to whether what was produced in
court was an original will. As mentioned before, the trial judge regarded as not
credible Sasedai’s evidence that the original wills were stolen, and copies returned
to her. The trial judge did not t hink however that this affected Sasedai’s credibility
on the main issues raised for the determination of the court. In those circumstances,
she reviewed her decision given earlier in a separate ruling not to allow a copy of
the will to be probated. She ordered that the will tendered through Mr Parmesar and
marked GP 3 (a) and (b) be admitted to probate in solemn form. We believe that the
trial judge was seeking to do justice in this case. In our view, the exercise of the
discretion of th e trial judge to adm it to probate in solemn form a copy of the
Guyana will, cannot be faulted.

Disposal

[82] For all the foregoing reasons, it is hereby ordered as follows:
(1) This appeal is allowed.

(2) The decision of the Court of Appeal is hereby set aside and the judgment of
George J in the High Court dated 16 December 2016 is hereby restored.

(3) The consent order granted by this Court on 3 May 2023 whereby it was
ordered that Sherene  Mungroo, Zenobia Rosenberg and Indrani e Mulchand
(the Respondents) sh all not distribute the assets  of the deceased pending the
determination of this appeal is hereby discharged with no order as to costs.

(4) The First and Second Respondents shall pay to the Appellant and the Third
Respondent the following costs:

(a) costs of this appeal calculated in accordance with Rule 17.15(3)(b) of
the Caribbean Court of Justice (Appellate Jurisdiction) Rules 2021;

(b) costs in the Court of Appeal to be assessed; and

(c) costs in the High Court as ordered by George J.

(5) There shall be no order as to costs against the Third Respondent.

/s/ A Saunders
