items.full_text:
[2024] CCJ 7 (AJ) GY

IN THE CARIBBEAN COURT OF JUSTICE
APPELLATE JURISDICTION

ON APPEAL FROM THE COURT OF APPEAL OF
THE CO-OPERATIVE REPUBLIC OF GUYANA

CCJ Appeal No GYCV2023/002
GY Civil Appeal No 101 of 2017

BETWEEN

MAURICE ARJOON                APPELLANT

AND

THE NEW BUILDING SOCIETY LTD
TRUST COMPANY (GUYANA) LTD
EXECUTOR OF THE ESTATE OF
AHMAD KHAN, DECEASED
SEEPAUL NARINE
NIZAM MOHAMED           RESPONDENTS

Before:   Mr Justice Saunders, President
Mme Justice Rajnauth-Lee
Mr Justice Barrow
Mr Justice Burgess
Mr Justice Jamadar

Date of Reasons:  19 March 2024

Appearances

Mr Edward A Luckhoo SC with Mr C V Satram, Mr Ron Motilal and Ms Eleanor
Luckhoo for the Appellant

Mr Stephen Fraser SC with Mr Teni Housty and Ms Shantel Scott-Lall for the
Respondents

Employment law – Breach of employment contract – Wrongful dismissal – Good faith
obligation in employment relationships – Implied obligation of trust and confidence in
employment relationships – Whether particular instances of wrongful dismissal can be
deemed involuntary retirement – Award of pension contributions as relief for wrongful
dismissal – Award of pension benefits as relief for wrongful dismissal – Pension as
deferred wages for service already rendered to an employer – Whether severance benefits
can be awarded in addition to pension benefits as relief for wrongful dismissal – Exemplary
damages – Termination of Employment and Severance Pay Act, Cap 96:01

SUMMARY

On 14 August 2007, the First Respondent terminated the Appellant ’s employment as
company Director/Secretary/CEO on the ground of ‘serious misconduct’. Pursuant to the
First Respondent’s Pension Scheme Rules, the Appellant was due to retire six months later,
on 24 February 2008, at age 60 and had applied for early retirement on 12 June 2007. The
circumstances surrounding the Appellant ’s dismissal concerned withdrawal of
approximately GYD70 million  from a member’s account at the First Respondent, by an
individual using a fraudulent Power of Attorney.

While employed with the First Respondent from 1 December 1979 to 13 August 2007,
pension contributions were made by the Appellant and on his behalf by the First
Respondent. In the letter of dismissal dated 14 August 2007, the First Respondent advised
the Appellant that a refund of his contributions to the Pension Scheme based on its rules
would be settled by the Trustees  after his indebtedness to the First Respondent had been
determined.

The Appellant initiated proceedings before the High Court, asserting that he had been
wrongfully dismissed , and seeking inter alia  full pension benefits and termination and
severance benefits under the Termination of Employment and Severance Pay Act , Cap
96:01 (‘TESPA’).

Reynolds J in the High Court ruled that the Appellant had been ‘wrongfully and unlawfully
dismissed’ by the First Respondent by its letter dated 14 August 2007.  The trial judge
awarded the Appellant payment in lieu of notice  of GYD4,144,797, severance benefits
amounting to  GYD16,104,723, and  pension benefits amounting to  GYD59,033,281,
calculated up to 30 June 2017 , and from 1 July 2017 a monthly pension of GYD372,498
to continue until the death of the Appellant. Reynolds J also awarded interest and costs to
the Appellant.

On appeal, the Court of Appeal agreed with the trial judge’s finding that the Appellant had
been wrongfully dismissed. The court however reversed the trial judge’s award of full
pension benefits to the Appellant. The Court of Appeal was of the view that having regard
to the fact that the Appellant’s employment had ceased, ‘no further pension contribution or
pension rights are in place’. The Court of Appeal however noted that the evidence was that
the Appellant ’s pension contributions amounted to  GYD6,287,872, and the First
Respondent’s pension contributions amounted to  GYD12,529,560. The Court of Appeal
therefore ordered that the  Appellant was entitled to receive the total sum of the pooled
contributions amounting to GYD18,817,432.

By Notice of Appeal filed on 11 April 2023, the Appellant appealed the decision of the
Court of Appeal . The Respondents filed a notice of cross -appeal (amended on 20 June
2023). This Court heard the appeal and the cross-appeal on 10 October 2023, and by order
dated 23 October 2023, the Court allowed the Appellant’s appeal and dismissed the cross-
appeal with reasons to follow. The Court also reversed the decision of the Court of Appeal
that the Appellant was not entitled to full pension benefits. The Court restored the judgment
and order of Reynolds J, save that a decision on the issue of the Appellant’s entitlement to
severance pay was reserved. Further, the Court ordered that  the First Respondent pay to
the Appellant the additional sum of GYD1,602,459 as leave pay and passage assistance for
the years 2006 and 2007, and standard costs.

The Court now delivers its reasons in support of its order made on 23 October 2023, and
its decision on the issue of severance. The Judges are agreed that the Appellant ha s been
wrongfully dismissed, and that the Appellant is entitled to full pension benefits as ordered
by Reynolds J.  On the issue of the Appellant’s entitlement to severance payment under
TESPA, the Court is divided 3-2. Barrow J has written for the majority and Saunders P and
Jamadar J concur.

Barrow J asserted that as a matter of law in Guyana and for the purposes of an award of
pension benefits, resign ation may in particular circumstances be regarded as retirement.
He reasoned that it may therefore legitimately be said that what took place with the
Appellant was that he involuntarily retired, or in other words, that he was required to retire
in line with the First Respondent’s Pension Scheme Rules allowing for entitlement to
pension. Having concluded that the Appellant was to be deemed as having retired, and that
he did so in line with the Pension Scheme Rules providing for entitl ement to pension,
Barrow J explained that it remained only to determine the pension that would be paid in a
normal case of retirement before the scheduled retirement date. Given that the calculation
of pension entitlement which was done in the High Court was not disputed  before this
Court, the award was upheld by Barrow J.

Barrow J turned to the question of the Appellant’s entitlement to receive severance pay in
addition to pension benefits. According to Barrow J, in view of the conclusion reached by
the Court that pension is to be paid to the Appellant as if retired, the Appellant’s argument
that severance pay should be paid because he was terminated and was thus unable to retire,
cannot succeed. Barrow J explained that were such an argument to succeed, the Appellant
would be getting exactly what the statute creating this be nefit of severance pay intended
that he should not, that is, both severance pay and pension.

In separate opinions , Saunders P and Jamadar J agreed with the conclusion of Barrow J
that where the Appellant is deemed to have retired, and entitled to pension benefits on this
basis, he cannot also be entitled  to severance pay under TESPA. Jamadar J  further
expressed the view that the Appellant was entitled, from the record and in the exceptional
circumstances of this case, to a consideration of additional heads of damage, including (i)
compensation and/or damages payable and/or other relief under s 20 of TESPA, and/or (ii)
exemplary damages.

Rajnauth-Lee and Burgess JJ concurred with the majority save on the issue of  the
Appellant’s entitlement to severance pay. The y agreed that the Appellant was entitled to
receive pension benefits, but their reasoning differed  from the majority. According to
Rajnauth-Lee and Burgess JJ , under s 3(2) of TESPA , accrued or earned pension  is
protected to the extent it is a ‘higher standard of benefit’ contained in an employment
agreement. They considered that the Appellant’s pension rights were a higher standard of
benefit to which he was entitled by virtue of his contract of employment with the First
Respondent. Accordingly, they concluded that the Appellant’s pension benefit s were
accrued or earned wages and he was entitled to full pension rights under the First
Respondent’s Pension Scheme and the Rules.

In relation to severance, Rajnauth-Lee and Burgess JJ were of the view that the Appellant
was wrongfully dismissed as distinct from ‘being retired’, and that a severance allowance
was a separate and distinct entitlement to pension benefits. Given what they considered the
policy behind s 21(1) of TESPA as to the payment of severance, they thought it  strange
that the legislature would have intended to take away an employee’s accrued compensation
for doing service over the years, that is, his severance payment, in circumstances where the
employee had been wrongfully dismissed , on the sole ground that he was entitled to a
pension. They therefore concluded that there was nothing in s 21(4)  (d) of TESPA which
precluded the Appellant receiving his full severance entitlement under TESPA, as well as
his accrued pension benefits under his contract of employment.

Cases referred to:

A v Bottrill [2003] 1 AC 449;  Addis v Gramophone Co Ltd [1908-1910] All ER Rep 1;  A-
G v Blake  [2001] 1 AC 268;  Air Jamaica Ltd v Charlton  (1999) 54 WIR 359;  Apsara
Restaurants (Barbados) Ltd v Guardian General Insurance Ltd [2024] CCJ 3 (AJ) BB;
Banking, Insurance and General Workers Union v PriceSmart Trinidad Ltd  TT 2008 IC
43 (CARILAW), (17 March 2008);  Barrow v A -G of Saint  Lucia  LC 2014 CA 6
(CARILAW), (27 October 2014);  Blyth v Scottish Liberal Club  [1983] IRLR 245;  Burn
v Alder Hey Children’s NHS Foundation Trust [2022] IRLR 306;  Chefette Restaurants
Ltd v Harris [2020] CCJ 6 (AJ) (BB), (2020) 98 WIR 79;  Christofidou v House of Fraser
(2015) UKEAT/0083/15;  Commissioner of Police v Alleyne [2022] CCJ 2 (AJ) BB, [2022]
2 LRC 590;  Courage Group’s Pension Schemes, Re  [1987] 1 WLR 495;  Guyana Sugar
Corp Inc v Dhanessar [2015] CCJ 4 (AJ) (GY), GY 2015 CCJ 1 (CARILAW);  Imperial
Group Pension  Trust Ltd v Imperial Tobacco Ltd [1991] 1 WLR 589;  Investors
Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896;  Jarvis
v Swans Tours Ltd [1973] 1 All ER 71;  King v University Court of the University of St
Andrews [2002] IRLR 252;  London Export Corp v Jubilee Coffee Roasting Co [1958] 2 All
ER 411;  Macari v Celtic Football and Athletic Co Ltd  [1999] IRLR 787;  Mihlenstedt v
Barclays Bank International Ltd [1989] IRLR 522;  OO v BK [2023] CCJ 10 (AJ) BB;
Paragon Properties Ltd v Magna Envestments Ltd [1972] 24 DLR (3d) 156;  Parry v
Cleaver [1970] AC 1;  Persaud v  Mongroo [2023] CCJ 16 (AJ) GY;  Republic Bank Ltd
v Tri-Star Caribbean Inc TT 2020 CA 50 (CARILAW), (9 September 2020);  Rookes v
Barnard [1964] 1 All ER 367;  Rubel Bronze and Metal Co Ltd, Re  [1918] 1 KB 315;
Sandy Lane Hotel Co Ltd v Cato [2022] CCJ 8 (AJ) (BB), BB 2022 CCJ 2 (CARILAW);
Shove v Downs Surgical plc [1984] ICR 532;  Stevens v Bell [2002] All ER [D] 301 (May);
Torres v Point Lisas Industrial Port Development Corp Ltd (2007) 74 WIR 431;  Trust Co
(Guyana) Ltd v Guyana Securities Council [2021] CCJ 11 (AJ) GY, (2021) 99  WIR 422;
Vorvis v Insurance Corp of British Columbia [1989] 1 SCR 1085;  Whiten v Pilot Insurance
Co [2002] 1 SCR 595.

Legislation referred to:

Guyana –  High Court Act, Cap. 3:02,  Insurance Act, Cap 91:02,  Law Reform
(Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, Cap 6:02,  Securities Industry Act Cap 73:04,  Supreme
Court of Guyana Civil Procedure Rules 2016,  Termination of Employment and Severance
Pay Act, Cap 96:01.

Treaties and International Materials referred to:

Agreement Establishing the Caribbean Court of Justice (adopted 14 February 2001, entered
into force 23 July 2002) 2255 UNTS 319.

Other Sources referred to:

Corthésy N and Harris -Roper C-A, Commonwealth Caribbean Employment and Labour
Law (Routledge 2014) ;  Cumberbatch J, ‘The Termination of Employment Statutory
Reform in Guyana’ (1999) 1 Guy L R 79;  Guest A G (ed), Chitty on Contracts (25th edn,
Sweet & Maxwell 1983);  Holzmann R and others, ‘Severance Pay Programs Around the
World: History, Rationale, Status and Reforms’ (Institute of Labor Economics Discussion
Paper No 5731, May 2011) 54.
Lepaulle P, ‘The Function of Comparative Law’ (1921-1922) 35(7) Harv L R 838;  Pollard
D, Employment Law and Pensions (2nd edn, Bloomsbury Publishing 2023).

REASONS FOR DECISION

Barrow J

Saunders P (concurring)

Jamadar J (concurring)

Rajnauth-Lee and Burgess JJ (concurring, except on the issue of the Appellant’s
entitlement to severance pay)

BARROW J:

[1] The Judgment of this Court was delivered on 23 October 2023 allowing th e
appeal and dismissing the cross-appeal in the termination of employment dispute
which gave rise to these proceedings , with reasons to follow. The judgment
reversed, in part, the decision of the Court of Appeal that Mr Maurice Arjoon, the
Appellant, was not entitled to pension benefits; it restored the Judgment and
Order of Reynolds J delivered on 20 July 2017 awarding pension benefits save
that it reserved decision on the issue of entitlement to severance  payment; and
ordered the First named Respondent to pay to the Appellant an additional sum for
leave pay and passage assistance for two years. The Respondent was ordered to
pay standard costs.

[2] These are the promised reasons and the decision on the issue of the entitlement to
severance pay that was reserved.

The Parties and the Legal Dispute

[3] The Appellant was elevated to the position of Director Secretary/CEO at the New
Building Society  (‘NBS’), the First Respondent, after some 24 years of
employment. H is written contract of employment provided for mandatory
pension contributions and for summary dismissal in circumstances of ‘gross
misconduct’. The First Respondent carried on business as a savings and mortgage
institution. The other Respondents, stated to be represented by the same
attorneys-at-law as the First Respondent, took no apparent part in the
proceedings, they are variously : Trust Company (Guyana) Ltd, Executor of the
Estate of Ahmad Khan, Seepaul Narine and Nizam Mohamed.

[4] On 14 August 2007, the First Respondent terminated the Appellant’s employment
on the ground of ‘serious misconduct’. The Appellant was due to retire six months
later, on 24 February 2008, at age 60 and had applied for early retirement on 12
June 2007. The circumstances surrounding the Appellant’s dismissal concerned
the withdrawal from a member’s account at the New Building Society of
approximately GYD70 million, using a fraudulent Power of Attorney.

[5] While employed with the First Respondent from 1 December 1979 to 13 August
2007, pension contributions were made by the Appellant and on his behalf by the
employer. In the letter of dismissal of 14 August 2007 sent by the First
Respondent to the Appellant, he was advised that a refund would be issued in
respect of pension contributions pooled over the course of his employment.
According to New Building Society, this sum amounted to GYD18,817,432, less
any indebtedness. The letter of dismissal stated:

As you are aware unauthorised withdrawals took place from Account No.
… amounting to the loss of funds to the Society in excess of  $69M, due
to fraud, dereliction of duty, negligence and/or serious misconduct.

Following investigations on the part of the Society and procedures in
which you decided not to personally participate, the Society's Board has
taken a decision to summarily dismiss you as Director/Secretary of the
Society with immediate effect for serious misconduct.

[6] The Appellant commenced proceedings before the High Court by Statement of
Claim dated 16 July 2010 and this Cour t, while not  repeating its many earlier
deprecations of judicial and systemic delays , must once again regret that the
parties and especially the Claimant have had to suffer the hardship and injustice
of having to wait so long for a final determination of this claim. It is important
that the courts do not become  resigned to accepting delay as the norm  and
something simply beyond our power to avoid. The Claimant sought the following
reliefs: (a) One Month’s pay in lieu of notice to terminate employment; (b)
Outstanding Leave Pay and Passage Allowance; (c) Loss of Earnings (salary) for
breach of contract; (d) Loss of Earnings (allowances) for breach of contract; (e)
Full pension benefits (accrued and continuing pension); and  (f) Severance
benefits under the Termination of Employment and Severance Pay Act 1 (‘TESP
Act’).

Finding of No Fault

[7] It was never alleged by NBS in these proceedings that the Appellant was
complicit in the withdrawal and both lower courts were clear that the Appellant
was not to be faulted , simply because he bore ul timate management
responsibility, for the deficienc ies in th e system , of which  the directors were
aware, that allowed the fraud to be perpetrated , if indeed there was fraud.  That
notwithstanding, the submissions to this Court for the Respondents still attempted
to throw some shade on the Appellant. The High Court found, and was upheld on
appeal, that there was not just and probable cause for summary dismissal of the
Appellant.

The Reliefs in the High Court and Court of Appeal

[8] Accordingly, the High Court ruled that the Appellant had been ‘wrongfully and
unlawfully dismissed’ by the New Building Society  by its letter of 14 August
20072.  The court awarded the Appellant severance benefits under TESP  Act,
three months’ payment in lieu of notice and pension benefits to which the
Appellant was entitled , calculated up to 30 June 2017 and thereafter at
GYD372,498 per month to continue until the death of the Appellant , as well as
interest under the Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act , Cap 6:02. The
trial judge disallowed the claim for loss of earnings, loss of allowances, leave pay

1 Cap 96:01.
2 Record, 898.
and passage allowances due to the Appellant as well as general damages for
breach of contract.

[9] In making the award of severance payment under TESP Act, the court noted that
under s 3(2) of the Act, provision is made for circumstances where a party has an
entitlement under the Act and also under the terms of his contract of employment.
The court explained that a party effectively has the option whether to ground his
claim for severance on the Act or to rely on the terms of his contract of
employment, and decided that based on the Appellant’s pleadings, he had claimed
under the Act. As indicated, the High Court held that the Claimant was entitled to
be paid pension benefits as prescribed by the terms of his contract of
employment.3

[10] The court dismissed the Respondents’ counter claim because it found that the First
Respondent had failed to prove that there were losses attributable to the action or
inaction of the Appellant.

[11] On appeal by NBS to the Court of Appeal , that court  reversed the trial judge’s
award of pension benefits and found that the Appellant was limited to receiving
pension contributions in the sum of GYD18,817,432. The court decided that ‘…
his employment having ceased, no further pension contributions or pension rights
are in place ’.4 The court, therefore, allowed in part the appeal of NBS , as to
pension; it dismissed the other parts of their appeal, including the appeal against
the decision of the trial judge that the Appellant had been wrongfully dismissed.

The Appeal and the Cross-Appeal

[12] The Appellant appealed to th is Court and NBS cross -appealed. The substantial
challenge of the Appellant to the decision of the Court of Appeal was to the
finding of the Court of Appeal that notwithstanding that the Appellant was

3 ibid, 901.
4 At [69].
wrongfully dismissed, the result of the dismissal was that his employment having
ceased, even though wrongfully , he was not to be awarded accrued pension
benefits.

[13] The cross-appeal by NBS was that the Court of Appeal erred in law and in fact in
failing to hold that the Appellant was properly dismissed  and in holding that the
Appellant was entitled to pension payment over and above the sum of his
contributions. To be clear, the First Respondent claimed that the Appellant was
not entitled to the contributions made by the employer; he was entitled only to
those contributions he made.  This was a departure from the statement as to the
amount to which the Appellant was entitled  that was made by the First
Respondent in the letter of dismissal.

The Dismissal

[14] The Court directed that the cross-appeal be heard first, and it became pellucid that
the case for NBS, as could be gathered on a closer reading of the letter of dismissal
(at [5] above), was that the serious misconduct of the Appellant that led to his
dismissal was his refusal to attend a disciplinary hearing by the board of directors.

[15] Counsel for the respondents offered his full view of the  background with
supporting argument in tracing ‘the path to dismissal’, beginning, of course, with
the loss suffered by the First Respondent from the withdrawal. The submissions
could not resist  including the now -wholly irrelevant  information that the
Appellant had been  criminally charged with conspiracy to defraud , but the
submissions managed to resist stating that the case was dismissed on a no case
submission. The relevant parts of the submissions beg an with the assertion that
despite there being no obligation under a contract of employment to afford an
employee a hearing prior to dismissal, the First Respondent thought it prudent to
offer the Appellant an opportunity to be heard before making any decision on
disciplining or dismissing him.

[16] The submissions  stated that by letter dated 12 June 2007  the Appellant was
interdicted from duty without pay or benefits and requested to attend a meeting
fixed for Friday , 15 June 2007 to explain why serious disciplinary action,
including dismissal, should not be taken against him for failing to observe the
rules and policies of the Society , and gross negligence resulting in loss of a
member's funds.

Refusal to Attend

[17] As counsel characterised it, t he Appellant made a pre -emptive strike  at the
meeting and the interdiction  by filing on the day immediately preceding the
meeting an ex  parte application for an interim injunction restraining the First
Respondent from interdicting him without pay and benefits and from proceeding
with the hearing proposed for the following day. Counsel submitted, ‘this was the
Appellant's first and most combative challenge to the authority of the Board and
to the First Respondent. By filing the action, the Appellant violated almost every
covenant contained in the contract of employment. Although no injunction order
was issued, the Appellant did not appear as requested at the scheduled meeting of
the Board of 15 June 2007.

[18] When it was clear that no interim injunction was granted, ‘the First Respondent
once again, gratuitously, offered the Appellant an opportunity to be heard’.  On 3
August 2007 the First Respondent wrote the Appellant inviting him to a hearing
fixed for 8 August, again to explain why serious disciplinary action including
dismissal should not be taken against him. The Appellant did not respond.
Instead, he had his lawyer write asking that the Board reconsider its decision to
proceed with the proposed hearing . In a further letter, counsel for the Appellant
stated that he was ‘coerced into the ignominious position of advising my client
not to accept your invitation to attend the proposed meeting ’ and indicated that
the Appellant would appear by Counsel.

[19] The Appellant did not attend the meeting. The submissions contended that ‘by
refusing to attend the Board meeting and participate in the Board's process for a
second time once again in violation of almost every tenet of … the aforesaid
employment contract, the Appellant had once again repudiated the said contract
of employment. Acting on legal advice is no excuse.’

[20] The submissions continue: ‘But the Appellant went yet a step further. He sent his
lawyer to attend the hearing in his stead, to answer the issues raised by the Board.
… A characterisation of the Appellant's conduct could be expressed in the
following terms, "Don't talk to me, talk to my lawyer". This is the pinnacle of
insubordination. It does not help, that it appears that the Board had received at
least three investigative reports, none flattering of the Appellant.’

Fundamental Breach of Contract

[21] Counsel submitted that ‘by refusing to attend to his place of work to respond  to
questions which may or may not lead to his reinstatement , [the Appellant] acted
in a manner inconsistent with his duty  to the First Respondent’ . Mr Fraser SC
submitted, ‘… this single act of defiance was a fundamental breach of contract’.
He relied on the decision in the not-eponymous case of Christofidou v House of
Fraser5 for the proposition that the failure of the employee in that case , a store
attendant, to attend a meeting that was investigating the theft  from the premises
of the employer of items that the employer sold, and which were being offered on
the internet for sale from the address of the employee, was misconduct sufficient
to warrant termination of the employment.

[22] The stark distinction in the facts of the two cases makes the case cited more telling
as authority against rather than in favour of the First Respondent. In that case, an
investigation was on foot, and it had been established that items apparently stolen
from the employer were being offered for sale on an eBay account , from an

5 (2015) UKEAT/0083/15.
address that was the employee’s address. This situation clearly led to an inference
against the employee of dishonesty. To persuade the employer of her innocence,
the employee had told the investigation that her former husband had established
the account and used her address without her knowledge . But the employee had
refused to provide contact information for the former husband  (which she had),
failed to adduce evidence from the former husband (with whom she was in
contact), and failed to attend a second meeting of the investigating  tribunal. In
those circumstances, the Employment Appeal Tribunal held, the employer was
reasonable to conclude that trust and confidence was undermined , and as that
went to the heart of the contract of employment, it would be perverse to find other
than that the employer was justified in terminating the contract summarily.

[23] In the instant case, the hearing to which the Appellant was being invited was no
investigation; th e necessary investigation had been completed by the internal
auditor who absolved the Appellant of any misconduct or negligence and the First
Respondent had expressed full confidence in the Appellant. In what Mr Luckhoo
SC, counsel for the Appellant, described as inexplicable, in defiance of logic, and
a volte-face the first respondent required the Appellant to appear before its Board
of Directors to answer unparticularised allegations and be present for its
determination of why serious disciplinary action including dismissal should not
be taken against him.

Lawfulness of the Appellant’s Response

[24] This Court considers it was perfectly reasonable for the Appellant, through his
attorney-at-law, to request particulars of the allegations that were being made
against him. We would similarly regard the statement by the Appellant to the
Board that he would have his attorney-at-law attend and represent him at their
meeting - which they thereupon cancelled. As a matter of reason , we see the
Appellant’s response as fair and appropriate.

[25] Blyth v  Scottish Liberal Club6 on which the First Respondent also sought to rely
is similarly unhelpful to them because the facts were so very different. Mr Blyth
was hired as Managing Secretary by a club for a number of years but in the
following year the club began winding up operations, and soon Mr Blyth's
functions had nearly ended. Questions arose about the legality of Mr Blyth's
fixed-term contract and before long he sought damages for breach of contract,
while still receiving his full salary. However, he refused to attend meetings or
follow instructions and claimed the contract justified this. His employment was
promptly terminated. The court dismissed the claim Mr Blyth brought, finding
his actions materially breached his contract  and justified his dismissal. In
upholding the decision on appeal, Clerk LJ stated as follows:

In the state of affairs of the Club at the time when the breaches took place
I can think of nothing which would strike more at the root of the contract
than the refusal by the pursuer to service the Review Committee and to
carry out orders in connection wi th the affairs of the Management
Committee. Once it is accepted that those were duties which the pursuer
was obliged to carry out under his contract, and were virtually the only
ones at the time, the Lord Ordinary's finding on the materiality of the
breaches is prima facie clearly confirmed.

[26] In Blyth the court thus found that the Appellant breached his contract by failing
to attend meetings when he was obliged to do so as part of his function as Director
and Secretary. It should not need to be  stated, but apparently it does, that in the
present appeal there was no failure or refusal of the Appellant to carry out a ny
lawful order of the Board . What the Appellant refused to do was to participate
blindly, which is to say without basic information as to  reasons or cause , in a
meeting that was called to decide upon the punishment to be imposed upon him,
including his dismissal. Nor did he simply refuse to attend; he stated he would be
attending by his attorney -at-law – whereupon the Respondent cancelled the
meeting.

6 [1983] IRLR 245.
Trust and Confidence

[27] The lawfulness of the Appellant’s response merits some discussion, and the
research of Mr Luck hoo SC for the Appellant has been helpful.  In
Commonwealth Caribbean Employment and Labour Law7 the authors note that
in the Commonwealth Caribbean there is standard application of the principles of
natural justice , especially in the context where there is a dearth of  statutory
provisions regarding the actual steps to be taken in terms of procedural fairness.
The text refers to the case of Banking, Insurance and General Workers Union v
PriceSmart Trinidad Ltd8 where no investigations were made into the employee’s
alleged misconduct before summoning her to a meeting, and she was not advised
of the charges against her , even when she requested them. The employer
subsequently demanded her resignation. The court held the employer’s actions
were reprehensible, in breach of the rules of natural justice and qui te contrary to
all known tenets of what can be regarded as good industrial practice.

[28] More pointedly, counsel submitted that this Court decided that a term of mutual
trust and confidence would be implied into a contract of employment, in Sandy
Lane Hotel Co Ltd v Cato .9 This necessarily requires that an employer must
furnish an employee with particulars of allegations in circumstances similar to
those in the instant case, it was submitted, and the employer cannot refuse to do
so and then allege fundamental breach by the employee for opting not to appear
in person but by counsel. In this vein, the court in King v University Court of the
University of St Andrews 10  determined that the implied duty of trust and
confidence subsisted whilst the investigation procedures were being carried out.
Therefore, it was held, t he pursuer in that case was entitled to be given a fair
opportunity to reply to the complaints made against him. Another recent decision
is Burn v Alder Hey Children’s NHS Foundation Trust 11 in which Underhill LJ
agreed that a separate duty of procedural fairness could readily be implied into

7 Natalie Corthésy and Carla-Anne Harris-Roper, Commonwealth Caribbean Employment and Labour Law (Routledge 2014) 229.
8  TT 2008 IC 43 (CARILAW), (17 March 2008).
9 [2022] CCJ 8 (AJ) BB, BB 2022 CCJ 2 (CARILAW).
10 [2002] IRLR 252.
11  [2022] IRLR 306.
the contract of employment in the context of the disciplinary process, apart from
the implied duty of trust and confidence.

[29] In the instant case, the trial judge examined the sequence of events leading to the
Appellant’s decision to appear by counsel and held that in the circumstances the
Appellant was entitled to seek counsel and to be afforded beforehand , as his
counsel requested , the details and specific nature of the infractions allegedly
committed by him. The Court of Appeal endorsed the findings of the trial judge.
As the  material offered by counsel for the Appellants has confirmed, the
jurisprudence fully supports the finding.

Repudiatory Breach

[30] Although the prec eding discussion settles the matter because it was strongly
argued, it would be fitting to deal briefly with the issue of repudiatory breach, of
which counsel for the Respondents accused the Appella nt.  The matter was
addressed by McCardie J in Re Rubel Bronze and Metal Co Ltd12 as follows:

In every case the question of repudiation must depend on the character of
the contract, the number and weight of the wrongful acts or assertions, the
intention indicated by such acts or words, the deliberation or otherwise
with which they are committed or uttered, and on the general
circumstances of the case. If the matters alleged to constitute a repudiation
are contained in written documents, then it is for the Court to determine
whether such documents evince a determination not to be bound by the
contract. But if such matters consist of acts or conduct, then it is for the
jury as judges of fact to determine whether repudiation is established: see
George D. Emery Co. v. Wells.

[31] In considering the f actors adumbrated, the contrast with the situation in Blyth v
Scottish Liberal Club13 relied on by the Respondents is again apposite. Clerk LJ
at [2] of his judgment found that Mr Blyth refused to carry out duties that he was
required to perform under his contract; ‘they were virtually the only duties which

12 [1918] 1 KB 315 at 322-323.
13 Blyth (n 6).
were left for him to perform in return for the salary which the defenders were
obliged to pay to him under the contract.’

[32] Considered against factors such as the weight of the wrongful act , the intention
manifested by the action,  and the deliberateness of that conduct , Mr Blyth’s
behaviour was a textbook case of repudiation. In Macari v Celtic Football and
Athletic Co Ltd14 Lord Caplan noted:

…looking to the legitimacy of the instruction it is possible that such an
order may also justify the employee in ignoring what he was asked to do,
on the basis that it is not within the scope of the employee's employment
to carry out instructions not truly connected with his proper function; nor
for that matter instructions which are fundamentally unreasonable.

[33] As we have stated, it was reasonable and sensible of the Appellant not to blindly
attend what he may well have regarded as a sentencing hearing. On the advice of
his attorney, he chose to appear by counsel. There is no breach in that response ;
no refusal to perform any contractual obligation. Accordingly, the dismissal of
the Appellant was plainly wrong, unlawful and in breach of his contract of
employment and having so concluded we dismissed the cross-appeal against the
finding that the Appellant was wrongfully dismissed.

The Pension Entitlement

[34] The appeal and cross-appeal on the  issue of pension payment are conveniently
dealt with together as the Respondents contended that apart from a return of the
pension contributions that the Appellant paid, he is entitled to no payment from
the pension fund; whereas the Appellant sought restoration of the award made by
the High Court of full pension benefits. This reduces the dispute to the single
question: to what payment from the pension fund is the Appellant entitled?

14 [1999] IRLR 787 at 798.
The Pension Rules

[35] The case for the Respondent was that the Pension Rules made no provision for
payment of any benefit to a dismissed pension contributor and, therefore, the
Appellant could be entitled to none. The relevant Pension Scheme was constituted
under a Trust Deed and the Rules of the New Building Society’s Pension Scheme
govern its operation. First, a digression : the Respondents submitted that the
pension scheme terminated by effluxion of time and, therefore, the Appellant has
no claim to pension under the scheme. This was not a matter that was pleaded nor
litigated in the courts below, and it is puzzling and disappointing that counsel for
the Respondents sought to advance this proposition at the level of this Court.
Especially so since counsel was quite unable to tell this Court what was the
consequence of his assertion that this was the fact  and offered no explanation of
how it was that the trustees continued to  collect pension contributions to this
supposedly extinguished pension scheme and continued to administe r it .
Accordingly, the Court treated the submission as immaterial.

[36] As highlighted by the Respondents, the rules of the scheme provide that members
should retire at the normal retirement age, that is on the six tieth birthday of the
member. Various provisions are made for retirement at earlier or later dates .
There is provision for a member to be refunded if he resigns and does not qualify
for pension. In such a case the member is entitled to the refund of his contributions
plus interest together with a percentage of the employer’s contribution depending
on the member ’s years of service . Where a member is dismissed for cause, or
voluntarily leaves employment , or resigns to forestall or avoid dismissal , the
Managing Trustee may forfeit any benefit arising from the employer ’s
contribution. As an alternative, they may deduct any amount the member may
owe to the employer or the fund, or any shortage in funds for which the member
is responsible or any amount misappropriated or defa lcated as may be certified
by the employer’s auditors.

Benefits on Termination

[37] The Respondents submitted that r 21.00 provides that the termination of
employment of a member  should be effective as if the scheme were not in
operation. Therefore, a member who is terminated shall not be entitled to claim
or recover anything by way of compensation in respect of any benefit arising
under the scheme.

[38] The Respondents submit that the obligation to make pension payments fall on the
trustees and not the employer  and quote Lord Millet in Air Jamaica Ltd v
Charlton15 who said of the obligation to make pension payments the following:

The obligation to make pension payments was not a contractual obligation
undertaken by the company, but a trust obligation imposed on the trustees.
Their lordships agree with the observation of Carey JA , … that each
employee becomes a member of the pension scheme by virtue of his
employment, but that his entitlement to a pension arises under the trusts
of the scheme.

[39] Further, it was submitted,  the employee has no contractual right to pension as was
said in the same case . From this proposition , the Respondent argue d that the
Appellant had no claim to pension or indeed any other entitlement under the pension
scheme against the First Respondent. The Respondents also drew attention to the
distinction between the situation in Guyana , where there is no relevant legislation ,
and the situation in England and Canada from which jurisdictions the Appellant relies
on authorities regarding pension rights. In those jurisdictions, the Respondents
submitted, the rights to pension are preserved in a case of early termination of
employment, by  the enabling pension -preservation legislation that has been
introduced in the respective jurisdictions . Not so in Guyana, the Respondents
submitted.

15 (1999) 54 WIR 359 at 367.
[40] In conclusion on this point, the Respondents submitted that as the Appellant did
not attain the normal age of retirement, and did not qualify for any measure of
reduced pens ion under r 10.00 , he was not entitled to any pension . The
Respondents further submitted that neither was the Appellant entitled to the
payment of any contributions made to the scheme by the employer, since r 11.00
does not apply in this case. Furthermore, the Respondents submitted , ‘if
terminated for cause the trustees are invested with the discretion to forfeit the
pension’ and submitted as well that r 21.00 excludes any claim for compensation
for loss of pension benefits on dismissal.

Provisions Relating to Pension on Termination

[41] It is appropriate to consider first the submissions of the Respondent that if an
employee is terminated for cause the trustees have a discretion to forfeit ‘the
pension.’ 16  This statement in the concluding paragraph of the Respondent’s
submission was quite an overreach from the Respondent’s earlier, and accurate,
submission that ‘the Managing Trustee may forfeit any benefit arising from the
First Respondent’s contribution.’17  The Respondents relied on this provision, in
r 11.00, as part of the foundation for their submission that the Appellant had no
right to pension under the First Respondent’s pension scheme. The rule provides:

11:02 If a member is dismissed b y the society for fraud, dishonesty,
defalcation or serious misconduct and voluntarily leaves the employment
of the Society or resigns to forestall or avoid dismissal  the Managing
Trustee may forfeit any benefit arising from the contributions of the
Society under the Scheme to which he might otherwise be entitled or may
withhold from any such benefit to which he is entitled any amount owing
to the Fund or the Society or any shortage of funds for which he is
responsible or the amount of any defalcation or misappropriation  as
certified by the auditor of the Society and pay that sum to the society.

16 Maurice Arjoon, ‘Submissions on behalf of the Respondents’, Submissions in Arjoon v New Building Society Ltd, GYCV2023/002,
21 July 2023, para 21.
17 ibid, para 7.
[42] The reliance on r 11.00 by the Respondent is  either confused or adventurous
because, as the submissions  earlier accepted, the rule has no application to this
case. The rule speaks to refund of contributions and payment of reduced benefits
consequent on resignation other than as provided for in r 10.00, or consequent on
dismissal by the Society for cause. The Appellant was seeking neither a refund of
contributions or reduced benefit and was making no claim to have resigned. The
rule simply has no application in this case , whatever the intention in referring to
it.

[43] In any case, there was no purported forfeiture by the trustees, as made clear by
the testimony of Mr Seepaul Narine, a director of the First Respondent, who
stated that ‘the Board decided that the pension of the Appellant ought to settle
after his indebtedness to the NBS was settled.’  That decision was taken  on the
day the Board dismissed the Appellant, so clearly there had been  no decision by
the Respondents to seek forfeiture.

[44] The position is all the stronger  when it is considered that there can be forfeiture
only where the employee is terminated for cause. The determination of this Court,
above, that there was no cause for termination of the Appellant puts the matter
beyond argument.  There was no forfeiture and there could  not have been
forfeiture.

[45] Rule 21.00 was relied upon by the Respondents, as another part of its foundation
for denying the right to pension,  because it provides that the termination of
employment of a member should be effective as if the scheme were not in
operation. Therefore, it was said, the rule provides that a terminated employee
shall not be entitled  to claim or recover anything by way of compensation in
respect of benefits under the scheme. The rule states:

21:00 The rights of the Society to terminate the employment of any
Member shall in no way be restricted by any of the provisions of the rules
and any such termination shall be effect ed as if the Scheme were not in
operation and accordingly any such Member shall not be entitled to claim
or recover any such sum by way of compensation or otherwise in respect
of any benefit arising from any provision of the scheme.

[46] This provision appears at the end of the rules along with others of a general nature
under the heading ‘Miscellaneous Provisions’. It would seem reasonable to
expect that, whatever is its intended application, the provision was not intended
to operate in all circumstances to disentitle to pension a member whose
employment is terminated in circumstances where the rules provide that pension
must be paid.

[47] Rule 10.00, reproduced at [49] below, expressly provides for payment of pension
on termination of employment of a member under various circumstances . Rule
21.00 does not purport to make a nonsense of the entitlement. How to apply this
general provision in r 21.00 was not argued, and the Court will not engage,
unassisted by the submissions of counsel,  with any broad interpreting of its
purpose and operation. However, it requires no effort at interpretation to gather
that what that rule does  is to express that the Society  is free to terminate the
employment of a member, unrestricted by the provisions of the rules. It excludes
claims for compensation for loss of benefits arising from the provisions of the
scheme—as opposed to claims for payment of pension due to a member under
the scheme. In other words, pension is paid as a matter of entitlement under the
rules, not as a matter of compensation for termination.

No Provision in Respect of Wrongful Termination

[48]  It was a common premise in the submissions that r 10.00 provides that an
employee retires on pension on his normal retirement date and that the rule then
goes on to state additional circumstances of retirement on pension. It is a
straightforward statement that a member retires on pension: this, after all, is the
whole purpose of a pension scheme. But it is easy to overlook the seminal nature
of the statement as a declaration of the fundamental principle of the pension
scheme: when an employee retires, he is entitled to pension. That principle must
be faithfully served in this and all cases. The principle applies fully to the
additional circumstances specified of a member being entitled to pension apart
from the entitlement at the retirement age.

[49] As provided in r 10.00, the additional circumstances include:

10.00 …
(ii) if the society permits him to retire at any time not more than 5 years
before his Normal Retirement Date;

(iii)  if the society requires him to retire at any time after he has attained
the age of 55 years …

[50] It is not surprising that the rules make no provision for payment of pension where
the Society  wrongfully terminates  the employment . The draftsperson could
hardly have been required to provide for the employer acting wrongfully  and,
indeed, nor were they competent to so provide. Provision for the consequences of
a wrongful termination is necessarily a matter left to the courts.

[51] This litigation is concerned with exactly that situation  – what is the provision to
be made in this case regarding the entitlement to pension of a wrongful
termination of employment. The fair provision, in this case, as we have found was
the straightforward remedy that the High Court granted . In effect, the Court
treated the Appellant’s entitlement as being the same  as if the employer had
permitted or required him to retire , in accordance with r 10.00. As a matter of
law, resignation may be treated as the same as retirement18 and thus it may
legitimately be said that what happened with the Appellant was that he
involuntarily retired, in the language of r 10.00, he was required to retire.

18 Barrow v A-G of Saint Lucia LC 2014 CA 6 (CARILAW), (27 October 2014).
[52] That conclusion having been established , it remained only to determine the
pension that would be paid in a normal case of retirement before the scheduled
retirement date. There was no disputing the calculation of the pension entitlement
that was done in the High Court, and we therefore upheld the award, with interest.

Severance Pay and Other Benefits

[53] Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal decided that the Appellant was
entitled to severance pay under the TESP Act but it was left uncertain, because of
the mixed result in the Court of Appeal,  whether that entitlement applied where
an employee was entitled to pension , as we have found to be the entitlement of
the Appellant. The relevant provision is s 21 of that Act, which states as follows:

(1) On termination of his employment, an employee who has completed
one or more years of continuous employment with an employer shall be
entitled to be paid by such employer a severance or redundancy allowance
equivalent to …
…

(4) Subsection (1) shall not apply where the employee... (emphasis
added)
 …
(d)  is being retired from his employment having attained the age
of sixty years or such other age as may be agreed upon
between the parties and is entitled to a gratuity or pension or
both from his employer under any law collective , labour
agreement or contract of employment whether such
entitlement is under any contributory or non-contributory
pension scheme , excluding benefits from the National
Insurance Scheme.

Provided however that where any gratuity payable on his retirement is less
than the amount the employee would have received under section 21 (1),
the amount under section 21 (1) shall be paid instead of the gratuity.

[54] The intent ion expressed by this section is that where an employment is
terminated, severance pay shall be paid, but where there is retirement, and the
employee is entitled to pension, it shall not be paid. The Appellant argues that he
was terminated, he did not retire, so severance pay should be paid. It is a credible
argument but in view of the  determination made above, that the Appellant shall
be paid pension as if he retired, it cannot succeed. If it did, the Appellant would
be getting exactly what the statute creating this benefit of severance pay intended
he should not get: he should not get severance pay and pension.

[55] The purpose of a severance payment is not to punish an employer; it is to reward
an employee for the service they gave to the employer and compensate them for
the loss they have suffered by the termination  of their employment , whether
wrongfully or not  – whether fairly or unfairly.19 At common law , there was no
obligation to make a severance payment  and it developed as a practice of good
employment relations . The practice having become standard  in employmen t
contracts, the legislature decided to put it on a statutory footing and make it
obligatory as a matter of general fairness .20 In this case , the Appellant is being
awarded pension and by that award he is being put in the position he would have
been in if his employment had  properly terminated by his retirement.  As s 21
provides, a properly terminated employee  who retires on pension is not entitled
to pension. Therefore, with the award of pension having been made to him by this
Court, the employee can be in no better position than to get what he was properly
entitled to upon a harmonious termination. The Appellant is now in exactly the
position he would have been in had his request for early retirement been
processed.

[56] Before leaving the issue of severance pay,  the Court observes for the sake of
future reference  that the present determination of when severance pay is not
payable must not be treated as a determination of principle or general application
across different countries . The present determination is no more than an
interpretation and  application of the specific legislative provision in this

19 Chefette Restaurants Ltd v Harris [2020] CCJ 6 (AJ) (BB), (2020) 98 WIR 79 at [124].
20 R Holzmann and others, ‘Severance Pay Programs Around the World: History, Rationale, Status and Reforms ’ (Institute of Labor
Economics Discussion Paper No 5731, May 2011) 54.
jurisdiction that severance pay is not an entitlement when the employee is entitled
to and receives pension.

[57] Finally, on this Court’s award for leave pay and passage assistance for two years,
there was no resistance to the appeal for these to be awarded by this Court, which
the Court of Appeal failed to do , possibly by oversight in the view of counsel.
These were outstanding entitlements in the normal course of the employment, as
the evidence showed, and there was no good reason to omit them from the sum
due to the Appellant and, accordingly, they were awarded.

SAUNDERS P (concurring):

[58] This Court heard the appellant’s appeal in this matter on Tuesday , 10 October
2023. On 23 October we issued an Order indicating that our reasons would
follow. That Order allowed Mr Arjoon’s appeal and dismissed the Building
Society’s cross-appeal. In it, we reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeal
which had held, in its judgment dated 16 September 2022, that Mr Arjoon was
not entitled to pension benefits. Instead, we restored the Judgment and Orders of
Brassington Reynolds J made on 20 July 2017 save that we reserved our decision
on the issue of Mr Arjoon’s entitlemen t to severance pay. We also held that the
Building Society must pay to Mr Arjoon the additional sum of GY D1,602,459
being leave pay and passage assistance for the years 2006 and 2007.

[59] We reserved our decision on severance pay in order to address the question
whether the Termination of Employment and Severance Pay Act ( ‘the Act ’)
contemplates that, in principle, it is permissible for an employee to receive both
a pension and gratuity as well as severance pay.   I agree entirely with the views
expressed by Barrow J above on how this question should be resolved.

[60] It seems to me that when s21( 4) (d) of the Act disapplied from entitlement to
severance pay an employee who was:

…being retired from his employment having attained the age of sixty years
or such other age as may be agreed upon between the parties and is entitled
to a gratuity or pension or both from his employer…

the Legislature must be taken as having indicated that eligibility to severance pay
is lost when an employee is entitled to receive a pension. Severance pay is
appropriate when your term of employment has been prematurely ended. But if
you have been retire d (or as in this case, treated as having been retired) and are
entitled to a gratuity and a pension, you are ineligible for ‘severance pay’. You
can’t be ‘severed’ and simultaneously be ‘retired’. By our Order we quashed the
Building Society’s disallowance of a pension for Mr Arjoon and we granted him
his pension as if he had attained the retirement age.

[61] In my view, two aspects of the Act lend support to this notion that the Act does
not countenance the receipt of both pension and gratuity, on the one hand, and as
well severance pay on the other. Firstly, the proviso to s 21 states that where any
gratuity payable on an employee’s retirement is less than the amount the
employee would have received as severance pay, then in lieu of the gratuity
severance pay shall be paid. This suggests to me that a dismissed employee must
receive either pension/gratuity or severance pay.

[62] Secondly, in circumstances where an employee has made out a complaint of
either unfair dismissal or the imposition of unreasonable disciplinary action, the
Act grants to the courts the very wide and unconstrained power to provide the
employee with compensa tion in ‘such amount as the Court considers just and
reasonable in all the circumstances having regard to the loss sustained by the
employee as a consequence of the dismissal or discipline…’ as well as ‘any other
just remedy in addition to or in lieu of th e award ’ already granted. There is
therefore no need, as it were, to top up with ‘severance pay’ an unfairly dismissed
employee, who is entitled to receive a pension and gratuity,  if a court is of the
view that the employee deserves compensation that is greater than what the
employee may have received in an ordinary action for wrongful dismissal or for
severance pay. It seems to me that the proper thing for an employee to do is to
seek enhanced compensation in keeping with s 20. If the court is persuaded that
the employee deserves such enhanced compensation,  then the ultimate dollar
figure awarded could be more or it could be less than what would have been
calculated as severance pay if the employment had come to a premature end and
severance payment was due.

[63] In this case, Mr Arjoon continually claimed exemplary damages before the High
Court. No exemplary damages were awarded by Reynolds  J. Among other
complaints, Mr Arjoon appealed against the judge’s failure to award him
exemplary damages. The Court of Appeal neglected to reverse the trial judge on
this issue. Mr Arjoon again raised the issue of exemplary damages in his notice
of appeal t o this Court but precious little was said about it in oral argument.
Indeed, before this Court, counsel neglected to press for such damages.

[64] In my view, given the width of s  20 it is unnecessary to consider whether any
particular common law remedies should be awarded even in an egregious case of
unfair dismissal or unreasonable imposition of disciplinary action. It is merely
necessary for a litigant to a) indicate that additional damages are being sought in
keeping with the section, b) provide the facts and circumstances that justify the
additional award and c) establish to the Court one’s entitlement.

[65] Given that this Court has already issued its Order confirming Reynold J’s
judgment subject only to the question whether the appellant should receive
severance pay, the issue of any further additional award comparable to exemplary
damages is moot. I therefore support the order made by Barrow J.

JAMADAR J (concurring):

Introduction

‘To see things in their true light, we must see them from a certain distance, as strangers,
which is impossible when we study any phenomena of our country [in isolation].’21

[66] I agree with the reasoning of Barrow J and with the decision that the Appellant,
Maurice Arjoon, was wrongfully dismissed. I also agree with the reasoning of
Rajnauth-Lee and Burgess JJ and with the outcome that the Appellant is entitled
to his full pension benefits. I further agree that he is entitled to leave pay and
passage assistance for the years 2006 and 2007, as ordered. On the issue of
severance, I agree that he is not also entitled to severance having been awarded
his pen sion, but in my opinion, he is entitled to damages under s 20 of the
Termination of Employment and Severance Act ( ‘the Act’)22 and/or exemplary
damages. In relation to severance and damages, I make the following comments
and recommendations.

Statutory Interpretation

[67] As a matter of strict statutory interpretation and applying a purely textual
approach, the analysis of Rajnauth-Lee and Burgess JJ on the issue of severance
cannot be flawed. Section 21(1) of the Act specifies that on termination of
employment, provided the continuous employment criteria are met, an employee
is entitled to a severance allowance (calculated as provided for). 23  This is
consistent with the overall purpose and objective of the Act – to provide for the
grant of redundancy or severance payment to employees. 24 It is the overarching
intention of the Act.

21 Pierre Lepaulle, ‘The Function of Comparative Law’ (1921-1922) 35(7) Harv L R 838, 858.
22  Cap 96:01 (n 1).
23 See also s 2 (definition of ‘severance of employment’) and s 7(a) and (c)(ii).
24 Long title.
[68] This overarching goal is not absolute and is subject to certain statutory exceptions
(as well as the qualifying criteria). Section 21(4) sets out these exceptions. For
example, s 21(4) (a) disapplies the payment of severance in cases of summary
dismissal ( under s  10) and termination under s 9 (termination during a
probationary period) or s 11 (termination for misconduct, breach of contract, or
unsatisfactory performance) of the Act. Significantly, s 21(4) (d) also provides a
ground of disentitlement, when a n employee ‘is being retired from his
employment having attained the age of sixty years or such other age as may be
agreed upon between the parties and is entitled to a gratuity or pension …’.

[69] On a strict application of the facts of this case as determined by this Court: (i) the
Appellant was wrongfully dismissed (negating any application of s 21(4) (a) of
the Act), and (ii) the Appellant did not retire at age 60 or pursuant to any
agreement between the contracting parties. Thus, on the face of it, the disentitling
provisions of s 21(4) do not apply. Indeed, the First Respondent has steadfastly
maintained as a matter of fact and law, that the Appellant is not entitled to any
pension. In fact, the  Appellant’s employment was prematurely and unilaterally
terminated by the First Respondent, albeit unlawfully.  It follows, logically and
on a strict textual interpretation, that he is entitled to a severance allowance under
the Act.

An Exceptional Case

[70] However, that is not the end of the matter. This case is unique and exceptional,
because this Court has decided both that the Appellant was wrongfully dismissed
and is entitled to his full pension. In this case the consequential and pragmatic
effect of this Court’s judgment is that the Appellant will receive his full pension
benefits. If that had happened in  the normal course of events (without any
termination of employment prior to attaining age 60), he would have been an
employee covered by s 21(4) (d) and disentitled to a severance allowance. This is
a clear and unequivocal statutory policy.

[71] In fact, the Act intends as a policy, both that severance allowance be paid to
employees provided certain conditions are met and also that it is not to be paid in
certain circumstances. As explained, one such policy circumstance of
disentitlement is receipt of full pension, in the ordinary course of events, at age
60 or as may be otherwise agreed. This case has introduced extraordinary
circumstances.

[72] How then is this legal conundrum to be resolved as a matter of law and justice?
How is the strict textual interpretation to be reconciled with a clear and contrary
policy intent? What is this Court to do if the strict circumstances of disentitlement
are not met?

[73] In my opinion , the solution lies in the application of the lens of fundamental
rights, as juridic values, and as a guiding light to show the interpretative way
forward. Wit J, in Guyana Sugar Corp Inc v Dhanessar ,25 alluded to this as
follows:

It cannot be assumed that the legislature intended to make ineffective
legislation; certainly not in Guyana whose Constitution tells us that it is a
“state in the course of transition from capitalism to socialism” (section 1)
and gives special recognition to the role and value of labour: “The source
of the growth of social wealth and of the well-being of the people, and of
each individual, is the labour of the people” (section 21). Workers in
Guyana have a fundamental right to be protected by the law. This means
that legislation must be interpreted so as to effectuate the protection it is
intended to offer.

[74] Thus, ‘looking at the entire structure of the Act and given the constitutional
background’,26 and bearing in mind that ‘it cannot be assumed that the legislature
intended to make ineffective legislation’,27 the question that arises is: How is the
constitutional standard of the protection of the law to be applied in this case so as

25 Guyana Sugar Corp Inc [2015] CCJ 4 (AJ) (GY), GY 2015 CCJ 1 (CARILAW) at [48] (Emphasis added). See also, OO v BK [2023]
CCJ 10 (AJ) BB.
26 ibid at [49].
27 ibid at [48].
to effectively afford a worker due recognition and regard, and in doing so, to meet
fundamental benchmarks of fairness and equality while adhering to the intent and
policy of the Act?

[75] In my opinion, the Appellant has derived the benefit of the protection of the law
by receiving his full pension. There is no undermining of that protection if he
does not also receive a severance allowance, as the statutory regime ultimately
intends such a result. Put another way, to award the Appellant both a full pension
and a severance allowance would be contrary to the policy of the law. A
purposive, policy-driven, interpretation should only permit the Appellant either
his pension or a severance allowan ce, and in this case, we having all agreed on
the former, then any claim to the latter is to be disallowed.

[76] Does such an interpretation provide a contextually just outcome in this case, given
its unique circumstances? Is the fullness of the protection of the law satisfied? In
my opinion, no.

Context is Everything

[77] Part of the factual matrix in this case is the unlawfulness of the First Respondent’s
actions, clearly intended to have the effect of depriving the Appellant of both his
pension and any severance allowance. That is to say, to leave the employee with
neither the benefit of deferred wages for services already rendered (a pension) ,
nor any compensation for services rendered (severance). Actions intended to
effectively punish the Appellant at the end of a lifetime of professional service
and to leave him without any economic support in the latter years of his life – to
deprive him o f his hard -earned expectation of a pension and/or alternatively
severance.

[78] To put the First Respondent’s conduct in context and from the perspective of the
Appellant’s experience, the following is noteworthy. The Appellant is an
accountant. He was initially employed by the First Respondent in 1977. By 2002
he had ascended through the ranks to the position of Director/Secretary/CEO of
the First Respondent and held that position of trust and confidence until his
termination on 14 August 2007. This was after 30 years of undisputed prior
meritorious service. His sudden and inexplicable summary dismissal, by letter,
took place six months before he would have reached the normal retirement age of
60, and was done on the basis of alleged ‘serious misconduct’. An alleg ation
which if proven, by virtue of the conjoint effects of ss 10 and 21(4) (a) of the Act,
would have disentitled him from receiving any severance allowance, and could
have also denied him pension.

[79] Barrow J explains some further important context, as follows:28

It was never alleged by NBS in these proceedings that the Appellant was
complicit in the withdrawal and both lower courts were clear that the
Appellant was not to be faulted, simply because he bore ultimate
management responsibility, for the deficiencies i n the system, of which
the directors were aware, that allowed the fraud to be perpetrated, if
indeed there was fraud. That notwithstanding, the submissions to this
Court for the Respondents still attempted to throw some shade on the
Appellant. The High Cou rt found, and was upheld on appeal, that there
was not just and probable cause for summary dismissal of the Appellant.

[80] The First Respondent’s conduct is well summarised by Barrow J, when he
describes the process it adopted in relation to the Appellant, as akin to ‘a
sentencing hearing’.29  In his opinion, with which we all agree:30

In the instant case, the hearing to which the Appellant was being invited
was no investigation; the necessary investigation had been completed by
the internal auditor who absolved the Appellant of any misconduct or
negligence and the First Respondent had expressed full confidence in the
Appellant.

29 At [33] above.
30 At [23] above.
[81] Yet, and as Barrow J also explains:31

… in defiance of logic, and a volte-face the First Respondent required the
Appellant to appear before its Board of Directors to answer
unparticularised allegations and be present for its determination of why
serious disciplinary action including dismissal should not be taken against
him.

[82] Indeed, as Barrow J would conclude with the unanimous approval of all members
of this panel: ‘Accordingly, the dismissal of the Appellant was plainly wrong,
unlawful and in breach of his contract of employment …’.32

[83] Rajnauth-Lee and Burgess JJ, for their part, explain in relation to the First
Respondent’s contention that the Appellant was not entitled to pension: ‘ In any
case, we recoil from any suggestion that the rules can be interpreted to allow NBS,
as the employer, to deprive Arjoon, as the employee, of his entitlement to pension
benefits by wrongfully terminating his contract of employment six months before
his normal retirement date .’33 Yet, this is exactly what the First Respondent set
about to do! In fact, the Appellant testified that he was not able to continue his
employment until his normal retirement age of 60 because of the dismissal. 34 In
my opinion, Rajnauth-Lee and Burgess JJ, correctly reason and hold that the First
Respondent breached its good faith obligation to the Appellant in wrongfully
dismissing him, thereby destroying his rights to pension. And, that such unlawful
conduct could not operate to do so.

[84] What is a just and proportionate response to such egregious behaviour on the part
of the First Respondent? What does the protection of the law demand?

Good Faith

[85] The behaviour of the First Respondent in this case is particularly egregious. It is
best understood in the context of the implied obligation of good faith that is
inherent in all employment contracts. It too, as a principle, is a part of the
protection of the law to which the Appellant is entitled, operating as an informing
interpretive value-lens and substantively. This Court, in Sandy Lane Hotel Co Ltd
v Cato,35 has unreservedly affirmed the fundamental value of good faith and its
corollary, the implied obligation of trust and confidence, as underpinning
principles in the context of employment contracts. Saunders P and Rajnauth-Lee
J explained the implications as  follows: ‘… a court must be astute to secure the
interests of … [e]mployees and not leave them at the complete mercy of the
actions of their employer’.36

[86] The implications of the obligation of good faith go even further. Capricious and
injurious action by an employer against employees, can potentially found a claim
in contract for breach of the implied obligation of good faith. 37 Thus, if an
employer without reasonable and proper cause behaves in ways that are intended
(on an objective standard) and/or calculated and/or reasonably likely (on a
probability standard) to cause serious injury to an employee, contrary to their
good faith obligations, such conduct can be actionable.

[87] In this case, the consequence is that the First Respondent can be liable for a breach
of its implied good faith obligations towards the Appellant, because of the
circumstances and manner in which he was treated and unlawfully dismissed.
Such a breach can attract an award of damages.

35 Sandy Lane Hotel (n 9) at [68]-[71].
36 ibid at [72].
37 See Imperial Group Pension Trust Ltd v Imperial Tobacco Ltd [1991] 1 WLR 589 at 597.
Section 20

[88] Within the scheme and policy of the Act this good faith obligation finds
independent and statutory recognition and expression, though unacknowledged
as such. Section 20(1) intends that where an employee is unfairly dismissed or a
wrongful imposition of disciplinary action is imposed by an employer, and it is
so held by the courts, ‘it shall award the employee compensat ion as specified in
sub-ss (2) and (3).’ Conceptually, both of these circumstances are breaches of the
good faith principle, grounded as they are in unfairness and wrongful action.
Thus, s 20 provides an independent statutory head of damage in the stated
circumstances.

[89] What damages? Subs ection (2) provides that ‘compensation shall be such an
amount as the Court considers just and equitable in all the circumstances having
regard to the loss sustained …’, and sub -s (3) allows the Court a discretion ‘if it
deems fit, (to) award any other just remedy in addition to or in lieu of the award’
made pursuant to sub-s (1). The governing principles in determining whether, and
if so, what additional compensation, damages, or relief, ought to be granted are:
the demands of contextual contractual (i) justice and (ii) equity. These include
fundamental rule of law considerations.

[90] There does not seem to me to be any reason why, in principle and in the
circumstances of this case, this additional compensatory award should not apply
in favour of the Appellant. This is so especially since the Appellant has pleaded
and prayed in aid for breach of the Act and claimed damages accordingly. 38
Section 20 relief was a live issue throughout these proceedings and is therefore
an open issue before this Court, because it is part and parcel of the issue of
severance under the Act.39 Further, in principle exemplary damages may also be

as the Court may think just, all the remedies or relief whatsoever to which any of the parties appear to be entitled in respect of any and

awarded under s  20, given the discretionary open -endedness of the relief that a
court may grant under sub-s (3).

Exemplary Damages

[91] The common law development of contract law is well known. In Jarvis v Swans
Tours Ltd,40 the Court of Appeal in England held that for the breach of a holiday
contract, damages were not limited to the costs of the holiday and could include
general damages for inconvenience, disappointment, and distress. Thus,
establishing a principle that in contracts of enjoyment or entertainment damages
can be awarded for failing to provide the promised enjoyment and/or
entertainment.

[92] The Appellant in his Statement of Claim, at para 9, asserted and claimed: ‘The
dismissal of the Plaintiff by the first defendant was oppressive arbitrary and was
malicious without any reasonable grounds entitling the Plaintiff to aggravated,
punitive and e xemplary damages.’ In fact, and as a specific head of relief, the
Appellant claimed: ‘Exemplary and punitive damages …’. 41 The trial judge did
not award any exemplary damages. The Appellant cross-appealed asserting that:
‘The Trial Judge ought to have awarded general damages … as well as punitive
and exemplary damages having regard to the circumstances of dismissal.’ 42 The
Court of Appeal also did not award exemplary damages. Neither court gave any
reasons for declining to consider or award punitive or exemplary damages.

[93] On appeal to this Court, the Appellant at Ground 2(p) asserted that; ‘The Court
of Appeal failed to make an award for general damages … and/or exemplary or
punitive damages having regard to the circumstances of the wrongful dismissal
of the Appellant.’43 In written submissions filed before this Court, the Appellant

his wrongful dismissal was erroneously and knowingly based on (i)

[94] In my opinion, the Appellant was entitled to a considered determination of his
claim for exemplary damages. Non-treatment, or dismissal by default, in the face
of unequivocal findings of wrongful dismissal and the repeated raising of the
issue by the Appellant at every level of the court system, cannot suffice
juridically.

[95] Exemplary damages can be awarded in employment contracts. This is rooted in
the obligation of good faith and also stands on independent bases. Such a claim
forms part of the protection of the law to which the Appellant is entitled. It also
advances the rule of law in liberal democratic societies, where freedom to contract
is anchored in good faith and essential for effective societal functioning.

[96] The development of the law in this area has not been uniform, and there are some
jurisdictions that hesitate, agonising as to whether to restrict the use of exemplary
damages to torts. 48 However, in parts of the Caribbean this development of the

[97] It is well established that exemplary damages can be awarded in the law of tort.50
It is also well established that whereas the general objective of damages is
compensatory, the real purpose of exemplary damages is to denounce and deter,
and in that sense, also punitive. 51 This purpose advances compliance with legal
norms and practices. In doing so, it supports and sustains the rule of law.

[98] Classically, and in tort, exemplary damages are awarded to show that the law
cannot be broken with impunity, to demonstrate that tort does not pay, and to
vindicate the rule of law.52 Most importantly, exemplary damages are a response
to the conduct of a wrongdoer. This improper conduct has been described in many
ways, and maybe the single most apt descriptor is ‘outrageous conduct’.53

[99] In A v Bottrill,54 outrageous conduct was explained conceptually, as follows:55

Exceptionally, a defendant’s conduct in committing a civil wrong is so
outrageous that an order for payment of compensation is not an adequate
response. Something more is needed from the court, to demonstrate that
such conduct is altogether unacceptable to society. Then the wrongdoer
may be ordered to make a further payment, by way of condemnation and
punishment.

Caribbean jurisprudence …’.

[100] Once one considers the real purpose of exemplary damages, to denounce and
deter, and to punish conduct that undermines the rule of law in a democratic
society, its applicability to the law of employment contracts is evident. Contracts
are the backbone of m odern societies, whether as employment contracts,
commercially, or more generally. Public and private human affairs are conducted
contractually. The society therefore has a deep interest in the maintenance of
contractual legal standards. One legal mechanis m for doing so, in the area of
employment contracts, is to condemn conduct that undermines normative legal
practices. Exemplary damages, when justified, is one tool in the judicial toolkit
for maintaining the rule of law in this area.

[101] Two Supreme Court of Canada decisions are illustrative. The first is Vorvis v
Insurance Corp of British Columbia.56 Vorvis was a wrongful dismissal case in
which a plaintiff was dismissed prior to the vesting of pension benefits, although
no complaint had been made about the quality of their work. It was not in dispute
that the employer’s conduct was worthy of condemnation. I t was held that
punitive damages may be awarded where the employer’s conduct had been harsh,
vindictive, reprehensible, or malicious, provided the employer’s conduct that
gave rise to the claim was an actionable wrong.

[102] In Vorvis the underlying principles are set out. T he entire court agreed that (i)
exemplary damages were available for breach of contract, and (ii) the focus was
on the conduct of the wrongdoer (not on its legal category). McIntyre J who
delivered the majority judgment of the court , cited Clement JA in Paragon
Properties Ltd v Magna Envestments Ltd 57  on the underlying principles
governing an award of exemplary damages in contract:

The basis of such an award is actionable injury to the plaintiff done in
such a manner that it offends the ordinary standards of morality or decent
conduct in the community in such marked degree that censure by way of
