Practice and procedure ‒ Special leave – Hearing of application for special leave to be
treated as hearing of appeal ‒ Extradition proceedings – Natural justice – Procedural
fairness ‒ Rule against bias – Presumed bias – Apparent bias – Ministerial decision to
issue Authority to Proceed ‒Whether the Minister was biased – Whether the Attorney
General was biased – Whether advice given by the Attorney General invalidated the
Authority to Proceed – Fugitive Offenders Act, Cap 10:04.

SUMMARY

General elections were held in the Co-operative Republic of Guyana on 1 September 2025.
The Second Applicant , Mr Azruddin Mohamed, was elected as the Leader of the
Opposition and was sworn into that office in January 2026. The First Applicant, Mr Nazar
Mohamed, is his father.

On 28 October 2025, the Government of Guyana received a request from the Government
of the United States of America for the extradition of both Applicants to that country. The
request resulted in the Minister of Home Affairs of Guyana (‘the Minister’ or ‘MOHA’)
issuing, on 30 October 2025, an Authority to Proceed (‘ATP’) pursuant to s 12 of the
Fugitive Offenders Act (‘the Act’ or ‘FOA’), which gave effect to extradition treaty
arrangements between Guyana and the United States of America. The ATP signified to the
magistrate that the request for extradition had been received and required the magistrate
to proceed with extradition proceedings in accordance with the provisions of the Act.

While those extradition proceedings were ongoing, the Applicants brought an action for
judicial review in the High Court on 23 December 2025, seeking, inter alia, an order that
the ATP was null and void because of bias, both actual and apparent. The Applicants also
sought a stay of the extradition proceedings. The alleged bias was said to have arisen from
the Minister’s affiliation with the governing political party, the People’s Progressive
Party/Civic (‘PPP/C’) in circumstances where the most senior represent atives of that
party, including the President, Vice -President, and the Attorney General, had publicly
described the Applicants as criminals and in other derogatory terms during the electoral
campaign. It was also alleged that the ATP was fatally defective because, prior to issuing
it, the Minister had consulted with the Attorney General, who was allegedly biased.

On 4 February 2026, Singh CJ (Ag) (‘the Chief Justice’), sitting in the High Court,
dismissed the application and refused the stay of the extradition proceedings. The Chief
Justice held that in issuing the ATP, the Minister was exercising an executive rather than
a judicial function and therefore the rule against bias did not apply to its fullest extent.
The Chief Justice also found that the allegations of bias had not been established, since it
had not been alleged that the Minister herself made any of the adverse statements against
the Applicants, and the expression by her colleagues of disdain for the Applicants could
not be attributed to her so as to taint her decision with bias. Costs were awarded to each
of the three Respondents to be paid on or before 27 February 2026.

On appeal, the Court of Appeal similarly dismissed the appeal and refused the request for
a stay of the extradition proceedings. Like the High Court, the Court of Appeal held that
the Minister was exercising an administrative function in issuing the ATP an d therefore
the issue of bias did not arise. All that was required was for the Minister to address her
mind to and comply with the statutory requirements regarding the issuance of the ATP.
Notwithstanding the Court of Appeal’s determination that the rule against bias did not
apply to the challenged decision, that court considered the submissions on bias. The court
found there was no direct proprietary, pecuniary or equivalently close personal interest
that would warrant automatic disqualification for bias.  Additionally, the Court of Appeal
found that the fair -minded observer would not conclude that there was apparent bias on
the part of the Minister, would appreciate that the ATP was merely a preliminary step in
the extradition process, and that the Applicants would have the benefit of all the safeguards
against bias provided under the Act. The Court of Appeal also rejected the argument that
the Minister and/or the Attorney General should have delegated their statutory functions
and powers to issue the ATP eith er pursuant to the Carltona principle or s 27 of the
Interpretation and General Clauses Act.
Dissatisfied with the decision of the Court of Appeal, the Applicants sought special leave
to appeal to the Caribbean Court of Justice. On 25 March 2026, this Court granted an
interim stay of the extradition proceedings and ordered that the hearing of the application
for special leave be treated as the hearing of the substantive appeal. The hearing focussed
on two central issues, namely:

(1) whether the Minister and/or the Attorney General was tainted with bias, actual or
apparent, such as to tarnish the issuance of the ATP, and, if so,

(2) whether the law required the Minister and/or the Attorney General to delegate their
statutory powers and functions in respect of the issuance of the ATP, in the
circumstances.

In a joint decision delivered by Anderson P and Barrow J, their Honours held that the
Applicants had met the threshold of arguability needed for the grant of special leave. That
is, it was arguable that the court below was wrong to decide that the rule against bias did
not apply to the issuance of the ATP.

In adjudicating the appeal, their Honours found that the rule against bias does apply to the
ministerial grant of the ATP but that the question of whether there had been a violation of
that rule had to be determined by the context in which that question ar ose. In the instant
case, the judges found that the ATP process does not import the full panoply of procedural
rights available in judicial proceedings. There was no general right to be heard prior to the
issuance of the ATP. There was no requirement for the Minister issuing the ATP to be free
from political bias. What was required was for the Minister to engage in a process that
allowed for consideration of the factors contemplated by the Act.  Their Honours found
that the Applicants had not challenged the process that led to the issuance of the ATP save
for the allegation that the Minister was politically biased. There was no allegation that the
Minister omitted to consider a relevant factor or that she considered an irrelevant one.
While the Attorney General, as chief legal adviser to the Government, must necessarily
be circumspect in any comment on extradition requests upon which his advice may be
sought, the decision to issue the ATP was statutorily vested in and was, as a matter of fact,
exercised by the MOHA with very minimal advice from the Attorney General. In these
circumstances, determination of whether the Attorney General was biased served no
probative value.

Their Honours expressed the considered view that it should become the practice in our
courts, except where it is manifestly clear that the extradition proceedings must fail (as
for example, where the ATP was issued by the wrong person), that while challenges to the
issuance of the ATP may be brought at any time, such challenges should only be heard
after completion of the committal proceedings. This practice would be consistent with the
international framework for extradition, encourage prompt performance o f extradition
treaty obligations, and provide a reasonable balance between the interest of the person
whose extradition is requested, and that of the State. This practice would also be in line
with the normal judicial processes envisaged by Parliament in, for example, ss 17 and 21
of the Act.

In the opinion of Anderson P and Barrow J, the challenge on grounds of bias having failed,
it was not necessary to consider the other ground of appeal concerning whether the
Minister and the Attorney General ought to have delegated their statutory powers i n the
circumstances. However, their Honours expressed grave doubts that there could properly
be delegation of the power under the Act to issue the ATP to any person who was not a
minister. Additionally, in light of their finding that the issuance of the ATP was not tainted
with bias, their Honours similarly found it unnecessary to address the arguments on waiver
and the doctrine of necessity raised by the Minister on her cross-appeal.

Rajnauth-Lee, Jamadar and Bulkan JJ delivered a separate opinion on several key aspects
of this matter. They were satisfied that the test for special leave was met by the Applicants
to the standard of arguability.

On jurisdiction and prematurity, they held that there is no legal basis that prevents the
Applicants from commencing these judicial review proceedings to quash the decision of
the MOHA to issue the ATP where bias is alleged in the decision-maker and/or decision-
making process. Prematurity does not arise in the circumstances of this case. There is
pragmatic good sense to the issue being raised at the earliest stage possible.

On the issue of waiver, they were of the view that it cannot be said that the Applicants
were plainly aware of all the relevant facts, or that by their conduct they clearly and
unequivocally waived their right to object on the ground of bias. Furthermore, the
Applicants did not delay and at the earliest opportunity questioned its lawfulness on the
ground of bias.

On the salient issue of bias, they underscored that the rights guaranteed under the
Constitution of Guyana permeate the entire extradition process, requiring a heightened
standard of scrutiny where implicated. They held that the rule against bias can apply  to
the issuance of an ATP under s 12 of the FOA and the fair-minded and informed observer
(apparent bias) test is the appropriate one.

On the facts, they concluded that there is no appearance of bias established against the
MOHA as the decision-maker or by reason of the larger ecosystem in which the Minister
operated. However, in relation to the Attorney General, they concluded that there  was a
real possibility that the Attorney General was biased. Despite this, they were of the view
that the Attorney General’s apparent bias has not so contaminated the process as to raise
a real possibility that the decision of the MOHA to issue the ATP was vitiated by bias.

On delegation, they determined that the doctrine of necessity does not arise in the
circumstances of this case, and delegation in relation to both the Attorney General and the
Minister is arguably permissible under the General Clauses and Interpretation Ac t of
Guyana.

On costs, they ordered that each party must bear their own costs in this appeal . Their
reasons highlighted that these proceedings are situated at the intersection of public law
and criminal law, raising issues of considerable public interest. Further, this action is not
frivolous or vexatious, or plainly hopeless, or an abuse of the court’s process, and has led
to important clarifications on the applicable law.

In conclusion, they highlighted the importance of judicial independence for all courts in
Guyana and opined that the public statements by the Vice -President and the Attorney
General referencing the existing judicial proceedings can undermine the independence of
the Judiciary and have deleterious effects on the administration of justice and the rule of
law in Guyana. They are to be denounced.

In a separate opinion of Ononaiwu and Eboe -Osuji JJ delivered by Eboe -Osuji J, they
opined that the dismissal of the appeal is borne out by difficulties attending both the
substantive content of the complaint of bias, as well as by procedural policy considerations
concerning the ripeness of the litigation.

They grant that fairness must attend decisions in public office, and fairness abjures bias.
But the law eschews the blinkered view in the appraisal of bias. That appraisal is not done
exclusively from the complainant’s point of view, registering only his g rievances, and
disregarding everything else. Bias is assessed from the point of view of the fair -minded,
reasonable observer fully informed of all the material facts and circumstances. It means
that the complainant’s grievance of bias must be appraised through the spectrum of all the
facts and circumstances in the given case. While a fair -minded and informed observer
should be a man or woman of the world, (s)he is also not to be led astray by ‘conspiracy
theories’ in the absence of credible evidence.

In this case, the approach outlined above thus requires account to be taken of both the
hostile comments that senior Government officials made against the Second Appellant,
and, all the considerations that bear on the Minister’s issuance of the ATP. Foremost in
that regard is the question whether the Minister who issued the ATP had a real discretion
to decline issuing it. If not, the complaint against the Minister accused of bias  becomes
largely academic, because no Minister would have free rein to decline issuing the ATP. In
that regard, some of the main considerations would include the incidence of external
factors that pressed against the Minister presented with the extradition request received in
a case like this. These include not only the sovereign acts of the Requesting State
(evidenced by the accompanying indictments and arrest warrants) that culminated  in the
extradition request that was made; but, also, the incidence of international obligations
(arising through extradition treaties or treaties on transnational crimes) implicated in the
notion of extradition.

Then again, the fact that the fair -minded and informed observer accepts that the case of
bias is fully made out in relation to the issuance of an ATP, does not mean that procedural
policy considerations would accept an attack against the ATP as ripe for litigation in every
case—outside the judicial proceedings that are an integral part of the extradition process.
This is because the extradition process, beginning with the committal proceedings, is
amply equipped with precisely the facility of judicial revie w, to remedy any injustice
occasioned by a biased issuance of an ATP. There is no need, as a general proposition, for
a separate track of judicial review for the ATP alone. At the inception of the committal
proceedings, it is enough for the Requested Perso n to register an early preliminary
objection against the ATP. Thereafter, any appeal or judicial review of the ruling on the
preliminary objection attacking the ATP should await the completion of the committal
proceedings. It is at the proper time when the challenge to the ATP is ripe for litigation
that the fair-minded and informed observer’s assessment of bias will be fully brought to
bear.

At the appropriate time for the inquiry into bias, the fair -minded and informed observer
must consider all the facts and circumstances of the case: including, as in this case,
whether the conducts complained against as indicia of bias were gratuitous on the part of
those impugned; or whether the impugned conduct was provoked by the complainant, thus
depriving him of clean hands in the overall circumstances of the case. On the facts and
circumstances of the present case, the Second Appellant does not have cl ean hands. He
provoked verbal attacks against him, by his own earlier attacks against Government
officials or his own willing participation in a general brawl of political calumny.

Having regard to the opinions expressed, this Court decides:

(1) The application for special leave to appeal from the decision of the Court of Appeal
is granted.

(2) The substantive appeal is dismissed.

(3) The interim stay of the extradition proceedings imposed by this Court on 25 March
2026 is hereby lifted.

(4) There shall be no order as to costs before this Court.

(5) The question of costs in the courts below is reserved.

ANDERSON P AND BARROW J:

Introduction

[1] By an urgent application dated 20 March 2026, the Applicants sought special leave
from this Court pursuant to s 8 of the Caribbean Court of Justice Act1 (‘CCJ Act’)
to challenge a judgment of the Court of Appeal of Guyana. That judgment upheld
the decision of the High Court that extradition committal proceedings against the
Applicants could continue; proceedings which were commenced pursuant to the
issuance by the Minister of Home Affairs of an Authority to Proceed ( ‘ATP’)
requiring the magistrate to proceed with extradition  proceedings against the
Applicants in accordance with the Fugitive Offenders Act 2 (‘the Act’). Section
12(1) of the Act authorised the Minister to issue the ATP, but s 12(2) prohibited the
Minister from doing so, ‘if it appears to him that an order for the extradition of the
person concerned could not lawfully be made, or would not in fact be made, … in
accordance with this Act.’

[2] In judicial review proceedings brought before them, the courts below held that the
committal proceedings could continue because the Applicants had not established
that in issuing the ATP , the Minister was affected by bias . Before this Court the
Applicants sought special leave to appeal that decision. Should such leave be
granted, the Applicants invited this Court to treat the hearing for leave as the
hearing of the intended appeal  and to overturn the finding that bias had not been
established. The Applicants also sought a stay of  the committal proceedings
pending the determination of their special leave application.

[3] At a Case Management Conference held on  25 March 2026, this Court ordered
that the hearing of the application for special leave be treated as the hearing of the
substantive appeal and fixed the hearing date for 21 April 2026. Further, this Court
granted an interim stay of the  extradition proceedings before  the court of
committal. Those proceedings were stayed  until the determination of the special
leave application or of the substantive appeal, or further order of this Court.

1 Cap 3:07.
2 Cap10:04.
[4] The Court has now read and considered the written submissions and heard lengthy
and skilful oral arguments from the parties, together with cited statutory, judicial,
and other authorities. Counsel on both sides are to be commended for the cogency
and erudition of their written and oral arguments which have provided very
considerable assistance to the Court in this matter.

[5] Upon deliberate and mature reflection, the Court has concluded that special leave
to appeal ought to be granted , but that the substantive appeal must be dismissed.
In consequence, the interim stay of the extradition committal proceedings must be
lifted. The following are our reasons for these decisions.

Background

(a) Authority to Proceed with Committal Proceedings

[6] A request for extradition dated 28 October 2025, was submitted by the Government
of the United States of America  (‘USA’) to the Government of the Co-operative
Republic of Guyana pursuant to the 1931 Extradition Treaty between the USA and
the United Kingdom. That treaty continued to govern the extradition arrangements
between the USA and Guyana after Guyana obtained independence  from the
United Kingdom in 1966. The request was for the Applicants to be extradited to
the USA to stand trial on federal indictments. Documents supporting that request
were conveyed to the Minister of  Home Affairs, the First Respondent  in this
application.

[7] On 30 October 2025, the Minister issued the ATP pursuant to s 12 of the Act.
Pursuant to the ATP, Principal Magistrate Judy Latchman, the Third Respondent
in this application, issued warrants of arrest for the Applicants who were duly
arrested and appeared before the Magistrate. They were granted bail pending the
hearing and determination of the committal proceedings, which commenced on 6
January 2026 . As described earlier, these  committal proceedings were stayed
pending the determination by this Court of the lawfulness of the issuance of the
ATP.

[8] The sole ground on which the Applicants sought to challenge the continuation of
committal proceedings against them was bias. They alleged that the bias was both
actual and apparent . The circumstances  which g ave rise to that bias, as the
Applicants contend, can be stated succinctly.

(b) Circumstances Giving Rise to Alleged Bias

[9] The Applicants were at one time close asso ciates and supporters of the People’s
Progressive Party/Civic ( ‘PPP/C’) coalition which currently forms the
Government of Guyana. A rupture in that relationship occurred after  the United
States Government imposed sanctions on the Applicants for alleged criminal
activities. Those activities were said to include evasion of import and export duty,
taxes, and bribery of Governmental officials. The Applicants have never been
convicted of these or any other offences under the laws of Guyana or any other
country.

[10] From about June 2024, the Applicants became outspoken and fierce critics of the
PPP/C Government. Subsequently, the Second Applicant entered the political fray
and formed his own political party , ‘We Invest in Nationhood’ (‘WIN’). He was
supported financially by his father, the First Applicant. WIN contested the general
election of 1 September 2025, and its list of candidates was successful in gaining
16 seats in Parliament, sufficient to have the Second Applicant appointed as the
Leader of the Opposition. He was sworn into that office on 26 January 2026. The
First Applicant holds no political office.

[11] During the election campaign, the current President, Vice-President and Attorney
General of Guyana made repeated reference in speeches and interviews to the
Applicants’ alleged criminal activities.  The Applicants were labelled as
‘criminals’, ‘tax frauds’, ‘dishonest’ , ‘robbers’ and ‘guilty’ of the very offences
which formed the subject of the ATP. The Attorney General, the Second
Respondent in this application, is alleged to have stated that the Second Applicant
was a ‘criminal’ and that there would be ‘repercussions’ if he was elected to
Parliament. The now Minister of Home Affairs was  present when some of these
statements were made but there is no allegation that she herself made any reference
to the Applicants’ alleged criminal activities. The only specific allegation  made
against her was that she mocked the Second Applicant during one of her campaign
speeches. We return to the nature of that ridicule at [99].

Proceedings before the High Court

[12] The proceedings before the High Court were initiated on 23 December 2025, when
the Applicants brought an action for judicial review. Among the orders sought were
declarations that the issuance of the ATP, the advice from the Second Respondent
on the preparation of the ATP, and the issuance of the warrants for the arrest of the
Applicants were all in breach of natural justice . Orders of certiorari were sought
to quash the ATP and the warrants. Orders of prohibition were requested to prohibit
the First and Second Respondents from making any further determination or taking
any further step to facilitate the extradition of the Applicants, save and except duly
delegating their functions in respect of the extradition pursuant to s 27 of the
Interpretation and General Clauses  Act,3 the Carltona principle, or any other
lawful mechanism. A stay of the committal proceedings , costs, and such further
relief as the court may see fit, were also sought.

[13] On 4 February 2026, Singh CJ (Ag) (‘the Chief Justice’) dismissed the application
and refused the stay of the extradition proceedings. The Chief Justice held that in
issuing the ATP the Minister was exercising an executive and not a judicial
function and that ‘bias in the judicial sense is not transposed automatically to
executive decision-making.’ The Chief Justice also found that the allegations of
bias had not been established, since it would be ‘absurd’ to conclude that the fact

3 Cap 2:01.
that the Minister heard her colleagues ’ expressions of disdain for the Applicants
necessarily meant that she was tainted with bias . Costs were awarded to each of
the three Respondents to be paid on or before 27 February 2026.
Proceedings before the Court of Appeal

[14] On 5 February 2026, the Applicants appealed to the Court of Appeal . On 11
February 2026, they again applied for a stay of the extradition proceedings along
with an urgent hearing of the appeal  along with the other orders they had sought
in the High Court. On 16 February 2026, the Court of Appeal expedited the hearing
of the appeal but refused the stay of the committal proceedings. Accordingly, those
extradition proceedings progressed even while the appeal was pending.

[15] On 17 March 2026, George-Wiltshire, C  (Ag) ( ‘the Chancellor ’) delivered the
unanimous written  decision of the Court of Appeal  dismissing t he appeal. The
Notice of Appeal had set out  14 grounds but the court considered that the focus
was essentially on two issues: (i) whether the rule against bias applies at all to the
Minister’s decision to issue the ATP under s 12 of the Act; and (ii) whether having
regard to s 27 of the Interpretation and General Clauses Act and the Carltona
principle, there was any requirement for the Minister to delegate the statutory
power conferred on her by the Act, a nd for the advice in relation to the Act to be
delegated to another person other than the Attorney General.

[16] The court set out the provisions of s s 7, 11 and 12 of the Act and focussed on the
central issue of whether bias applies to the issuance of the ATP. The court decided
that in the context of the Act, the Minister exercised an administrative function and
therefore that the issue of bias did not arise. The court found support for this view
in the reasoning of Franklin v Minister of Town and Country Planning4 in which a
Minister at a public meeting prior to the enactment of The New Towns Act gave a
speech outlining the need to form new towns to relieve the density of the
population of London and the reasons the Stevenage area was well -suited to

4 [1948] AC 87.
accommodate such a new town. Following the passage of the Act, the Minister, in
the exercise of his duty to designate new towns under the Act, circulated a draft
order for the establishment of a new town in the Stevenage area. Objections
received by landow ners in the Stevenage area to the draft order triggered the
Minister’s obligation under the Act to appoint a person to hold a public inquiry.
After carefully considering the report of that public inquiry and the submissions
made to him by all concerned local authorities and parties, the Minister proceeded
to make the final order designating a new town in the Stevenage area, the
objections notwithstanding. The Applicants in that case challenged the order of the
Minister on the ground that the statements made by him at the public meeting prior
to the passage of the Act tainted his decision with bias. That challenge was
dismissed on the basis that, ‘no judicial or quasi-judicial duty was imposed on the
Minister in the discharge of his statutory duties, those duties being purely
administrative; the only question was whether he had complied with the statutory
direction regarding the appointment of a person to hold the public enquiry.’

[17] The Court of Appeal decided that all that was required was for  the Minister to
address her mind to and comply with the statutory considerations and requirements
regarding the issuance of an ATP . There was no evidence that the matters to be
considered regarding the issuance of the ATP were not considered by  her. The
Chancellor further characteri sed as ‘preposterous’ the contention that  bias was
evident in the minimal legal advice  provided to the Minister by the Attorney
General. There was ‘no evidence to support a finding that such advice could be
tainted with bias.’

[18] Having determined that bias could not arise, the court nevertheless, for
completeness, addressed whether a fair-minded person would consider that there
was bias in the  issuance of the ATP by the Minister.  The court rejected any
suggestion that the category of automatic disqualification from R v Bow Street
Metropolitan Stipendiary Magistrate , ex p Pinochet Ugarte (No 2) ,5 which

5 [2000] 1 AC 119.
required the existence of a direct proprietary, pecuniary, or equivalently close
personal interest in the outcome of the proceedings by the decision-maker, applied

[32] Before considering the issues, it is necessary to set out the statutory framework
governing and related to the issuance of the ATP.
Statutory Framework

[33] There are three distinct phases to the extradition process. The first is the issuance
of the ATP. This commences with a request for extradition made under s 9 of the
Act. Section 9 provides for the making of a request to the Minister and specifies
the documentation that should accompany the request. There is no allegation in
this case that there was non-compliance with s 9.

[34] As foreshadowed, s  12 authorises the Minister to issue the ATP . The section
provides as follows:

12. (1) On receipt of a request under section 9 the Minister may
issue an order in Form 1 (hereinafter referred to as ‘authority to proceed’)
signifying to a magistrate that the request for the extradition of the person
mentioned in the order has been received and requiring the magistrate to
proceed with the case in accordance with the provisions of this Act.

(2)  The Minister shall not issue an authority to proceed if it appears
to him that an order for the extradition of  the person concerned could not
lawfully be made, or would not in fact be made, in accordance with this
Act.

(3)  Subject to this Act, no person shall be dealt with by a magistrate
under this Act except in pursuance of an authority to proceed issued by the
Minister.

[35] It is evident from s 12(2) that the Minister is required to give some consideration
to whether the requirements for lawful extradition have been met  by the request
and accompanying documentation. Section 8 provides for the general restrictions
on extradition  of persons from Guyana . There was no complaint in these
proceedings that s 8 was not complied with  such that the ATP to the Magistrate
would be invalidated . But s 12(2) goes further and  prohibits the Minister from
issuing an authority to proceed if it appears to her that an order for the extradition
‘could not’ lawfully be made, or ‘would not’ in fact be made, in accordance with
the Act. The Minister must therefore exercise some discretion in weighing whether
those factors listed in s 17(2) and s 26, as appropriate , would in fact result in the
extradition order not being made. Again, no argument was made before us , or in
the courts below,  that these statutory provisions were not considered by the
Minister.

[36] The second phase is judicial and commences with the proceedings for committal
before the Magistrate. Section 15 contains the provisions for the committal
proceedings. Pertinently, s 15(4) provides:

(4) Where an authority to proceed has been issued in respect of a person
arrested as referred to in subsection ( 1) and the court of committal is
satisfied, after hearing any evidence tendered in support of the request for
the extradition of that person or on behalf of that person, that the offence
to which the authority relates is an extraditable offence and is furth er
satisfied, -

(a) where the person is accused of the offence, that the evidence
would be sufficient to warrant his trial for that offence if it
had been committed within the jurisdiction of that court; or

(b) where the person is alleged to be unlawfully at large after
conviction of the offence, that he has been so convicted and
appears to be so at large,

the court shall, unless his committal is prohibited by any other provision of
this Act, commit him to custody by warrant in Form 6 to await his
extradition under this Act, but if the court is not so satisfied or if  his
committal is so prohibited, the court shall discharge him from custody.

[37] Section 15(4) requires the Magistrate to consider whether the  extradition is
prohibited by s 8, because s 8 provides for  general restrictions on extradition of
persons from Guyana. The Magistrate must also consider whether the committal
is prohibited by any other provision of the Act.

[38] A further step in the judicial phase is the habeas corpus application. A person
committed to custody to await extradition is entitled to make a habeas corpus
application. Section 17 provides as follows:

17. (1) A person committed to custody under section 15 (4) may
make an application to the High Court for habeas corpus within fifteen days
from the day on which the order of committal is made and, on such
application, the High Court may, without prejudice to any other jurisdiction
of that Court, exercise any of the powers conferred upon it by this Act.

(2) On an application made by any person under subsection (1),
the High Court may order the person committed to be discharged from
custody if that court is satisfied that by reason of-

(a)  the trivial nature of the offence of which he is
accused or was convicted;

(b)  the passage of time since he is alleged to have
committed it or to have become unlawfully at large,
as the case may be;

(c)  the accusation against him being not made in good
faith or in the interests of justice; or

(d)  any other sufficient cause,

it would, having regard to all the circumstances, be unjust or oppressive to
extradite him.

[39] Section 21 gives a right of appeal to the Court of Appeal. As far as relevant, s 21(1)
provides that:

21. (1) Any person whose extradition is sought, or the Government
of any Commonwealth country or treaty territory which is seeking his
extradition, if dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court on an
application for habeas corpus under section 17 ... may, within fifteen days
of the pronouncing of the decision, appeal to the Court of Appeal on any
question of law.

[40] In determining the application for habeas corpus, the High Court and the Court of
Appeal must per force consider whether extradition is prohibited under s 8. This
is because s 8 itself requires that the High Court, where any application is made
under s 17(1), and the Court of Appeal, where any question of law arises in any
appeal under s 21, must consider the s 8 prohibitions.

[41] The third and final phase is the surrender of the fugitive. This phase consists of the
issuance of the warrant by the Minister under s 26 ordering the extradition. As far
as relevant, s 26 provides:

26. (1) Where a person is committed to custody under this Act to
await his extradition and is not discharged from custody by the High Court
on an application for habeas corpus or the Court of Appeal on appeal from
the decision of the High Court, the Minister may by  warrant in Form 7
order him to be extradited to the Commonwealth country or Treaty territory
by or on behalf of which the request for his  extradition was made unless
the extradition of that person is prohibited  by section 8 or this section or
the Minister decides under this section to make no such order in his case.

(2) The Minister shall not make an order under this section in
the case of any person if it appears to the Minister, on any ground
mentioned in section 17 (2), that it would be unjust or oppressive to
extradite that person.

[42] Section 26 contains other provisions prohibiting the Minister from making the
extradition order in certain cases and granting a broad discretion whether to grant
the extradition order in other cases.

(ii) Whether the Rule against Bias Applies to the Ministerial Grant of the ATP

[53] The rule against bias is an aspect of procedural fairness which is itself a
foundational principle of Caribbean public law. Procedural fairness ensures that
when the state exercises power over individuals, decisions are made fairly,

33 Ramdass (n 18).
34 (TT CA, 13 December 2007) at [56]‒[58].
transparently, and without prejudice. A fundamental principle running through the
common law and entrenched in Caribbean constitutions is that every exercise of
state power must be attended by procedural fairness. This principle must
necessarily apply to the issuance of the ATP which is a quin tessential exercise of
the power to initiate the machinery of the State to permit the extradition of citizens
to a foreign land. The extent of the application of the rule against bias, however,
must be determined by the context in which this state power is exercised.

[54] The common law foundational requirement of procedural fairness – sometimes
called natural justice – is underpinned by two core elements. One is the hearing
rule, which entails the right of a person to be heard before a decision affecting his
rights or interests is made. The other is the rule against bias which is the
requirement that decision-makers must act impartially.

[55] The rule against bias component of procedural fairness has deep historical roots.
It originated in Roman law reflecting the notion that it is unfair for a person to be
the judge of a matter in which he has a personal interest. This limit on adjudicative
power entered English common law through the natural law tradition and was
crystallised by Sir Edward Coke when he famously restated it in Latin as  nemo
judex in causa sua (‘no one should be a judge in his own cause’). In Dr Bonham’s
case35 in 160 9, Sir Edward held that the College of Physicians could not both
prosecute and adjudicate a case from which it benefited financially.

[56] In modern times it has been widely recognised that the rule against bias proscribes:
(1) actual bias, where the decision -maker has a personal interest or prejudice; (2)
apparent bias, where a reasonable observer might suspect partiality; and (3)
institutional bias, where structural arrangements create the clear risk of unfairness.
For present purposes, we are concerned only with (1) and (2), that is , actual or
apparent bias.

35 (1609) 8 Co Rep 113 b, 77 ER 646.
[57] Both types were involved in Dimes v Proprietors of the Grand Junction Canal 36
in which the decision by Lord Chancellor Cottenham in a case involving a canal
company was set aside after it emerged that he owned shares in the company. The
House of Lords held that any direct pecuniary interest in the outcome of a case, no
matter how small, automatically disqualifies a judge from deciding that case.
Further, the House considered that quite apart from actual bias, the conduct of the
Lord Chancellor also gave rise to the appearance of bias. The current formulation
of the test for apparent bias is generally taken to be that stated in Porter v Magill,37
namely, whether the fair -minded and informed observer, having considered the
facts, would conclude that there was a real possibility that the decision-maker was
biased.

[58] These common law principles are reified in the Caribbean constitutional legal
order which protects rights implicated in the extradition process. These include the
right to liberty38, security of the person 39, the right to freedom of movement 40, as
well as the right to respect for one’s private and family life. For comparison, the
Supreme Court of Canada has consistently held that extradition decisions must
comply with the principles of fundamental justice under the Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms which encompass procedural fairness and impartial
decision-making.41 The extradition process engages heightened scrutiny, such that
any substantive defect in fairness —including actual bias or the appearance of bias
— could well invalidate the process.42

[59] The direct question whether the rule against bias applies to the exercise of
ministerial power to grant the ATP allows, therefore, only one answer. It does ,
since the rule against bias is of general application in public law. The rule against
bias is not limited to judicial or quasi -judicial decision-making but applies to all

Respondent is not and cannot be immune from the sovereign principles embedded
in procedural fairness or natural justice, which include the rule against bias. This
is simply another way of saying that state power cannot be validly or properly
wielded for private interest or preferences.

[60] An important caveat is necessary, however. In law, the term ‘bias’ spans a wide
spectrum and may be personal, pecuniary, official, or implicit. Legislation
consistent with the Guyana C onstitution may require that certain decisions be
made by government officials and this could have an impact on the content and
application of the rule. This leads, then, to the fundamental principle, which we
examine immediately below, that the rule against bias must be interpreted
contextually.

Context for the Application of Procedural Fairness Including the Rule against
Bias

[61] Notwithstanding the omnipresence of the requirement for procedural fairness,
including the rule against bias, not every exercise of state power must be attended
by the same rigour or full application of the principle. Context is everything. The
requirements of procedural fairness, including the rule against bias, vary
depending on the circumstances in which it is applied. The standard required in
judicial decision -making may be di fferent from that required in ministerial
decision-making which may in turn differ from that required in relation to police
investigations and the prosecution of charges. As L’Heureux-Dubé J persuasively
stated in Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)44:

21.   The existence of a duty of fairness  … does not determine what
requirements will be applicable in a given set of circumstances.  As I wrote

in Knight v. Indian Head School Division No. 19 , … ‘the concept of
procedural fairness is eminently variable and its content is to be decided in
the specific context of each case ’.  All of the circumstances must be
considered in order to determine the content of the duty of procedural
fairness…

[62] The principle enunciated in 1999 in Baker v Canada echoed earlier decisions and
has been subsequently affirmed by courts in the Commonwealth. A significant
body of case -law to this effect exists in the Caribbean; 45 United Kingdom; 46
Australia;47 and Singapore. 48 Courts across the Commonwealth have routinely
affirmed that procedural fairness is a flexible, context -dependent concept whose
content must reflect the nature of the decision and decision-maker in question.

Application of Rule against Bias in Extradition

[63] It follows from the foregoing that, as regards extradition, the nature and content of
the rule against bias is determined by the nature of the decision -maker and the
stage at which the decision is being taken. The point was made with clarity by the
Supreme Court of Canada in United States of America v Dynar:49
128.    The principles of fundamental justice guaranteed under s. 7 of the
Charter vary according to the context of the proceedings in which they are
raised.  It is clear that there is no entitlement to the most favourable
procedures imaginable...   For example , more attenuated levels of
procedural safeguards have been held to be appropriate at immigration
hearings than would apply in criminal trials... The same approach is equally
applicable to an extradition proceeding.   While it was stated ... that the
committal hearing in the extradition process is ‘certainly judicial in its
nature and warrants the application of the full panoply of procedural
safeguards’, it was held that the extent and nature of procedural protection

45 A-G v Mohammed TT 1985 CA 56 (CARILAW), (11 November 1985); Bahamas Air Traffic Controllers Union v Government of
The Commonwealth of the Bahamas BS 2001 SC 23 (CARILAW), (18 April 2001); Adams v Commissioner of Police AI 2009 HC 19
(CARILAW), (28 August 2009).
46 Ridge v Baldwin [1964] AC 40; Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374; Lloyd v McMahon
[1987] 1 AC 625; R v Secretary of State for the Home Dept, ex p Doody [1994] 1 AC 531.
47 Kioa v West (1985) 159 CLR 550; Minister for Immigration and Border Protection v SZSSJ (2016) 259 CLR 180; AB v Independent
Broad-based Anti-Corruption Commission  (2024) 278 CLR 300.
48 Public Prosecutor v Pek Lian Guan [2026] SGHC 62; DSV v DSU [2026] SGHC 128.
49 [1997] 2 SCR 462 (citations omitted).
guaranteed by s. 7 of the Charter in an extradition proceeding will depend
on the context in which it is claimed....
129.    The context and purpose of the extradition hearing will shape the
level of procedural protection that is available to a fugitive....

[64] For present purposes, it is useful to consider just two of the categories of decision-
making involved in the extradition process traversed earlier: the ministerial and
judicial decision-making phases.

(a)  Judicial Decision-making in Extradition Proceedings

[65] The rule against bias finds its most rigorous application in the judicial decision -
making phase of the extradition process. As we have seen, the smallest direct
pecuniary interest in the outcome of a case is equated to actual bias and
automatically disqual ifies a judge. 50 But apparent bias will also be fatal to the
judge’s participation in extradition decision -making. In United States of America
v Dynar51 the Supreme Court of Canada confirmed that extradition hearings before
a judge are judicial proceedings and the rule against bias applies with maximum
rigour. Likewise, in Canada v  Schmidt52 the Court stressed that extradition
hearings are judicial in character, requiring strict adherence to impartiality.

[66] The most extreme example of strict adherence to impartiality in judicial decision-
making in extradition is probably the oft-cited case of R v Bow Street Metropolitan
Stipendiary Magistrate, ex p Pinochet Ugarte (No  2).53 Failure by Lord Hoffman
to disclose that he was an unpaid director and chairman of A.I.C. Ltd, a charity
wholly controlled by Amnesty International, which was an intervener supporting
Pinochet’s extraction, sufficed for the House of Lords to set aside its previous
ruling on which the Law Lord had sat. The House held that if the absolute
impartiality of the judiciary is to be maintained, there must be a rule which

50 Dimes (n 36).
51 [1997] 2 SCR 462.
52 [1987] 1 SCR 500.
53 Pinochet Ugarte (n 5).
automatically disqualified a judge who was involved, whether personally or as a
director of a company, in promoting the same causes in the same organi sation
which was a party to the suit. It thus extended the strict, absolute legal concept of
automatic disqualification on grounds of purely financial interests to non -
pecuniary interests. Even the appearance of partiality was sufficient to vitiate
judicial proceedings where liberty is at stake.

[67] It should be noted that the rule of automatic disqualification for bias is now under
strain. Lord Hope has described the Pinochet decision as ‘highly technical’54 and
Lord Bingham has stated that any extension would be ‘undesirable’.55 The
automatic disqualification rule has been rejected in Canada, 56 South Africa,57 and
Ireland58 on the ground that apparent bias was sufficient to ensure that justice was
seen to be done. This Court’s attention has been drawn to the severe academic
criticism of A Olowofoyeku, ‘The Nemo Judex Rule: The Case Against Automatic
Disqualification’59 as follows:

…automatic disqualification is draconian, disproportionate and
unnecessary. There is nothing that can be achieved by automatic
disqualification that cannot be achieved by an application of the real
danger/reasonable apprehension test. On the other hand, application of the
automatic disqualification rule may well lead to the disqualification of
judges in situations wherein a closer inspection of the circumstances would
reveal that there was never any realistic possibility of bias.

[68] However, these criticisms concern the automaticity of disqualification and argue
that the informed objective observer provides a better test for debarment from
judicial decision-making on the ground of impartiality. They do not detract from
the principle that t he rule against bias applies in full at the committal, habeas
corpus, and judicial review stages. Extradition hearings are court proceedings
governed by procedural fairness, applied with maximum rigo ur; a principle

54 Meerabux v A-G of Belize (2005) 66 WIR 113 (BZ PC) at [21].
55 Locabail (UK) Ltd v Bayfield Properties Ltd [2000] QB 451 at 465.
56 Wewaykum Indian Band v Canada [2003] 2 SCR 259 at [72]‒[73].
57 Bernert v Absa Bank Ltd [2011] 4 LRC 395 at [52]‒[55].
58 Goode Concrete v CRH plc [2015] 3 IR 493.
59 Abimbola A Olowofoyeku, ‘The Nemo Judex Rule: The Case Against Automatic Disqualification’ [2000] PL 456. See, also, R v
Governor of Pentonville Prison, ex p Osman [1989] 3 All ER 701.
reinforced by comparative authority from final courts of appeal around the
Commonwealth.60

(b)  Ministerial Decision-making in the Extradition Process

[69] It has been suggested that the rule against bias does not apply to ministerial
decision-making. In the case of  Franklin v Minister of Town and Country
Planning, the Minister was allowed to designate areas for a new town. Objectors
challenged the designation order arguing that the Minister had publicly stated that
his mind was ‘already made up’ before considering the objections. The House of
Lords ruled that the Minister’s duty was purely administrative and therefore that
the statutory requirement to hold a public inquiry was merely to ensure the
Minister was properly informed, not to subject hi m to the same strict impartiality
standards expected of a court of law. Lord Thankerton stated61:

My Lords, I could wish that the use of the word ‘bias’ should be confined
to its proper sphere. Its proper significance, in my opinion, is to denote a
departure from the standard of even-handed justice which the law requires
from those who occupy judicial office, or those who are commonly
regarded as holding a quasi -judicial office, such as an arbitrator . The
reason for this clearly is that, having to adjudicate as between two or more
parties, he must come to his adjudication with an independent mind,
without any inclination or bias towards one side or other in the dispute. As
Lord Cranworth L.C. says in Ranger v. Great Western Ry. Co. (1): “A judge
ought to be, and is supposed to be, indifferent between the parties. He has,
or is supposed to have, no bias inducing him to lean to the one side rather
than to the other. In ordinary cases it is a just ground of exception to a judge
that he is not indifferent, and the fact that he is himself a party, or interested
as a party, affords the strongest proof that he cannot be indifferent.” … But,
in the present case, the respondent having no judicial duty, the only
question is what the respondent actually did, that is, whether in fact he did
genuinely consider the report and the objections.

[70] It is not necessary to rehash the evolution in the law. Suffice it to say that it is now
widely conceded that the law has moved on over the past 78 years and that there
is now no longer any attempt to classify decisions as judicial, quasi -judicial,

60 Pinochet Ugarte (n 5); United States of America v Cobb [2001] 1 SCR 587; United States v Ferras [2006] 2 SCR 77.
61 Franklin (n 4) at 103‒104 (emphasis added).
administrative, or executive for the purpose of determining the applicability of
natural justice including the rule against bias. No category of decision -making is
truly exempt: R v Secretary of State for the Environment, ex p Kirkstall Valley
Campaign Ltd62.

[71] The matter was recently considered at length by the Judicial Committee of the
Privy Council in Ramdass v Minister of Finance where it was urged that there was
a hard and fast principle of law that the rule against bias does not apply to non -
adjudicative decisions and was inapplicable as a matter of law to the Minister’s
decisions in that case. It was further urged that even if the Minister’s motives might
have been political or self -interested, the fact remained that he merely made a
recommendation to set up an investigation and moreover that the investigation
team is itself independent and that its independence had not been challenged. The
Privy Council disagreed and stated63:

The Board does not accept that the question whether the rule against bias
applies in this case is a pure question of law. The rule against bias forms
an essential requirement of procedural fairness or natural justice. It is well-
established that what proce dural fairness requires in any given situation
depends on the specific facts and context of the individual case. Moreover,
the authorities cited by the appellants make clear that, in deciding whether
it is arguable that the rule against bias applies to the  decisions that are
challenged in this judicial review, the question is not whether those
decisions are of a certain type or category – whether judicial, quasi -
judicial, or in some looser sense, adjudicative. Rather, the focus is on the
facts of the case a nd the context in which the impugned decisions were
taken. None of the cases cited by the appellants establish, as a matter of
law, that the rule against bias can never apply in a non -adjudicative
context, no matter the facts.

[72] Respectfully, this is clearly correct. A decision adopted because of the bias of the
decision-maker is necessarily a decision for an improper purpose. Public power
may only be wielded for proper purposes and not for improper or private purposes.
Procedural fairness serves to discipline state power, enhance the legitimacy of
public decisions, and protect individual dignity by ensuring that those whose rights

62 Kirkstall Valley Campaign Ltd (n 20) at 323‒324.
63 Ramdass (n 18) at [51].
or interests are affected are treated fairly and impartially. A public decision
actuated without justification and purely by malice or bias breaches the guarantee
of procedural fairness.

[73] It should be pointed out for perspective, en passant , that decision -making
regarding prosecutions, the laying of criminal charges, and the launching of
investigations has been said to be an obvious area in which the rule against bias
does not apply. A leading case often cited for this proposition is R v Secretary of
State for Trade ex p Perestrello  in which a complaint of bias on the ground of a
pre-determined decision to launch an investigation, was commented upon by Wolff
J in the following terms64:

When one considers the functions of those officers, it really is wholly
inappropriate to talk about them not being regarded as biased if they are
performing their functions properly. Take this very case – it is, in my view,
almost inevitable that before the powers under section 109 are exercised,
the officers  concerned, and through his officers, the Secretary of State ,
must regard the situation as one where there are matters to be investigated.
They are acting in a policing role. Their function is to see whether their
suspicions are justified by what they find, and that being so, it is wholly
inappropriate for the case to be approached in the same way as one would
approach a person performing a n ormal judicial role or quasi -judicial
role; a situation where the person is making a determination.

[74] Also, in Law Association of Trinidad and Tobago ( ‘LATT’) v Chief Justice of
Trinidad and Tobago,65 the LATT had resolved to establish a committee to inquire
into allegations made against the Chief Justice who brought judicial review
proceedings challenging the inquiry on grounds including apparent bias. The Court
of Appeal rejected this challenge on the basis t hat apparent bias did not apply to
LATT given that it was not proposing to determine the rights or liabilities of the
Chief Justice. The LATT was not a decision -maker in relation to any rights,
liabilities, or responsibilities exercisable by the Chief Justice.

64 Perestrello (n 30) at 35B (emphasis added).
65 LATT (n 32).
[75] Comparably, as was stated by the court in Perestrello, it would be inappropriate to
apply the bias rule to police officers ‘if they are performing their functions
properly.’66 Similarly, in LATT, Mendonca JA noted that a prosecutor has no
liability to the accused even where the prosecution does not result in a conviction,
‘unless he acts with malice .’67  The fairness of this approach is  reinforced by
recalling the point that upon acquittal of a criminal charge the tort of malicious
prosecution is always available to a person targeted by the police or prosecutor or
investigator because of personal grudge  or bias. Accordingly, even in the laying
and prosecution of criminal charges and in the commencement or continuation of
investigations there is room for the application of the procedural fairness and the
rule against bias, albeit ex post facto.

[76] In any event, any inapplicability of the rule against bias to prosecutorial decisions
does not operate in the present case because, as several Commonwealth decisions
have made clear, ministerial decision -making at the ATP stage is subject to
procedural fairness. A good starting place is the older English concept of ‘order to
proceed’ under s 7 of the Extradition Act of 1989 (equivalent to authorit y to
proceed). In R v Secretary of State for the Home Dept, ex p Norgren 68 Lord
Bingham accepted that the legality of the order could be challenged on judicial
review grounds although he ultimately concluded that the Home Secretary was not
guilty of procedural unfairness in acting as he did.

[77] Norgren was relied upon in Warner v Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago69
to subject the issuance of the ATP to judicial review for procedural fairness. The
Privy Council made clear that i n ‘considering the requirements of fairness in this
case all of [the relevant] factors need to be taken into account ’.70 As the Attorney
General had voluntarily offered the appellant an opportunity to make
representations (which was declined), the court ruled that no procedural unfairness
had occurred in this specific factual instance. And in Ferguson v Attorney General

66 Perestrello (n 30) at 35B (Woolf J) (emphasis added).
67 LATT (n 32) at [102] (emphasis added).
68 [2000] QB 817.
69 [2022] UKPC 43 (TT).
70 ibid at [92].
of Trinidad and Tobago71 the Trinidadian courts extensively mapped out the ‘due
process of law’ required across the entire life cycle of extradition proceedings. It
was emphasised that because an extradition request could infringe upon
constitutional rights to liberty and freedom of movement, any executive
decisions—including the initial evaluation leading to an ATP —fall within the
strict bounds of reviewable executive discretion.

[78] Another way of approaching the applicability of bias in the ministerial issuance of
the ATP is to consider the levels of permissible judicial scrutiny. In judicial
decision-making the rule against bias applies in its purest form as illustrated in the
Pinochet case and the courts will intervene at the slightest impropriety. Ministerial
decision-making is not immune from the need for procedural fairness —including
the rule against bias  but ministers are politic al officials  accountable to the
parliament and must be accorded a wider margin for decision-making by the courts
particularly where their decisions do not have a direct effect on rights.

[79] It follows, therefore, that the appropriate question is not whether the rule against
bias applies to the ministerial decision to issue the ATP but rather the extent of
that application. Having established that procedural fairness including the rule
against bias is a flexible and context -dependent concept, the relevant
circumstances must be highlighted to determine the degree of applicability  of the
rule. Several factors may be identified that are important in defining the context
for the issuance of the ATP.

(i) The International Context of Extradition
[80] The rise of transnational organised crime and terrorism has necessitated
multilateral cooperation embodied in such formal global frameworks as the UN
Model Law on Extradition, but the backbone of modern international extradition
law remains the bilateral treaty. The 1931 Treaty between the United Kingdom
and the United States, to which Guyana succeeded after attaining independence

71 Ferguson (n 34). See also various judgments spanning 2008–2011.
from the United Kingdom, embodies the international obligations in respect of
extraditions on the contracting parties. Failure by Guyana to perform its
obligations under the 1931 Treaty to arrest, detain, and extradite persons in respect
of whom its co -contracting state has made the proper request, could result in
international state liability.

[81] Unreasonable delay in the performance of obligations under the 1931 Treaty could
also signal a breach. The international community has long expressed concern over
the chronic delay often encountered in extradition processes. That delay is
frequently caused through multiplicity of legal challenges. 72 Protection of the
rights of the accused does not require multiplicity of litigation and courts must be
alive to the  very real risk that the extradition infrastructure of legislation and
institutional procedures can be used simply to delay the process.

[82] Of course, it must not be forgotten that the law applicable in Guyana is the
legislation which domesticates the treaty by incorporating it into the national legal
order.  The FOA should, as far as possible, be interpreted to comply with the
Guyana’s international obligations under the 1931 Treaty. Any interpretation that
frustrates those obligations should, unless the statute clearly requires it, be
avoided. In short, judicial construction of the FOA should seek to aid the good
faith performance of Guyana’s treaty obligation, although in right of the
parliamentary power, it is the legislative requirements in the FOA that are
imperative and dispositive.

(ii) Limited Discretion Granted by FOA to the Minister in the Issuance of the
ATP

[83] Although other factors are relevant, such as the maintenance of public confidence,
the proper control of the exercise of discretion is an important indicator of the

72 United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime  (UNODC), ‘Report of the Informal Expert Working Group on Effective Extradition
Casework Practice’ (Vienna 2004).
existence and operation of the rule against bias. The greater the discretion the more
numerous the possibilities for the intrusion of bias and the more pressing the
necessity to guard against it. Correspondingly, where there is no discretion in the
decision-making there is little room for bias to be a factor and correspondingly
little scope for the operation of the rule against bias.

[84] Under the FOA m any of the functions of the Minister are indeed administrative
involving little discretion. But this is not true for all ministerial functions at the
ATP stage. As discussed earlier at [34]‒[35], s 12(2) plainly locates in the Minister
the power not to issue an ATP ‘if it appears to him’ that certain conditions for the
extradition ‘could not lawfully be made, or would not in fact be made, in
accordance with this Act ’. This wording invests the Minister with the
responsibility of making a qualitative judgment. It is, admittedly, a limited
discretion hemmed in by considerations of , for example,  compliance with
Guyana’s international obligations and purely administrative functions such as
those relating to checking that the requesting state has presented the appropriate
documentation. But it is a discretion, nonetheless,  in that s 12(2) calls for a
subjective assessment of likely statutory effects and possible judicial attitudes.

[85] Mr Mendes for the First Respondent  frankly conceded that procedural fairness
applied to the ATP process to the extent of requiring, ‘that the Minister carry out
her functions genuinely and with an open mind ’.73 This involves the Minister
having and adhering to a process that allows for the giving of genuine
consideration to the relevant factors at the issuance of the ATP stage, particularly,
those matters arising from provisions in s 12(2) of the Act (above at [34]‒[35]).
That process also accounts for both limbs of the procedural fairness requirement:
the fair hearing rule and the rule against bias.

73 Minister of Home Affairs Oneidge Walrond, ‘Submissions on behalf of the First Respondent’, Submission in Mohamed v Minister of
Home Affairs, Oneidge Walrond, GY/A/CV2026/001, 10 April 2026, [38].
[86] Perspective as to the limited purpose and effect of the ATP is obtained by referring
to s 70 of the English Extradition Act 2003 which has been the subject of several
recent amendments. That Act now provides that, in the case of requests from
certain terri tories, if the Secretary of State receives a valid extradition request
which is made in the approved way and contains the required information, he must
issue a certificate and send the request and the certificate to the judge. There are
only very limited circumstances (s 70(2)) in which the Secretary of State may
refuse to issue the certificate.  In the case of requests from other territories , the
Secretary of State is removed altogether from the process by s 2 of the Act so that
when a warrant is received by the designated authority, it is forwarded directly to
the appropriate judge if the formalities required by the section are complied with.

[87] The Canadian process indicates a similar view of the ATP as authorising an
extradition hearing to be held before the court to consider whether an individual
should be committed for extradition.74 The determination is made by counsel with
the Department of Justice Canada on behalf of the Federal Minister of Justice after
considering the request and supporting documents. Their function is simply to
decide whether to issue the ATP in accordance with the requirements of the
applicable extradition treaty, if any, and the Extradition Act.

[88] It must therefore be accepted that the ATP process attracts some , but does not
import the full panoply , of procedural rights available in judicial proceedings.
There is no right to be heard; there is no right to a decision-maker free of political
bias. There is, however, a right to a process that allows for the proper carrying out
of the ministerial function contemplated by the FOA. That is a process for the
minister’s purview bearing in mind the international and diplomatic context. It will
only be challengeable if it is clearly and manifestly a sham or  if it ‘shocks the
conscience’75 resulting in an ATP that is fatally defective.

74 Department of Justice Canada, ‘Extradition in Canada : General Overview of the Canadian Extradition Process ’ (1 March 2019 )
<https://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/cj-jp/emla-eej/extradition_eng.pdf> accessed 26 May 2026.
75 The ‘shock the conscience’ test is adopted in related aspects of Canadian extradition law: Schmidt (n 52); United States v Burns
[2001] 1 SCR 283.
(iii) Political Bias and Actual or Automatic Disqualification

[89] The legislative context represented by the FOA, has important implications for the
rule of automatic disqualification for bias. The common law rule on actual or
apparent bias, illustrated in Pinochet, has no direct applicability to political bias in
the issuance of the ATP. This necessarily follows from the deliberate investiture in
a political officeholder by parliament of the power to initiate the extradition
process. It would clearly have been within the contemplation of parliament that the
minister may well possess political bias against his or her political opponents and
in favour of his or her political allies.

[90] Therefore, a utomatic exclusion from performance of the ministerial function
because of political bias would destroy the policy design of the Act. Such exclusion
would effectively create classes of persons in respect of whom the Minister is
prohibited from exercising the ministerial functions dictated by the Act. Absent a
successful challenge to its constitutionality, the provisions and objectives of the
Act informed, as far as possible, by the terms of the treaty it was intended t o
implement, must be upheld by this Court.

(iv) Context and the Timing of the Challenge

[91] The ATP is a preliminary step in the extradition process. It is followed by the
judicial phase in which there is an adversarial contest regarding whether an
extradition order should be granted. There then follows possible habeas corpus
proceedings. Finally, there is the surrender phase in which the Minister decides
whether the fugitive should be yielded up for extradition. The sequencing of these
events provides the context for the examination of the timing of the challenge for
procedural fairness, including bias. The ministerial decision to issue the ATP does
not itself result in extradition; that very decision is subject to judicial scrutiny when
the matter comes before the courts.

[92] The matter was put into perspective in the affidavit of First Respondent , the
Minister of Home Affairs, where the following appears at [44]:

 … it did not appear to me that I was adjudicating on any dispute. There
was not yet put before me any information which contradicted any of my
conclusions. The exercise I was performing was more administrative in
nature. It involved running through a chec k list of requirements. I
appreciated that the Applicants are free to raise any question whether their
extradition is prohibited before the

items.full_text:
[2026] CCJ 1 (AJ) GY

IN THE CARIBBEAN COURT OF JUSTICE
APPELLATE JURISDICTION

ON APPEAL FROM THE COURT OF APPEAL OF
THE CO-OPERATIVE REPUBLIC OF GUYANA

CCJ Application No GYCV2025/002
GY Civil Appeal Nos 69 of 2010 and 70 of 2010

BETWEEN

 ESLENE VIGILANCE suing in her personal
  capacity and in the capacity as the executrix of the
  estate of her late husband Albert Vigilance, deceased                 APPELLANT

AND

 ROOPNARINE PERSAUD             RESPONDENT

Before:   Mr Justice Barrow
Mr Justice Jamadar
Mme Justice Ononaiwu
Mr Justice Eboe-Osuji
Mr Justice Bulkan

Date of Judgment:  20 February 2026

Appearances

Mr Teni Housty, Ms Shantel Scott-Lall and Ms Sydney Fraser for the Appellant

Mr C V Satram, Mr Mahendra Satram and Mr Ron Motilall for the Respondent

Land  — Prescriptive title — Adverse possession — Fraud — Irregularities — Application
to amend statement of claim  — Concurrent findings of lower courts  — Indefeasibility of
title — Whether trial judge erred in refusing application to amend statement of claim to
include particulars of fraud and to adduce further evidence  — Deeds Registry Act , Cap
5:01, s 22 — Title to Land (Prescription and Limitation) Act, Cap 60:02.

SUMMARY

This appeal concerns the attempt of the Vigilance estate, represented over decades by
successive personal representatives and attorneys -at-law, to overturn the prescriptive title
granted to George Estrick and the subsequent transport of the land to Roopnarine Persaud,
the respondent. The estate alleged that Estrick obtained the land by fraud, but never pleaded
or proved any fraud against Persaud, who merely purchased the land from Estrick.

The High Court dismissed the claim in 2010, finding no evidence of fraud and holding that
alleged irregularities in the Land Court process did not amount to fraud capable of
invalidating a registered title. On the day set for judgment  delivery, new counsel in the
matter made an oral application to amend the pleadings to advance a claim of fraud against
Persaud and include particulars of fraud  and to adduce further evidence. The trial judge
refused the application as far too late and prejudicial.  On appeal, the Court of Appeal
affirmed the decision of the trial judge.

Before the Caribbean Court of Justice  (‘CCJ’), the appellant sought that the Court of
Appeal’s decision be set aside  as well as costs in this Court and the courts below . The
appellant contended  that the refusal to allow amendments and admit further evidence
amounted to a miscarriage of justice, and that the courts below erred in failing to properly
assess the alleged fraudulent acquisition by  Estrick and its impact on the subsequent sale
to the respondents..

Before the CCJ, the appellant argued that the trial judge should have allowed the
amendment and considered additional evidence. Barrow J (Jamadar, Ononaiwu, Eboe -
Osuji and Bulkan JJ concurring) held that the appeal was bound to fail because the
appellant’s case rested entirely on allegations of fraud against Estrick  which were
dismissed and the claim against Estrick  was not  pursued on appeal . By the time new
counsel sought to amend the pleadings , the trial judge had already determined that there
was no evidence of fraud. Without proof of fraud by Estrick, there could be no basis for
alleging fraud against the respondent, who had acquired a derivative title from Estrick.
Therefore, the proposed amendment was both impermissibly late and legally futile.

Barrow J further emphasised the principle of indefeasibility of registered title  under s 22
of the Deeds Registry Act . Even if there were irregularities in the prescriptive title
proceedings, such defects cannot invalidate a registered title unless actual fraud is
established. Further, in the context of this appeal which was brought solely against Persaud
and not the Estricks , certain contentions as to an outdated plan, missing documents, or
alleged non-service of notices were meaningless.

Bulkan J (Barrow, Jamadar, Ononaiwu and Eboe-Osuji JJ concurring) agreed with Barrow
J that the appeal must be dismissed but went further in analysing the underlying defects in
the prescriptive title proceedings. He observed that although the estate failed procedurally
to pursue on appeal claims against Estrick, the evidence at trial revealed several troubling
features of Estrick’s claim. These matters, while incapable of assisting the appellant at this
stage, raised legitimate concerns about the standards applied in the Land Court and the
need for stronger safeguards in prescriptive title applications.

Bulkan J stressed that prescriptive title requires rigorous proof of actual, exclusive, and
undisturbed possession, and that applicants must provide full, frank disclosure of all
material facts. He compared Guyana’s system with the more structured approach  used in
Trinidad and Tobago, which includes detailed guidelines, up -to-date surveys, and
independent field investigations. In light of the prevalence of land fraud and procedural
failures affecting litigants like the Vigilance estate, he called for more s tringent judicial
oversight and legislative reform.

The appeal was dismissed with costs to the respondent.

Cases referred to:
Adams v London  [1964] LRBG 188 ; Apsara Restaurants (Barbados) Ltd v Guardian
General Insurance Ltd [2024] CCJ 3 (AJ) BB, BB 2024 CCJ 1 (CARILAW) ; Bisnauth v
Shewprashad [2009] CCJ 8 (AJ) (GY), (2009) 79 WIR 339 ; Brandis v Craig (1981) 30
WIR 136 (GY CA); Dey v Ramdhanny [2003-2004] GLR 37; Dipcon Engineering Services
Ltd v A-G of Trinidad and Tobago (TT HC, 9 January 2026) ; Glen v Sampson (1972) 19
WIR 237 (GY CA); Inc Trustees of the Diocese of Guiana v McLean  [1939] LRBG 182;
Lachana v Arjune [2008] CCJ 12 (AJ) (GY), GY 2008 CCJ 15 (CARILAW); Li v Walker
(1968) 12 WIR 195 ; Madhoo v Ramdass  [1954] LRBG 191 ; Mathan v Kujal  (2014) 85
WIR 383 (GY CA); Singh v Mossai [2019] CCJ 1 (AJ) (GY), (2020) 95 WIR 450  (GY
CA); Tackorie v Port Mourant Ltd  [1954] LRBG 108 ; Todd v Price [2021] CCJ 2 (AJ)
GY; Toolsie Persaud Ltd v Andrew James Investments Ltd [2008] CCJ 5 (AJ) (GY), (2008)
